CHAPTER 3

![](images/00295.jpg)

*Friends and Enemies*

랜드 did not run far, only as far as the sally gate around the corner from the stable. He slowed to a walk before he got there, trying to appear casual and unhurried.

The arched gate was closed tight. It was barely big enough for two men to ride through abreast, but like all the gates in the outer wall, it was covered with broad strips of black iron, and locked shut with a thick bar. Two guards stood before the gate in plain conical helmets and plate-and-mail armor, with long swords on their backs. Their golden surcoats bore the Black Hawk on the chest. He knew one of them slightly, Ragan. The scar from a 트롤록 arrow made a white triangle against Ragan’s dark cheek behind the bars of his face-guard. The puckered skin dimpled with a grin when he saw 랜드.

“Peace favor you, 랜드 al’Thor.” Ragan almost shouted to be heard over the bells. “Do you intend to go hit rabbits over the head, or do you still insist that club is a bow?” The other guard shifted to stand more in front of the gate.

“Peace favor you, Ragan,” 랜드 said, stopping in front of them. It was an effort to keep his voice calm. “You know it’s a bow. You’ve seen me shoot it.”

“No good from a horse,” the other guard said sourly. 랜드 recognized him, now, with his deep-set, almost-black eyes that never seemed to blink. They peered from his helmet like twin caves inside another cave. He supposed there could be worse luck for him than Masema guarding the gate, but he was not sure how, short of a Red 에스 세다이. “It’s too long,” Masema added. “I can shoot three arrows with a horsebow while you loose one with that monster.”

랜드 forced a grin, as if he thought it was a joke. Masema had never made a joke in his hearing, nor laughed at one. Most of the men at 팔 다라 accepted 랜드; he trained with 란, and Lord Agelmar had him at table, and most important of all, he had arrived at 팔 다라 in company with 모이라인, an 에스 세다이. Some seemed unable to forget his being an outlander, though, barely saying two words to him, and then only if they had to. Masema was the worst of those.

“It’s good enough for me,” 랜드 said. “Speaking of rabbits, Ragan, how about letting me out? All this noise and bustle is too much for me. Better to be out hunting rabbits, even if I never see one.”

Ragan half turned to look at his companion, and 랜드’s hopes began to lift. Ragan was an easygoing man, his manner belying his grim scar, and he seemed to like 랜드. But Masema was already shaking his head. Ragan sighed. “It cannot be, 랜드 al’Thor.” He gave a tiny nod toward Masema as if to explain. If it were up to him alone. . . . “No one is to leave without a written pass. Too bad you did not ask a few minutes ago. The command just came down to bar the gates.”

“But why would Lord Agelmar want to keep *me* in?” Masema was eyeing the bundles on 랜드’s back, and his saddlebags. 랜드 tried to ignore him. “I’m his guest,” he went on to Ragan. “By my honor, I could have left anytime these past weeks. Why would he mean this order for me? It is Lord Agelmar’s order, isn’t it?” Masema blinked at that, and his perpetual frown deepened; he almost appeared to forget 랜드’s packs.

Ragan laughed. “Who else could give such an order, 랜드 al’Thor? Of course, it was Uno who passed it to me, but whose order could it have been?”

Masema’s eyes, fixed on 랜드’s face, did not blink. “I just want to go out by myself, that’s all,” 랜드 said. “I’ll try one of the gardens, then. No rabbits, but at least there won’t be a crowd. 빛 illumine you, and peace favor you.”

He walked away without waiting for an answering blessing, resolving not to go near any of the gardens on any account. *Burn me, once the ceremonies are done there could be 에스 세다이 in any of them.* Aware of Masema’s eyes on his back—he was sure it was Masema—he kept his pace normal.

Suddenly the bells stopped ringing, and he skipped a step. 민utes were passing. A great many of them. Time for the 아미를린 석좌 to be shown to her chambers. Time for her to send for him, to start a search when he was not found. As soon as he was out of sight of the sally gate, he began to run again.

Near the barracks’ kitchens, the Carters’ Gate, where all the foodstuffs for the keep were brought in, stood closed and barred, behind a pair of soldiers. He hurried past, across the kitchen yard, as if he had never meant to stop.

The Dog Gate, at the back of the keep, just high enough and wide enough for one man on foot, had its guards, too. He turned around before they saw him. There were not many gates, even as big as the keep was, but if the Dog Gate was guarded, they all would be.

Perhaps he could find a length of rope. . . . He climbed one of the stairs to the top of the outer wall, to the wide parapet with its crenellated walls. It was not comfortable for him, being so high and exposed if that wind came again, but from there he could see across the tall chimneys and sharp roofs of the town all the way to the city wall. Even after nearly a month, the houses still looked odd to his 두 강 eyes, eaves reaching almost to the ground as if the houses were all wood-shingled roof, and chimneys angled to let heavy snow slide past. A broad, paved square surrounded the keep, but only a hundred paces from the wall lay streets full of people going about their daily business, aproned shopkeepers out under the awnings in front of their shops, rough-clothed farmers in town to buy and sell, hawkers and tradesmen and townspeople gathered in knots, no doubt to talk about the surprise visit from the 아미를린 석좌. He could see carts and people flowing through one of the gates in the town wall. Apparently the guards there had no orders about stopping anyone.

He looked up at the nearest guardtower; one of the soldiers raised a gauntleted hand to him. With a bitter laugh, he waved back. Not a foot of the wall but was under the eyes of guards. Leaning through an embrasure, he peered down past the slots in the stone for setting hoardings, down the sheer expanse of stone to the drymoat far below. Twenty paces wide and ten deep, faced with stone polished slippery smooth. A low wall, slanted to give no hiding place, surrounded it to keep anyone from falling in by accident, and its bottom was a forest of razor-sharp spikes. Even with a rope to climb down and no guards watching, he could not cross that. What served to keep 트롤록s out in the last extreme served just as well to keep him in.

Suddenly he felt weary to the bone, drained. The 아미를린 석좌 was there, and there was no way out. No way out, and the 아미를린 석좌 there. If she knew he was there, if she had sent the wind that had seized him, then she was already hunting him, hunting with an 에스 세다이’s powers. Rabbits had more chance against his bow. He refused to give up, though. There were those who said 두 강 folk could teach stones and give lessons to mules. When there was nothing else left, 두 강 people hung on to their stubbornness.

Leaving the wall, he wandered through the keep. He paid no mind to where he went, so long as it was nowhere he would be expected. Not anywhere near his room, nor any of the stables, nor any gate—Masema might risk Uno’s tongue to report him trying to leave—nor garden. All he could think of was keeping away from *any* 에스 세다이. Even 모이라인. She *knew* about him. Despite that, she had done nothing against him. *So far. So far as you know. What if she’s changed her mind? Maybe she sent for the 아미를린 석좌.*

For a moment, feeling lost, he leaned against the corridor wall, the stone hard under his shoulder. Eyes blank, he stared at a distant nothing and saw things he did not want to see. *Gentled. Would it be so bad, to have it all over?* Really *over?* He closed his eyes, but he could still see himself, huddling like a rabbit with nowhere left to run, and 에스 세다이 closing round him like ravens. *They almost always die soon after, men who’ve been gentled. They stop wanting to live.* He remembered 톰 Merrilin’s words too well to face that. With a brisk shake, he hurried on down the hall. No need to stay in one place until he was found. *How long till they find you anyway? You’re like a sheep in a pen. How long?* He touched the sword hilt at his side. *No, not a sheep. Not for 에스 세다이 or anybody else.* He felt a little foolish, but determined.

People were returning to their tasks. A din of voices and clattering pots filled the kitchen that lay nearest the Great Hall, where the 아미를린 석좌 and her party would feast that night. Cooks and scullions and potboys all but ran at their work; the spit dogs trotted in their wicker wheels to turn the spitted meats. He made his way quickly through the heat and steam, through the smells of spices and cooking. No one spared him a second glance; they were all too busy.

The back halls, where the servants lived in small apartments, were stirring like a kicked antheap as men and women scurried to don their best livery. Children did their playing in corners, out of the way. Boys waved wooden swords, and girls played with carved dolls, some announcing that *hers* was the 아미를린 석좌. Most of the doors stood open, doorways blocked only by beaded curtains. Normally, that meant whoever lived there was open to visitors, but today it simply meant the residents were in a hurry. Even those who bowed to him did so with hardly a pause.

Would any of them hear, when they went to serve, that he was being sought, and speak of seeing him? Speak to an 에스 세다이 and tell her where to find him? The eyes that he passed suddenly appeared to be studying him slyly, and to be weighing and considering behind his back. Even the children took on sharper looks in his mind’s eye. He knew it was just his imagination—he was sure it was; it had to be—but when the servants’ apartments were behind him, he felt as if he had escaped before a trap could spring shut.

Some places in the keep were empty of people, the folk who normally worked there released for the sudden holiday. The armorer’s forge, with all the fires banked, the anvils silent. Silent. Cold. Lifeless. Yet somehow not empty. His skin prickled, and he spun on his heel. No one there. Just the big square tool chests and the quenching barrels full of oil. The hair on the back of his neck stirred, and he whipped round again. The hammers and tongs hung in their places on the wall. Angrily he stared around the big room. *There’s nobody there. It’s just my imagination. That wind, and the Amyrlin; that’s enough to make me imagine things.*

Outside in the armorer’s yard, the wind swirled up around him momentarily. Despite himself he jumped, thinking it meant to catch him. For a moment he smelled the faint odor of decay again, and heard someone behind him laughing slyly. Just for a moment. Frightened, he edged in a circle, peering warily. The yard, paved with rough stone, was empty except for him. *Just your bloody imagination!* He ran anyway, and behind him he thought he heard the laughter again, this time without the wind.

In the woodyard, the presence returned, the sense of someone there. The feel of eyes peering at him around tall piles of split firewood under the long sheds, darting glances over the stacks of seasoned planks and timbers waiting on the other side of the yard for the carpenter’s shop, now closed up tight. He refused to look around, refused to think of how one set of eyes could move from place to place so fast, could cross the open yard from the firewood shed to the lumbershed without even a flicker of movement that he could see. He was sure it was one set of eyes. *Imagination. Or maybe I’m going crazy already.* He shivered. *Not yet. Light, please not yet.* Stiff-backed, he stalked across the woodyard, and the unseen watcher followed.

Down deep corridors lit only by a few rush torches, in storerooms filled with sacks of dried peas or beans, crowded with slatted racks heaped with wrinkled turnips and beets, or stacked with barrels of wine and casks of salted beef and kegs of ale, the eyes were always there, sometimes following him, sometimes waiting when he entered. He never heard a footstep but his own, never heard a door creak except when he opened and closed it, but the eyes were there. *Light, I* am *going crazy.*

Then he opened another storeroom door, and human voices, human laughter, drifted out to fill him with relief. There would be no unseen eye here. He went in.

Half the room was stacked to the ceiling with sacks of grain. In the other half a thick semicircle of men knelt in front of one of the bare walls. They all seemed to wear the leather jerkins and bowl-cut hair of menials. No warriors’ topknots, no livery. No one who might betray him accidentally. *What about on purpose?* The rattle of dice came through their soft murmurs, and somebody let out a raucous laugh at the throw.

로이알 was watching them dice, rubbing his chin thoughtfully with a finger thicker than a big man’s thumb, his head almost reaching the rafters nearly two spans up. None of the dicers gave him a glance. 오지어 were not exactly common in the 국경지대, or anywhere else, but they were known and accepted here, and 로이알 had been in 팔 다라 long enough to excite little comment. The 오지어’s dark, stiff-collared tunic was buttoned up to his neck and flared below the waist over his high boots, and one of the big pockets bulged and sagged with the weight of something. Books, if 랜드 knew him. Even watching men gamble, 로이알 would not be far from a book.

In spite of everything, 랜드 found himself grinning. 로이알 often had that effect on him. The 오지어 knew so much about some things, so little about others, and he seemed to want to know everything. Yet 랜드 could remember the first time he ever saw 로이알, with his tufted ears and his eyebrows that dangled like long mustaches and his nose almost as wide as his face—saw him and thought he was facing a 트롤록. It still shamed him. 오지어 and 트롤록s. 미르드랄, and things from the dark corners of midnight tales. Things out of stories and legends. That was how he had thought of them before he left Emond’s Field. But since leaving home he had seen too many stories walking in the flesh ever to be so sure again. 에스 세다이, and unseen watchers, and a wind that caught and held. His smile faded.

“All the stories are real,” he said softly.

로이알’s ears twitched, and his head turned toward 랜드. When he saw who it was, the 오지어’s face split in a grin, and he came over. “Ah, there you are.” His voice was a deep bumblebee rumble. “I did not see you at the Welcome. That was something I had not seen before. Two things. The 시엔나르an Welcome, and the 아미를린 석좌. She looks tired, don’t you think? It cannot be easy, being Amyrlin. Worse than being an Elder, I suppose.” He paused, with a thoughtful look, but only for a breath. “Tell me, 랜드, do you play at dice, too? They play a simpler game here, with only three dice. We use four in the *stedding.* They won’t let me play, you know. They just say, ‘Glory to the Builders,’ and will not bet against me. I don’t think that’s fair, do you? The dice they use *are* rather small”—he frowned at one of his hands, big enough to cover a human head—“but I still think—”

랜드 grabbed his arm and cut him off. *The Builders!* “로이알, 오지어 built 팔 다라, didn’t they? Do you know any way out except by the gates? A crawl hole. A drain pipe. Anything at all, if it’s big enough for a man to wiggle through. Out of the wind would be good, too.”

로이알 gave a pained grimace, the ends of his eyebrows almost brushing his cheeks. “랜드, 오지어 built Mafal Dadaranell, but that city was destroyed in the 트롤록 전쟁. This”—he touched the stone wall lightly with broad fingertips—“was built by men. I can sketch a plan of Mafal Dadaranell—I saw the maps, once, in an old book in 스테딩 Shangtai—but of 팔 다라, I know no more than you. It *is* well built, though, isn’t it? Stark, but well made.”

랜드 slumped against the wall, squeezing his eyes shut. “I need a way out,” he whispered. “The gates are barred, and they won’t let anyone pass, but I need a way out.”

“But why, 랜드?” 로이알 said slowly. “No one here will hurt you. Are you all right? 랜드?” Suddenly his voice rose. “맷! 페린! I think 랜드 is sick.”

랜드 opened his eyes to see his friends straightening up out of the knot of dicers. 맷 카우톤, long-limbed as a stork, wearing a half smile as if he saw something funny that no one else saw. Shaggy-haired 페린 Aybara, with heavy shoulders and thick arms from his work as a blacksmith’s apprentice. They both still wore their 두 강 garb, plain and sturdy, but travel-worn.

맷 tossed the dice back into the semicircle as he stepped out, and one of the men called, “Here, southlander, you can’t quit while you’re winning.”
“Better than when I’m losing,” 맷 said with a laugh. Unconsciously he touched his coat at the waist, and 랜드 winced. 맷 had a dagger with a ruby in its hilt under there, a dagger he was never without, a dagger he could not be without. It was a tainted blade, from the dead city of Shadar Logoth, tainted and twisted by an evil almost as bad as the 어둠의 존재, the evil that had killed Shadar Logoth two thousand years before, yet still lived among the abandoned ruins. That taint would kill 맷 if he kept the dagger; it would kill him even faster if he put it aside. “You’ll have another chance to win it back.” Wry snorts from the kneeling men indicated they did not think there was much chance of that.

페린 kept his eyes down as he followed 맷 across to 랜드. 페린 always kept his eyes down these days, and his shoulders sagged as if he carried a weight too heavy even for their width.

“What’s the matter, 랜드?” 맷 asked. “You’re as white as your shirt. Hey! Where did you get those clothes? You turning 시엔나르an? Maybe I’ll buy myself a coat like that, and a fine shirt.” He shook his coat pocket, producing a clink of coins. “I seem to have luck with the dice. I can hardly touch them without winning.”

“You don’t have to buy anything,” 랜드 said tiredly. “모이라인 had all our clothes replaced. They’re burned already for all I know, all but what you two are wearing. Elansu will probably be around to collect those, too, so I’d change fast if I were you, before she takes them off your back.” 페린 still did not look up, but his cheeks turned red; 맷’s grin deepened, though it looked forced. They too had had encounters in the baths, and only 맷 tried to pretend it did not matter. “And I’m not sick. I just need to get out of here. The 아미를린 석좌 is here. 란 said . . . he said with her here, it would have been better for me if I were gone a week. I need to leave, and all the gates are barred.”

“He said that?” 맷 frowned. “I don’t understand. He’d never say *anything* against an 에스 세다이. Why now? Look, 랜드, I don’t like 에스 세다이 any more than you do, but they aren’t going to do anything to us.” He lowered his voice to say that, and looked over his shoulder to see if any of the gamblers was listening. Feared the 에스 세다이 might be, but in the 국경지대, they were far from being hated, and a disrespectful comment about them could land you in a fight, or worse. “Look at 모이라인. She isn’t so bad, even if she is 에스 세다이. You’re thinking like old 센 뷰이 telling his tall tales back home, in the Winespring Inn. I mean, she hasn’t hurt us, and they won’t. Why would they?”

페린’s eyes lifted. Yellow eyes, gleaming in the dim light like burnished gold. *모이라인 hasn’t hurt us?* 랜드 thought. 페린’s eyes had been as deep a brown as 맷’s when they left the 두 강. 랜드 had no idea how the change had come about—페린 did not want to talk about it, or about very much of anything since it happened—but it had come at the same time as the slump in his shoulders, and a distance in his manner as if he felt alone even with friends around him. 페린’s eyes and 맷’s dagger. Neither would have happened if they had not left Emond’s Field, and it was 모이라인 who had taken them away. He knew that was not fair. They would probably all be dead at 트롤록s’ hands, and a good part of Emond’s Field as well, if she had not come to their village. But that did not make 페린 laugh the way he used to, or take the dagger from 맷’s belt. *And me? If I was home and still alive, would I still be what I am now? At least I wouldn’t be worrying about what the 에스 세다이 are going to do to me.*

맷 was still looking at him quizzically, and 페린 had raised his head enough to stare from under his eyebrows. 로이알 waited patiently. 랜드 could not tell them why he had to stay away from the 아미를린 석좌. They did not know what he was. 란 knew, and 모이라인. And 에그웨인, and 니나브. He wished none of them knew, and most of all he wished 에그웨인 did not, but at least 맷 and 페린—and 로이알, too—believed he was still the same. He thought he would rather die than let them know, than see the hesitation and worry he sometimes caught in 에그웨인’s eyes, and 니나브’s, even when they were trying their best.

“Somebody’s . . . watching me,” he said finally. “Following me. Only. . . . Only, there’s nobody there.”

페린’s head jerked up, and 맷 licked his lips and whispered, “A 페이드?”

“Of course not,” 로이알 snorted. “How could one of the 눈 없는 자 enter 팔 다라, town or keep? By law, no one may hide his face inside the town walls, and the lamplighters are charged with keeping the streets lit at night so there isn’t a shadow for a 미르드랄 to hide in. It could not happen.”

“Walls don’t stop a 페이드,” 맷 muttered. “Not when it wants to come in. I don’t know as laws and lamps will do any better.” He did not sound like someone who had half thought 페이드s were only gleemen’s tales less than half a year before. He had seen too much, too.

“And there was the wind,” 랜드 added. His voice hardly shook as he told what had happened on the tower top. 페린’s fists tightened until his knuckles cracked. “I just want to leave here,” 랜드 finished. “I want to go south. Somewhere away. Just somewhere away.”

“But if the gates are barred,” 맷 said, “how do we get out?”

랜드 stared at him. “We?” He had to go alone. It would be dangerous for anyone near him, eventually. He would be dangerous, and even 모이라인 could not tell him how long he had. “맷, you know you have to go to 타르 발론 with 모이라인. She said that’s the only place you can be separated from that bloody dagger without dying. And you know what will happen if you keep it.”

맷 touched his coat over the dagger, not seeming to realize what he was doing. “ ‘An 에스 세다이’s gift is bait for a fish,’ ” he quoted. “Well, maybe I don’t want to put the hook in my mouth. Maybe whatever she wants to do in 타르 발론 is worse than if I don’t go at all. Maybe she’s lying. ‘The truth an 에스 세다이 tells is never the truth you think it is.’ ”

“You have any more old sayings you want to rid yourself of?” 랜드 asked. “ ‘A south wind brings a warm guest, a north wind an empty house’? ‘A pig painted gold is still a pig’? What about, ‘talk shears no sheep’? ‘A fool’s words are dust’?”

“Easy, 랜드,” 페린 said softly. “There is no need to be so rough.”

“Isn’t there? Maybe I don’t want you two going with me, always hanging around, falling into trouble and expecting me to pull you out. You ever think of that? Burn me, did it ever occur to you I might be tired of always having you there whenever I turn around? Always there, and I’m tired of it.” The hurt on 페린’s face cut him like a knife, but he pushed on relentlessly. “There are some here think I’m a lord. A lord. Maybe I like that. But look at you, dicing with stablehands. When I go, I go by myself. You two can go to 타르 발론 or go hang yourselves, but I leave here alone.”

맷’s face had gone stiff, and he clutched the dagger through his coat till his knuckles were white. “If that is how you want it,” he said coldly. “I thought we were. . . . However you want it, al’Thor. But if I decide to leave at the same time you do, I’ll go, and you can stand clear of me.”

“Nobody is going anywhere,” 페린 said, “if the gates are barred.” He was staring at the floor again. Laughter rolled from the gamblers against the wall as someone lost.

“Go or stay,” 로이알 said, “together or apart, it doesn’t matter. You are all three *ta’veren.* Even I can see it, and I don’t have that Talent, just by what happens around you. And 모이라인 Sedai says it, too.”

맷 threw up his hands. “No more, 로이알. I don’t want to hear about that anymore.”

로이알 shook his head. “Whether you hear it or not, it is still true. 시간의 수레바퀴 weaves the Pattern of the Age, using the lives of men for thread. And you three are *ta’veren*, centerpoints of the weaving.”

“No more, 로이알.”

“For a time, the Wheel will bend the Pattern around you three, whatever you do. And whatever you do is more likely to be chosen by the Wheel than by you. *Ta’veren* pull history along behind them and shape the Pattern just by being, but the Wheel weaves *ta’veren* on a tighter line than other men. Wherever you go and whatever you do, until the Wheel chooses otherwise you will—”

“No more!” 맷 shouted. The men dicing looked around, and he glared at them until they bent back to their game.

“I am sorry, 맷,” 로이알 rumbled. “I know I talk too much, but I did not mean—”

“I am not staying here,” 맷 told the rafters, “with a bigmouthed 오지어 and a fool whose head is too big for a hat. You coming, 페린?” 페린 sighed, and glanced at 랜드, then nodded.

랜드 watched them go with a stick caught in his threat. *I must go alone. Light help me, I have to.*

로이알 was staring after them, too, eyebrows drooping worriedly. “랜드, I really didn’t mean to—”

랜드 made his voice harsh. “What are you waiting for? Go on with them! I don’t see why you’re still here. You are no use to me if you don’t know a way out. Go on! Go find your trees, and your precious groves, if they haven’t all been cut down, and good riddance to them if they have.”

로이알’s eyes, as big as cups, looked surprised and hurt, at first, but slowly they tightened into what almost might be anger. 랜드 did not think it could be. Some of the old stories claimed 오지어 were fierce, though they never said how, exactly, but 랜드 had never met anyone as gentle as 로이알.

“If you wish it so, 랜드 al’Thor,” 로이알 said stiffly. He gave a rigid bow and stalked away after 맷 and 페린.

랜드 slumped against the stacked sacks of grain. *Well*, a voice in his head taunted, *you did it, didn’t you. I had to,* he told it. *I will be dangerous just to be around. Blood and ashes, I’m going to go mad, and. . . . No! No, I won’t! I will not use the Power, and then I won’t go mad, and. . . . But I can’t risk it. I can’t, don’t you see?* But the voice only laughed at him.

The gamblers were looking at him, he realized. All of them, still kneeling against the wall, had turned to stare at him. 시엔나르ans of any class were almost always polite and correct, even to blood enemies, and 오지어 were never any enemies of 시엔나르. Shock filled the gamblers’ eyes. Their faces were blank, but their eyes said what he had done was wrong. Part of him thought they were right, and that drove their silent accusation deep. They only looked at him, but he stumbled out of the storeroom as if they were chasing him.

Numbly he went on through the storerooms, hunting a place to secrete himself until some traffic was allowed through the gates again. Then he could hide in the bottom of a victualer’s cart, maybe. If they did not search the carts on the way out. If they did not search the storerooms, search the whole keep for him. Stubbornly he refused to think about that, stubbornly concentrated on finding a safe place. But every place he found—a hollow in a stack of grain sacks, a narrow alley along the wall behind some wine barrels, an abandoned storeroom half filled with empty crates and shadows—he could imagine searchers finding him there. He could imagine that unseen watcher, whoever it was—or whatever—finding him there, too. So he hunted on, thirsty and dusty and with cobwebs in his hair.

And then he came out into a dimly torch-lit corridor, and 에그웨인 was creeping along it, pausing to peer into the storerooms she passed. Her dark hair, hanging to her waist, was caught back with a red ribbon, and she wore a goose-gray dress in the 시엔나르an fashion, trimmed in red. At the sight of her, sadness and loss rolled over him, worse than when he had chased 맷 and 페린 and 로이알 away. He had grown up thinking he would marry 에그웨인 one day; they both had. But now. . . .

She jumped when he popped out right in front of her, and her breath caught loudly, but what she said was, “So there you are. 맷 and 페린 told me what you did. And 로이알. I know what you’re trying to do, 랜드, and it is plain foolish.” She crossed her arms under her breasts, and her big, dark eyes fixed him sternly. He always wondered how she managed to seem to be looking down at him—she did it at will—although she was only as tall as his chest, and two years younger besides.

“Good,” he said. Her hair suddenly made him angry. He had never seen a grown woman with her hair unbraided until he left the 두 강. There, every girl waited eagerly for the Women’s Circle of her village to say she was old enough to braid her hair. 에그웨인 certainly had. And here she was with her hair loose except for a ribbon. *I want to go home and can’t, and she can’t wait to forget Emond’s Field.* “You go away and leave me alone, too. You don’t want to keep company with a shepherd anymore. There are plenty of 에스 세다이 here for you to moon around, now. And don’t tell any of them you saw me. They’re after me, and I don’t need you helping them.”

Bright spots of color bloomed in her cheeks. “Do you think I would—”

He turned to walk away, and with a cry she threw herself at him, flung her arms around his legs. They both tumbled to the stone floor, his saddlebags and bundles flying. He grunted when he hit, sword hilt digging into his side, and again when she scrabbled up and plopped herself down on his back as if he were a chair. “My mother,” she said firmly, “always told me the best way to learn to deal with a man was to learn to ride a mule. She said they have about equal brains most of the time. Sometimes the mule is smarter.”

He raised his head to look over his shoulder at her. “Get off me, 에그웨인. Get off! 에그웨인, if you don’t get off”—he lowered his voice ominously—“I’ll do something to you. You know what I am.” He added a glare for good measure.

에그웨인 sniffed. “You wouldn’t, if you could. You would not hurt anybody. But you can’t, anyway. I know you cannot channel the 하나의 힘 whenever you want; it just happens, and you cannot control it. So you are not going to do anything to me or anybody else. I, on the other hand, have been taking lessons with 모이라인, so if you don’t listen to some sense, 랜드 al’Thor, I might just set your breeches on fire. I can manage that much. You keep on as you are and see if I cannot.” Suddenly, for just a moment, the torch nearest them on the wall flared up with a roar. She gave a squeak and stared at it, startled.

Twisting around, he grabbed her arm, pulled her off his back, and sat her against the wall. When he sat up himself, she was sitting there across from him, rubbing her arm furiously. “You really would have, wouldn’t you?” he said angrily. “You’re fooling with things you don’t understand. You could have burned both of us to charcoal!”

“Men! When you cannot win an argument, you either run away or resort to force.”

“Hold on there! Who tripped who? Who sat on who? And you threatened—tried!—to—” He raised both hands. “No, you don’t. You do this to me all the time. Whenever you realize the argument isn’t going the way you want, suddenly we are arguing about something else completely. Not this time.”

“I am not arguing,” she said calmly, “and I am not changing the subject, either. What is hiding except running away? And after you hide, you’ll run away for true. And what about hurting 맷, and 페린, and 로이알? And me? I know why. You’re afraid you will hurt somebody even worse if you let them stay near you. If you don’t do what you shouldn’t, then you do not have to worry about hurting anybody. All this running around and striking out, and you don’t even know if there’s a reason. Why should the Amyrlin, or any 에스 세다이 but 모이라인, even know you exist?”

For a moment he stared at her. The longer she spent with 모이라인 and 니나브, the more she took on their manner, at least when she wanted to. They were much alike at times, the 에스 세다이 and the Wisdom, distant and knowing. It was disconcerting coming from 에그웨인. Finally he told her what 란 had said. “What else could he mean?”

Her hand froze on her arm, and she frowned with concentration. “모이라인 knows about you, and she hasn’t done anything, so why should she now? But if 란. . . .” Still frowning, she met his eyes. “The storerooms are the first place they will look. If they do look. Until we find out if they are looking, we need to put you somewhere they would never think of searching. I know. The dungeon.”

He scrambled to his feet. “The dungeon!”

“Not in a cell, silly. I go there some evenings to visit Padan Fain. 니나브 does, too. No one will think it odd if I go early today. In truth, with everybody looking to the Amyrlin, no one will even notice us.”

“But, 모이라인. . . .”

“She doesn’t go to the dungeons to question Master Fain. She has him brought to her. And she has not done that very much for weeks. Believe me, you will be safe there.”

Still, he hesitated. Padan Fain. “Why do you visit the peddler, anyway? He’s a Darkfriend, admitted out of his own mouth, and a bad one. Burn me, 에그웨인, he brought the 트롤록s to Emond’s Field! 어둠의 존재’s hound, he called himself, and he has been sniffing on my trail since Winternight.”

“Well, he is safe behind iron bars now, 랜드.” It was her turn to hesitate, and she looked at him almost pleading. “랜드, he has brought his wagon into the 두 강 every spring since before I was born. He knows all the people I know, all the places. It’s strange, but the longer he has been locked up, the easier in himself he has become. It’s almost as if he is breaking free of the 어둠의 존재. He laughs again, and tells funny stories, about Emond’s Field folk, and sometimes about places I never heard of before. Sometimes he is almost like his old self. I just like to talk to somebody about home.”

*Since I’ve been avoiding you*, he thought, *and since 페린’s been avoiding everybody, and 맷’s been spending all his time gambling and carousing.* “I shouldn’t have kept to myself so much,” he muttered, then sighed. “Well, if 모이라인 thinks it’s safe enough for you, I suppose it is safe enough for me. But there’s no need for you to be mixed in it.”

에그웨인 got to her feet and concentrated on brushing off her dress, avoiding his eye.

“모이라인 *has* said it’s safe? 에그웨인?”

“모이라인 Sedai has never told me I could not visit Master Fain,” she said carefully.

He stared at her, then burst out, “You never asked her. She doesn’t know. 에그웨인, that’s stupid. Padan Fain’s a Darkfriend, and as bad as ever a Darkfriend was.”

“He is locked in a cage,” she said stiffly, “and I do not have to ask 모이라인’s permission for everything I do. It is a little late for you to start worrying about doing what an 에스 세다이 thinks, isn’t it? Now, are you coming?”

“I can find the dungeon without you. They are looking for me, or will be, and it won’t do you any good to be found with me.”

“Without me,” she said dryly, “you’ll likely trip over your own feet and fall in the 아미를린 석좌’s lap, then confess everything while trying to talk your way out of it.”

“Blood and ashes, you ought to be in the Women’s Circle back home. If men were all as fumble-footed and helpless as you seem to think, we’d never—”

“Are you going to stand here talking until they do find you? Pick up your things, 랜드, and come with me.” Not waiting for an answer, she spun around and started off down the hall. Muttering under his breath, he reluctantly obeyed.

There were few people—servants, mainly—in the back ways they took, but 랜드 had the feeling that they all took special notice of him. Not notice of a man burdened for a journey, but of *him*, 랜드 al’Thor in particular. He knew it was his imagination—he hoped it was—but even so, he felt no relief when they stopped in a passageway deep beneath the keep, before a tall door with a small iron grill set in it, as thickly strapped with iron as any in the outer wall. A clapper hung below the grill.

Through the grill 랜드 could see bare walls, and two top-knotted soldiers sitting bareheaded at a table with a lamp on it. One of the men was sharpening a dagger with long, slow strokes of a stone. His strokes never faltered when 에그웨인 rapped with the clapper, a sharp clang of iron on iron. The other man, his face flat and sullen, looked at the door as if considering before he finally rose and came over. He was squat and stocky, barely tall enough to look through the cross-hatched bars.

“What do you want? Oh, it’s you again, girl. Come to see your Darkfriend? Who’s that?” He made no move to open the door.

“He’s a friend of mine, Changu. He wants to see Master Fain, too.”

The man studied 랜드, his upper lip quivering back to bare teeth. 랜드 did not think it was supposed to be a smile. “Well,” Changu said finally. “Well. Tall, aren’t you? Tall. And fancy dressed for your kind. Somebody catch you young in the Eastern Marches and tame you?” He slammed back the bolts and yanked open the door. “Well, come in if you’re coming.” He took on a mocking tone. “Take care not to bump your head, my Lord.”

There was no danger of that; the door was tall enough for 로이알. 랜드 followed 에그웨인 in, frowning and wondering if this Changu meant to make some sort of trouble. He was the first rude 시엔나르an 랜드 had met; even Masema was only cold, not really rude. But the fellow just banged the door shut and rammed the heavy bolts home, then went to some shelves beyond the end of the table and took one of the lamps there. The other man never ceased stropping his knife, never even looked up from it. The room was bare except for the table and benches and shelves, with straw on the floor and another iron-bound door leading deeper in.

“You’ll want some light, won’t you,” Changu said, “in there in the dark with your Darkfriend friend.” He laughed, coarse and humorless, and lit the lamp. “He’s waiting for you.” He thrust the lamp at 에그웨인, and undid the inner door almost eagerly. “Waiting for you. In there, in the dark.”

랜드 paused uneasily at the blackness beyond, and Changu grinning behind, but 에그웨인 caught his sleeve and pulled him in. The door slammed, almost catching his heel; the latch bars clanged shut. There was only the light of the lamp, a small pool around them in the darkness.

“Are you sure he’ll let us out?” he asked. The man had never even looked at his sword or bow, he realized, never asked what was in his bundles. “They aren’t very good guards. We could be here to break Fain free for all he knows.”

“They know me better than that,” she said, but she sounded troubled, and she added, “They seem worse every time I come. All the guards do. Meaner, and more sullen. Changu told jokes the first time I came, and Nidao never even speaks anymore. But I suppose working in a place like this can’t give a man a light heart. Maybe it is just me. This place does not do my heart any good, either.” Despite her words, she drew him confidently into the black. He kept his free hand on his sword.

The pale lamplight showed a wide hall with flat iron grills to either side, fronting stone-walled cells. Only two of the cells they passed held prisoners. The occupants sat up on their narrow cots as the light struck them, shielding their eyes with their hands, glaring between their fingers. Even with their faces hidden, 랜드 was sure they were glaring. Their eyes glittered in the lamplight.

“That one likes to drink and fight,” 에그웨인 murmured, indicating a burly fellow with sunken knuckles. “This time he wrecked the common room of an inn in the town single-handed, and hurt some men badly.” The other prisoner wore a gold-embroidered coat with wide sleeves, and low, gleaming boots. “He tried to leave the city without settling his inn bill”—she sniffed loudly at that; her father was an innkeeper as well as Mayor of Emond’s Field—“nor paying half a dozen shopkeepers and merchants what he owed.”

The men snarled at them, guttural curses as bad as any 랜드 had heard from merchants’ guards.

“They grow worse every day, too,” she said in a tight voice, and quickened her step.

She was enough ahead of him when they reached Padan Fain’s cell, at the very end, that 랜드 was out of the light entirely. He stopped there, in the shadows behind her lamp.

Fain was sitting on his cot, leaning forward expectantly as if waiting, just as Changu had said. He was a bony, sharp-eyed man, with long arms and a big nose, even more gaunt now than 랜드 remembered. Not gaunt from the dungeon—the food here was the same as the servants ate, and not even the worst prisoner was shorted—but from what he had done before coming to 팔 다라.

The sight of him brought back memories 랜드 would just as soon have done without. Fain on the seat of his big peddler’s wagon wheeling across the Wagon Bridge, arriving in Emond’s Field the day of Winternight. And on Winternight the 트롤록s came, killing and burning, hunting. Hunting three young men, 모이라인 had said. *Hunting me, if they only knew it, and using Fain for their trail hound.*

Fain stood at 에그웨인’s approach, not shielding his eyes or even blinking at the light. He smiled at her, a smile that touched only his lips, then raised his eyes above her head. Looking straight at 랜드, hidden in the blackness behind the light, he pointed a long finger at him. “I feel you there, hiding, 랜드 al’Thor,” he said, almost crooning. “You can’t hide, not from me, and not from them. You thought it was over, did you not? But the battle’s never done, al’Thor. They are coming for me, and they’re coming for you, and the war goes on. Whether you live or die, it’s never over for you. Never.” Suddenly he began to chant.

> “Soon comes the day all shall be free.

> Even you, and even me.

> Soon comes the day all shall die.

> Surely you, but never I.”
He let his arm fall, and his eyes rose to stare intently at an angle up into the darkness. A crooked grin twisting his mouth, he chuckled deep in his throat as if whatever he saw was amusing. “Mordeth knows more than all of you. Mordeth knows.”

에그웨인 backed away from the cell until she reached 랜드, and only the edge of the light touched the bars of Fain’s cell. Darkness hid the peddler, but they could still hear his chuckles. Even unable to see him, 랜드 was sure Fain was still peering off at nothing.

With a shiver, he pried his fingers off his sword hilt. “Light!” he said hoarsely. “This is what you call being like he used to be?”

“Sometimes he’s better, and sometimes worse.” 에그웨인’s voice was unsteady. “This is worse—much worse than usual.”

“What is he seeing, I wonder. He’s mad, staring at a stone ceiling in the dark.” *If the stone weren’t there, he’d be looking straight at the women’s apartments. Where 모이라인 is, and the 아미를린 석좌.* He shivered again. “He’s mad.”

“This was not a good idea, 랜드.” Looking over her shoulder at the cell, she drew him away from it and lowered her voice as if afraid Fain might overhear. Fain’s chuckles followed them. “Even if they don’t look here, I cannot stay here with him like this, and I do not think you should, either. There is something about him today that. . . .” She drew a shaky breath. “There is one place even safer from search than here. I did not mention it before because it was easier to get you in here, but they will never look in the women’s apartments. Never.”

“The women’s . . . ! 에그웨인, Fain may be mad, but you’re madder. You can’t hide from hornets in a hornets’ nest.”

“What better place? What is the one part of the keep no man will enter without a woman’s invitation, not even Lord Agelmar? What is the one place no one would ever think to look for a man?”

“What is the one place in the keep sure to be full of 에스 세다이? It is crazy, 에그웨인.”

Poking at his bundles, she spoke as if it were all decided. “You must wrap your sword and bow in your cloak, and then it will look as if you are carrying things for me. It should not be too hard to find you a jerkin and a shirt that isn’t so pretty. You will have to stoop, though.”

“I told you, I won’t do it.”

“Since you’re acting stubborn as a mule, you should take right to playing my beast of burden. Unless you would really rather stay down here with him.”

Fain’s laughing whisper came through the black shadows. “The battle’s never done, al’Thor. Mordeth knows.”

“I’d have a better chance jumping off the wall,” 랜드 muttered. But he unslung his bundles and set about wrapping sword and bow and quiver as she had suggested.

In the darkness, Fain laughed. “It’s never over, al’Thor. Never.”

CHAPTER 4

*Summoned*

Alone in her rooms in the women’s apartments, 모이라인 adjusted the shawl, embroidered with curling ivy and grapevines, on her shoulders and studied the effect in the tall frame mirror standing in a corner. Her large, dark eyes could appear as sharp as a hawk’s when she was angry. They seemed to pierce the silvered glass, now. It was only happenstance that she had had the shawl in her saddlebags when she came to 팔 다라. With the blazing white Flame of 타르 발론 centered on the wearer’s back and long fringe colored to show her 아자—모이라인’s was as blue as a morning sky—the shawls were seldom worn outside 타르 발론, and even there usually only inside the 백색 탑. Little in 타르 발론 besides a meeting of the 탑의 회의실 called for the formality of the shawls, and beyond the Shining Walls a sight of the Flame would send too many people running, to hide or perhaps to fetch the 빛의 아이들. A Whitecloak’s arrow was as fatal to an 에스 세다이 as to anyone else, and the Children were too wily to let an 에스 세다이 see the bowman before the arrow struck, while she still might do something about it. 모이라인 had certainly never expected to wear the shawl in 팔 다라. She was slender and not at all tall, and smooth-cheeked 에스 세다이 agelessness often made her appear younger than she was, but 모이라인 had a commanding grace and calm presence that could dominate any gathering. A manner ingrained growing up in the Royal Palace of 케렌 had been heightened, not submerged, by still more years as an 에스 세다이. She knew she might need every bit of it today. Yet much of the calm was on the surface, today. *There must be trouble, or she would not have come herself*, she thought for at least the tenth time. But beyond that lay a thousand questions more. *What trouble, and who did she choose to accompany her? Why here? Why now? It cannot be allowed to go wrong now.*

거대한 뱀 ring on her right hand caught the light dully as she touched the delicate golden chain fastened in her dark hair, which hung in waves to her shoulders. A small, clear blue stone dangled from the chain, in the middle of her forehead. Many in the 백색 탑 knew of the tricks she could do using that stone as a focus. It was only a polished bit of blue crystal, just something a young girl had used in her first learning, with no one to guide her. That girl had remembered tales of *angreal* and even more powerful *sa’angreal*—those fabled remnants of the 전설의 시대 that allowed 에스 세다이 to channel more of the 하나의 힘 than any could safely handle unaided—remembered and thought some such focus was required to channel at all. Her sisters in the 백색 탑 knew a few of her tricks, and suspected others, including some that did not exist, some that had shocked her when she learned of them. The things she did with the stone were simple and small, if occasionally useful; the kind a child would imagine. But if the wrong women had accompanied the Amyrlin, the crystal might put them off balance, because of the tales.

A rapid, insistent knocking came at the chamber door. No 시엔나르an would knock that way, not at anyone’s door, but least of all hers. She remained looking into the mirror until her eyes stared back serenely, all thought hidden in their dark depths. She checked the soft leather pouch hanging at her belt. *Whatever troubles brought her out of 타르 발론, she will forget them when I lay this trouble before her.* A second thumping, even more vigorous than the first, sounded before she crossed the room and opened the door with a calm smile for the two women who had come for her.

She recognized them both. Dark-haired Anaiya in her blue-fringed shawl, and fair-haired Liandrin in her red. Liandrin, not only young-seeming but young and pretty, with a doll’s face and a small, petulant mouth, had her hand raised to pound again. Her dark brows and darker eyes were a sharp contrast to the multitude of pale honey braids brushing her shoulders, but the combination was not uncommon in 타라본. Both women were taller than 모이라인, though Liandrin by less than a hand.

Anaiya’s blunt face broke into a smile as soon as 모이라인 opened the door. That smile gave her the only beauty she would ever have, but it was enough; almost everyone felt comforted, safe and special, when Anaiya smiled at them. “빛 shine on you, 모이라인. It’s good to see you again. Are you well? It has been so long.”

“My heart is lighter for your presence, Anaiya.” That was certainly true; it was good to know she had at least one friend among the 에스 세다이 who had come to 팔 다라. “빛 illumine you.”

Liandrin’s mouth tightened, and she gave her shawl a twitch. “The 아미를린 석좌, she requires your presence, Sister.” Her voice was petulant, too, and cold-edged. Not for 모이라인’s sake, or not solely; Liandrin always sounded dissatisfied with something. Frowning, she tried to look over 모이라인’s shoulder into the room. “This chamber, it is warded. We cannot enter. Why do you ward against your sisters?”

“Against all,” 모이라인 replied smoothly. “Many of the serving women are curious about 에스 세다이, and I do not want them pawing through my rooms when I am not here. There was no need to make a distinction until now.” She pulled the door shut behind her, leaving all three of them in the corridor. “Shall we go? We must not keep the Amyrlin waiting.”

She started down the hallway with Anaiya chatting at her side. Liandrin stood for a moment staring at the door as if wondering what 모이라인 was hiding, then hurried to join the others. She bracketed 모이라인, walking as stiffly as a guard. Anaiya merely walked, keeping company. Their slippered footsteps fell softly on thick-woven carpets with simple patterns.

Liveried women curtsied deeply as they passed, many more deeply than they would have for the Lord of 팔 다라 himself. 에스 세다이, three together, and the 아미를린 석좌 herself in the keep; it was more honor than any woman of the keep had ever expected in her lifetime. A few women of noble Houses were out in the halls, and they curtsied, too, which they most certainly would not have done for Lord Agelmar. 모이라인 and Anaiya smiled and bowed their heads to acknowledge each reverence, from servant or noble equally. Liandrin ignored them all.

There were only women here, of course, no men. No 시엔나르an male above the age of ten would enter the women’s rooms without permission or invitation, although a few small boys ran and played in the halls here. They knelt on one knee, awkwardly, when their sisters dropped deep curtsies. Now and then Anaiya smiled and ruffled a small head as she passed.

“This time, 모이라인,” Anaiya said, “you have been gone from 타르 발론 too long. Much too long. 타르 발론 misses you. Your sisters miss you. And you are needed in the 백색 탑.”

“Three more false 용.” Liandrin bit the words off. “In 살다에아, 무란디, and 티어 false 용 ravage the land. The while, you Blues smile and talk of nothing, and try to hold on to the past.” Anaiya raised an eyebrow, and Liandrin snapped her mouth shut with a sharp sniff.

“Three,” 모이라인 mused softly. For an instant her eyes gleamed, but she masked it quickly. “Three in the last two years, and now three more at once.”

“As the others were, these will be dealt with also. This male vermin and any ragtag rabble who follow their banners.”

모이라인 was almost amused by the certainty in Liandrin’s voice. Almost. She was too aware of the realities, too aware of the possibilities. “Have a few months been enough for you to forget, Sister? The last false Dragon all but tore 게알단 apart before his army, ragtag rabble or not, was defeated. Yes, 로가인 is in 타르 발론 by now, gentled and safe, I suppose, but some of our sisters died to overpower him. Even one sister dead is more loss than we can bear, but 게알단’s losses were much worse. The two before 로가인 could not channel, yet even so the people of 캔도르 and 아라드 도만 remember them well. Villages burned and men dead in battle. How easily can the world deal with three at one time? How many will flock to their banners? There has never been a shortage of followers for any man claiming to be the 용의 환생. How great will the wars be this time?”

“It isn’t so grim as that,” Anaiya said. “As far as we know, only the one in 살다에아 can channel. He has not had time to attract many followers, and sisters should already be there to deal with him. The 타이런s are harrying their false Dragon and his followers through Haddon Mirk, while the fellow in 무란디 is already in chains.” She gave a short, wondering laugh. “To think the Murandians, of all people, would deal with theirs so quickly. Ask, and they do not even call themselves Murandians, but Lugarders, or Inishlinni, or this or that lord’s or lady’s man. Yet for fear one of their neighbors would take the excuse to invade, the Murandians leaped on their false Dragon almost as soon as he opened his mouth to proclaim himself.”

“Still,” 모이라인 said, “three at the same time cannot be ignored. Has any sister been able to do a Foretelling?” It was a slight chance—few 에스 세다이 had manifested any part of that Talent, even the smallest part, in centuries—so she was not surprised when Anaiya shook her head. Not surprised, but a little relieved.

They reached a juncture of hallways at the same time as the Lady Amalisa. She dropped a full curtsy, bowing deep and spreading her pale green skirts wide. “Honor to 타르 발론,” she murmured. “Honor to 에스 세다이.”

The sister of the Lord of 팔 다라 required more than a nod of the head. 모이라인 took Amalisa’s hands and drew her to her feet. “You honor us, Amalisa. Rise, Sister.”

Amalisa straighted gracefully, with a flush on her face. She had never as much as been to 타르 발론, and to be called Sister by an 에스 세다이 was heady even for someone of her rank. Short and of middle years, she had a dark, mature beauty, and the color in her cheeks set it off. “You honor me too greatly, 모이라인 Sedai.”

모이라인 smiled. “How long have we known each other, Amalisa? Must I now call you my Lady Amalisa, as if we had never sat over tea together?”

“Of course not.” Amalisa smiled back. The strength evident in her brother’s face was in hers, too, and no less for the softer line of cheek and jaw. There were those who said that as hard and renowned a fighter as Agelmar was, he was no better than an even match for his sister. “But with the 아미를린 석좌 here. . . . Anaiya *tsked.* “Sometimes formality is necessary, but men often make more of it than they must. Please, call me Anaiya, and I will call you Amalisa, if I may.”

From the corner of her eye, 모이라인 saw 에그웨인, far down the side hall, disappearing hurriedly around a corner. A stooped shape in a leather jerkin, head down and arms loaded with bundles, shambled at her heels. 모이라인 permitted herself a small smile, quickly masked. *If the girl shows as much initiative in 타르 발론,* she thought wryly, *she will sit in the 아미를린 석좌 one day. If she can learn to control that initiative. If there is an 아미를린 석좌 left on which to sit.*

When she turned her attention back to the others, Liandrin was speaking.

“. . . and I would welcome the chance to learn more of your land.” She wore a smile, open and almost girlish, and her voice was friendly.

모이라인 schooled her face to stillness as Amalisa extended an invitation to join her and her ladies in her private garden, and Liandrin accepted warmly. Liandrin made few friends, and none outside the 적색 아자. *Certainly never outside the 에스 세다이. She would sooner make friends with a man, or a 트롤록.* 모이라인 was not sure Liandrin saw much difference between men and 트롤록s. She was not sure any of the 적색 아자 did.

Anaiya explained that just now they must attend the 아미를린 석좌. “Of course,” Amalisa said. “빛 illumine her, and the Creator shelter her. But later, then.” She stood straight and bowed her head as they left her.

모이라인 studied Liandrin as they walked, never looking at her directly. The honey-haired 에스 세다이 was staring straight ahead, rosebud lips pursed thoughtfully. She appeared to have forgotten 모이라인 and Anaiya both. *What is she up to?*

It constantly amazed 모이라인 that Anaiya dealt as well as she did in the 백색 탑, but those who were devious always seemed to take her openness and honesty, her acceptance of everyone, as cunning devices. They were always caught completely off balance when she turned out to mean what she said and say what she meant. Too, she had a way of seeing to the heart of things. And of accepting what she saw. “The word from 안도르 is both good and bad. The street riots in Caemlyn died down with the coming of spring, but there is still talk, too much talk, blaming the Queen, and 타르 발론 as well, for the long winter. 모르가세 holds her throne less securely than she did last year, but she holds it still, and will so long as Gareth Bryne is Captain-General of the Queen’s Guards. And the Lady 엘레인, the Daughter-Heir, and her brother, the Lord 가윈, have come safely to 타르 발론 for their training. There was some fear in the 백색 탑 that the custom would be broken.”

Liandrin gave a little start, as if she had just awakened. “Pray that she continues to have breath. The Daughter-Heir’s party was followed to the River Erinin by the 빛의 아이들. Sometimes I think she pushes her daughter because of that, whatever the girl chooses.”

모이라인 sniffed disdainfully. “엘레인 was born with the spark in her; it was not a matter of choosing. 모르가세 would not risk letting the girl die from lack of training if all the 백의단 in 아마디시아 were camped outside Caemlyn. She would command Gareth Byrne and the Queen’s Guards to cut a path through them to 타르 발론, and Gareth Byrne would do it if he had to do it alone.” *But she still must keep the full extent of the girl’s potential secret. Would the people of 안도르 knowingly accept 엘레인 on the Lion Throne after 모르가세 if they knew? Not just a queen trained in 타르 발론 according to custom, but a full 에스 세다이?* In all of recorded history there had been only a handful of queens with the right to be called 에스 세다이, and the few who let it be known had all lived to regret it. Men from every land are already gathering, all eager to be part of the legend, eager to find the Horn. 무란디 and 알타라 are on their toes, of course, thinking it’s all a mask for a move against one of them. “Perhaps not the stories they expect,” 모이라인 said. Liandrin looked at her sharply, and she kept her face still.

“I suppose not,” Anaiya said placidly. “The stories they least expect will be exactly the ones they will add to the cycle. Beyond that, I have only rumor to offer. The Sea Folk are agitated, their ships flying from port to port with barely a pause. Sisters from the islands say the Coramoor, their Chosen One, is coming, but they won’t say more. The 아일 appear to be stirring, too, but no one knows why. No one ever knows with the 아일. At least there is no evidence they mean to cross the 세계의 척추 again, thank the Light.” She sighed and shook her head. “What I would not give for even one sister from among the 아일. Just one. “It would have to be 타라본 and 아라드 도만,” 모이라인 said, and shook her head. “They have squabbled over Almoth Plain for nearly three hundred years, but it has never come to open blows.” She looked at Liandrin; 에스 세다이 were supposed to throw off all their old loyalties to lands and rulers, but few did so completely. “Enough of idle talk,” the honey-haired woman broke in angrily. “For you, 모이라인, the Amyrlin waits.” She took three quick strides ahead of the others and threw open one of a pair of tall doors. “For you, the Amyrlin will have no idle talk.”

Unconsciously touching the pouch at her waist, 모이라인 went past Liandrin through the doorway, with a nod as if the other woman were holding the door for her. She did not even smile at the white flash of anger on Liandrin’s face. *What* is *the wretched girl up to?*

Brightly colored carpets covered the anteroom floor in layers, and the room was pleasantly furnished with chairs and cushioned benches and small tables, the wood simply worked or just polished. Brocaded curtains sided the tall arrowslits to make them seem more like windows. No fires burned in the fireplaces; the day was warm, and the 시엔나르an chill would not come until nightfall.

Fewer than half a dozen of the 에스 세다이 who had accompanied the Amyrlin were there. Verin 맷hwin and Serafelle, of the 갈색 아자, did not look up at 모이라인’s entrance. Serafelle was intently reading an old book with a worn, faded leather cover, handling its tattered pages carefully, while plump Verin, sitting cross-legged beneath an arrowslit, held a small blossom up to the light and made notes and sketches in a precise hand in a book balanced on her knee. She had an open inkpot on the floor beside her, and a small pile of flowers on her lap. The three other women already in the room turned, but they made no effort to approach 모이라인, only looked at her. One, a slender woman of the 황색 아자, she did not know; she spent too little time in 타르 발론 to know all the 에스 세다이, although their numbers were no longer very great. Carlinya was as pale of skin and cold of manner as the white fringe on her shawl, the exact opposite in every way of dark, fiery Alanna Mosvani, of the Green, but they both stood and stared at her without speaking, without expression. Alanna sharply snugged her shawl around her, but Carlinya made no move at all. The slender Yellow sister turned away with an air of regret.

“빛 illumine you all, Sisters,” 모이라인 said. No one answered. She was not sure Serafelle or Verin had even heard. *Where are the others?* There was no need for them all to be there—most would be resting in their rooms, freshing from the journey—but she was on edge now, all the questions she could not ask running through her head. None of it showed on her face.

The inner door opened, and 리안 appeared, without her gilt-flamed staff. The 연대기 수호자 was as tall as most men, willowy and graceful, still beautiful, with coppery skin and short, dark hair. She wore a blue stole, a hand wide, instead of a shawl, for she sat in the 탑의 회의실, though as Keeper, not to represent her 아자.

“There you are,” she said briskly to 모이라인, and gestured to the door behind her. “Come, Sister. The 아미를린 석좌 is waiting.” She spoke naturally in a clipped, quick way that never changed, whether she was angry or joyful or excited. As 모이라인 followed 리안 in, she wondered what emotion the Keeper was feeling now. 리안 pulled the door to behind them; it banged shut with something of the sound of a cell door closing.

The 아미를린 석좌 herself sat behind a broad table in the middle of the carpet, and on the table rested a flattened cube of gold, the size of a travel chest and ornately worked with silver. The table was heavily built, its legs stout, but it seemed to squat under a weight two strong men would have had trouble lifting.

At the sight of the golden cube 모이라인 had difficulty keeping her face unruffled. The last she had seen of it, it had been safely locked in Agelmar’s strongroom. On learning of the 아미를린 석좌’s arrival she had meant to tell her of it herself. That it was already in the Amyrlin’s possession was a trifle, but a worrisome trifle. Events could be outpacing her.

She swept a deep curtsy and said formally, “As you called me, Mother, so have I come.” The Amyrlin extended her hand, and 모이라인 kissed her Great Serpent ring, no different from that of any other 에스 세다이. Rising, she made her tone more conversational, but not too much so. She was aware of the Keeper standing behind her, beside the door. “I hope you had a pleasant journey, Mother.”

The Amyrlin had been born in 티어, of a simple fisherman’s family, not a noble House, and her name was 시우안 산체, though very few had used that name, or even thought of it, in the ten years since she had been raised from the 탑의 회의실. She was the 아미를린 석좌; that was the whole of it. The broad stole on her shoulders was striped in the colors of the seven 아자s; the Amyrlin was of all 아자s and of none. She was only of medium height, and handsome rather than beautiful, but her face held a strength that had been there before her elevation, the strength of the girl who had survived the streets of the Maule, 티어’s port district, and her clear blue gaze had made kings and queens, and even the Captain Commander of the 빛의 아이들, drop their eyes. Her own eyes were strained, now, and there was a new tightness to her mouth.

“We called the winds to speed our vessels up the Erinin, Daughter, and even turned the currents to our aid.” The Amyrlin’s voice was deep, and sad. “I have seen the flooding we caused in villages along the river, and the Light only knows what we have done to the weather. We will not have endeared ourselves by the damage we’ve done and the crops we may have ruined. All to reach here as quickly as possible.” Her eyes strayed to the ornate golden cube, and she half lifted a hand as if to touch it, but when she spoke it was to say, “엘라이더 is in 타르 발론, Daughter. 모이라인 was conscious of 리안 standing to one side, quiet as always in the presence of the Amyrlin. But watching, and listening. “I am surprised, Mother,” she said carefully. “This is no time for 모르가세 to be without 에스 세다이 counsel.” 모르가세 was one of the few rulers to openly admit to an 에스 세다이 councilor; almost all had one, but few admitted it.

“엘라이더 insisted, Daughter, and queen or not, I doubt 모르가세 is a match for 엘라이더 in a contest of wills. In any case, perhaps this time she did not wish to be. 엘레인 has potential. More than I have ever seen before. Already she shows progress. The Red sisters are swollen up like puff-fish with it. I don’t think the girl leans to their way of thinking, but she is young, and there is no telling. Even if they don’t manage to bend her, it will make little difference. 엘레인 could well be the most powerful 에스 세다이 in a thousand years, and it is the 적색 아자 who found her. They have gained much status in the Hall from the girl.”

“I have two young women with me in 팔 다라, Mother,” 모이라인 said. “Both from the 두 강, where the blood of Manetheren still runs strong, though they do not even remember there was once a land called Manetheren. The old blood sings, Mother, and it sings loudly in the 두 강. 에그웨인, a village girl, is at least as strong as 엘레인. I have seen the Daughter-Heir, and I know. As for the other, 니나브 was the Wisdom in their village, yet she is little more than a girl herself. It says something of her that the women of her village chose her Wisdom at her age. Once she gains conscious control of what she now does without knowing, she will be as strong as any in 타르 발론. With training, she will shine like a bonfire beside the candles of 엘레인 and 에그웨인. And there is no chance these two will choose the Red. They are amused by men, exasperated by them, but they do like them. They will easily counter whatever influence the 적색 아자 gains in the 백색 탑 from finding 엘레인.”

The Amyrlin nodded as if it were all of no consequence. 모이라인’s eyebrows lifted in surprise before she caught herself and smoothed her features. Those were the two main concerns in the 탑의 회의실, that fewer girls who could be trained to channel the 하나의 힘 were found every year, or so it seemed, and that fewer of real power were found. Worse than the fear in those who blamed 에스 세다이 for the 세계의 파멸, worse than the hatred from the 빛의 아이들, worse even than the workings of 어둠의 친구들, were the sheer dwindling of numbers and the lessening of abilities. The corridors of the 백색 탑 were sparsely populated where once they had been crowded, and what could once be done easily with the 하나의 힘 could now be done only with difficulty, or not at all.

“엘라이더 had another reason for coming to 타르 발론, Daughter. She sent the same message by six different pigeons to make sure I received it—and to whom else in 타르 발론 she sent pigeons, I can only guess—then came herself. She told the 탑의 회의실 that you are meddling with a young man who is *ta’veren*, and dangerous. He was in Caemlyn, she said, but when she found the inn where he had been staying, she discovered you had spirited him away.”

“The people at that inn served us well and faithfully, Mother. If she harmed any of them. . . .” 모이라인 could not keep the sharpness out of her voice, and she heard 리안 shift. One did not speak to the 아미를린 석좌 in that tone; not even a king on his throne did.

“You should know, Daughter,” the Amyrlin said dryly, “that 엘라이더 harms no one except those she considers dangerous. 어둠의 친구들, or those poor fool men who try to channel the 하나의 힘. Or one who threatens 타르 발론. Everyone else who isn’t 에스 세다이 might as well be pieces on a stones board as far as she is concerned. Luckily for him, the innkeeper, one Master Gill as I remember, apparently thinks much of 에스 세다이, and so answered her questions to her satisfaction. 엘라이더 actually spoke well of him. But she spoke more of the young man you took away with you. More dangerous than any man since 아투르 호크윙, she said. She has the Foretelling sometimes, you know, and her words carried weight with the Hall.”

For 리안’s sake, 모이라인 made her voice as meek as she could. That was not very meek, but it was the best she could do. “I have three young men with me, Mother, but none of them is a king, and I doubt very much if any of them even dreams of uniting the world under one ruler. No one has dreamed 아투르 호크윙’s dream since the 백년 전쟁.”

“Yes, Daughter. Village youths, so Lord Agelmar tells me. But one of them is *ta’veren.*” The Amyrlin’s eyes strayed to the flattened cube again. “It was put forward in the Hall that you should be sent into retreat for contemplation. This was proposed by one of the 의석자들 for the 녹색 아자, with the other two nodding approval as she spoke.”

리안 made a sound of disgust, or perhaps frustration. She always kept in the background when the 아미를린 석좌 spoke, but 모이라인 could understand the small interruption this time. The 녹색 아자 had been allied with the Blue for a thousand years; since 아투르 호크윙’s time, they had all but spoken with one voice. “I have no desire to hoe vegetables in some remote village, Mother.” *Nor will I, whatever the 탑의 회의실 says.*

“It was further proposed, also by the Greens, that your care during your retreat should be given to the 적색 아자. The Red 의석자들 tried to appear surprised, but they looked like fisher-birds who knew the catch was unguarded.” The Amyrlin sniffed. “The Reds professed reluctance to take custody of one not of their 아자, but said they would accede to the wishes of the Hall.”

Despite herself, 모이라인 shivered. “That would be . . . most unpleasant, Mother.” It would be worse than unpleasant, much worse; the Reds were never gentle. She put the thought of it firmly to one side, to deal with later. “Mother, I cannot understand this apparent alliance between the Greens and the Reds. Their beliefs, their attitudes toward men, their views of our very purposes as 에스 세다이, are completely opposite. A Red and a Green cannot even talk to each other without coming to shouts.”

“Things change, Daughter. Four of the last five women raised Amyrlin have come from the Blue. Perhaps they feel that is too many, or that the Blue way of thinking no longer suffices in a world full of false 용. After a thousand years, many things change.” The Amyrlin grimaced and spoke as if to herself. “Old walls weaken, and old barriers fall.” She shook herself, and her voice firmed. “There was yet another proposal, one that still smells like week-old fish on the jetty. Since 리안 is of the 청색 아자 and I came from the Blue, it was put forward that sending two sisters of the Blue with me on this journey would give the Blue four representatives. Proposed in the Hall, to my face, as if they were discussing repairing the drains. Two of the White Sisters stood against me, and two Green. The Yellow muttered among themselves, then would not speak for or against. One more saying nay, and your sisters Anaiya and Maigan would not be here. There was even some talk, open talk, that I should not leave the 백색 탑 at all.”

모이라인 felt a greater shock than on hearing that the 적색 아자 wanted her in their hands. Whatever 아자 she came from, the 연대기 수호자 spoke only for the Amyrlin, and the Amyrlin spoke for all 에스 세다이 and all 아자s. That was the way it had always been, and no one had ever suggested otherwise, not in the darkest days of the 트롤록 전쟁, not when 아투르 호크윙’s armies had penned every surviving 에스 세다이 inside 타르 발론. Above all, the 아미를린 석좌 was the 아미를린 석좌. Every 에스 세다이 was pledged to obey her. No one could question what she did or where she chose to go. This proposal went against three thousand years of custom and law.

“Who would dare, Mother?”

The 아미를린 석좌’s laugh was bitter. “Almost anyone, Daughter. Riots in Caemlyn. The Great Hunt called without any of us having a hint of it until the proclamation. False 용 popping up like redbells after a rain. Nations fading, and more nobles playing at the Game of Houses than at any time since 아투르 호크윙 cut all their plottings short. And worst of all, every one of us knows the 어둠의 존재 is stirring again. Show me a sister who does not think the 백색 탑 is losing its grip on events, and if she is not 갈색 아자, she is dead. Time may be growing short for all of us, Daughter. Sometimes I think I can almost feel it growing shorter.”

“As you say, Mother, things change. But there are still worse perils outside the Shining Walls than within.”

For a long moment the Amyrlin met 모이라인’s gaze, then nodded slowly. “Leave us, 리안. I would talk to my Daughter 모이라인 alone.”

There was only a moment’s hesitation before 리안 said, “As you wish, Mother.” 모이라인 could feel her surprise. The Amyrlin gave few audiences without the Keeper present, especially not to a sister she had reason to chastise.

The door opened and closed behind 리안. She would not say a word in the anteroom of what had occurred inside, but the news that 모이라인 was alone with the Amyrlin would spread through the 에스 세다이 in 팔 다라 like wildfire through a dry forest, and the speculation would begin.

As soon as the door closed the Amyrlin stood, and 모이라인 felt a momentary tingle in her skin as the other woman channeled the 하나의 힘. For an instant, the 아미를린 석좌 seemed to her to be surrounded by a nimbus of bright light.

“I don’t know that any of the others have your old trick,” the 아미를린 석좌 said, lightly touching the blue stone on 모이라인’s forehead with one finger, “but most of us have some small tricks remembered from childhood. In any event, no one can hear what we say now.”

Suddenly she threw her arms around 모이라인, a warm hug between old friends; 모이라인 hugged back as warmly.

“You are the only one, 모이라인, with whom I can remember who I was. Even 리안 always acts as if I had *become* the stole and the staff, even when we are alone, as if we’d never giggled together as 수련생s. Sometimes I wish we still were 수련생s, you and I. Still innocent enough to see it all as a gleeman’s tale come true, still innocent enough to think we would find men—they would be princes, remember, handsome and strong and gentle?—who could bear to live with women of an 에스 세다이’s power. Still innocent enough to dream of the happy ending to the gleeman’s tale, of living our lives as other women do, just with more than they.”

“We are 에스 세다이, 시우안. We have our duty. Even if you and I had not been born to channel, would you give it up for a home and a husband, even a prince? I do not believe it. That is a village goodwife’s dream. Not even the Greens go so far.”

The Amyrlin stepped back. “No, I would not give it up. Most of the time, no. But there have been times I envied that village goodwife. At this moment, I almost do. 모이라인, if anyone, even 리안, discovers what we plan, we will both be stilled. And I can’t say they would be wrong to do it.”
