CHAPTER 24

![](images/00381.jpg)

*New Friends and Old Enemies*

에그웨인 followed the 허락받은 자 through the halls of the 백색 탑. Tapestries and paintings covered walls as white as the outside of the tower; patterned tiles made the floor. The 허락받은 자’s white dress was exactly like hers, except for seven narrow bands of color at hem and cuffs. 에그웨인 frowned, looking at that dress. Since yesterday 니나브 had worn an 허락받은 자’s dress, and she seemed to have no joy of it, nor of the golden ring, a serpent eating its own tail, that marked her level. The few times 에그웨인 had been able to see the Wisdom, 니나브’s eyes had seemed shadowed, as if she had seen things she wished with all her heart not to have seen.

“In here,” the 허락받은 자 said curtly, gesturing to a door. Named Pedra, she was a short, wiry woman, a little older than 니나브, and with a briskness always in her voice. “You’re given this time because it is your first day, but I’ll expect you in the scullery when the gong sounds High, and not one moment later.”

에그웨인 curtsied, then stuck out her tongue at the 허락받은 자’s retreating back. It might have been only the evening before that 셰리암 had finally put her name in the 수련생 book, but already she knew she did not like Pedra. She pushed open the door and went in.

The room was plain and small, with white walls, and there was a young woman, with reddish gold hair spilling around her shoulders, sitting on one of two hard benches. The floor was bare; 수련생s did not get much use of rooms with carpets. 에그웨인 thought the girl was about her own age, but there was a dignity and self-possession about her that made her seem older. The plainly cut 수련생 dress appeared somehow more, on her. Elegant. That was it.

“My name is 엘레인,” she said. She tilted her head, studying 에그웨인. “And you are 에그웨인. From Emond’s Field, in the 두 강.” She said it as if it had some significance, but went right on anyway. “Someone who has been here a little while is always assigned to a new 수련생 for a few days, to help her find her way. Sit, please.”

에그웨인 took the other bench, facing 엘레인. “I thought the 에스 세다이 would teach me, now that I’m finally a 수련생. But all that’s happened so far is that Pedra woke me a good two hours before first light and put me to sweeping the halls. She says I have to help wash dishes after dinner, too.”

엘레인 grimaced. “I hate washing dishes. I never had to—well, that doesn’t matter. You will have training. From now on, you will be at training at this hour every day, as a matter of fact. From breakfast until High, then again from dinner to Trine. If you are especially quick or especially slow, they may take you from supper to Full, as well, but that is usually for more chores.” 엘레인’s blue eyes took on a thoughtful expression. “You were born with it, weren’t you?” 에그웨인 nodded. “Yes, I thought I felt it. So was I, born with it. Do not be disappointed if you did not know. You will learn to feel the ability in other women. I had the advantage of growing up around an 에스 세다이.”

에그웨인 wanted to ask about that—*Who grows up with 에스 세다이?*—but 엘레인 went on.

“And also do not be disappointed if it takes you some time before you can achieve anything. With the 하나의 힘, I mean. Even the simplest thing takes a little time. Patience is a virtue that must be learned.” Her nose wrinkled. “셰리암 Sedai always says that, and she does her best to make us all learn it, too. Try to run when she says walk, and she’ll have you in her study before you can blink.”

“I’ve had a few lessons already,” 에그웨인 said, trying to sound modest. She opened herself to *세다르*—that part of it was easier now—and felt the warmth suffuse her body. She decided to try the biggest thing she knew how to do. She stretched out her hand, and a glowing sphere formed over it, pure light. It wavered—she still could not manage to hold it steady—but it was there.

Calmly, 엘레인 held out her hand, and a ball of light appeared above her palm. Hers flickered, too.

After a moment, a faint light glowed all around 엘레인. 에그웨인 gasped, and her ball vanished.

엘레인 giggled suddenly, and her light went out, both the sphere and the light around her. “You saw it around me?” she said excitedly. “I saw it around you. 셰리암 Sedai said I would, eventually. This was the first time. For you, too?”

에그웨인 nodded, laughing along with the other girl. “I like you, 엘레인. I think we’re going to be friends.”

“I think so, too, 에그웨인. You are from the 두 강, from Emond’s Field. Do you know a boy named 랜드 al’Thor?”

“I know him.” Abruptly 에그웨인 found herself remembering a tale 랜드 had told, a tale she had not believed, about falling off a wall into a garden and meeting. . . . “You’re the Daughter-Heir of 안도르,” she gasped.

“Yes,” 엘레인 said simply. “If 셰리암 Sedai as much as heard I’d mentioned it, I think she would have me into her study before I finished talking.”

“Everyone talks about being called to 셰리암’s study. Even the 허락받은 자. Does she scold so fiercely? She seems kindly to me.”

엘레인 hesitated, and when she spoke it was slowly, not meeting 에그웨인’s eye. “She keeps a willow switch on her desk. She says if you can’t learn to follow the rules in a civilized way, she will teach you another way. There are so many rules for 수련생s, it is very hard not to break some of them,” she finished.

“But that’s—that’s horrible! I’m not a child, and neither are you. I won’t be treated as one.”

“But we are children. The 에스 세다이, the full sisters, are the grown women. The 허락받은 자 are the young women, old enough to be trusted without someone looking over their shoulders every moment. And 수련생s are the children, to be protected and cared for, guided in the way they should go, and punished when they do what they should not. That is the way 셰리암 Sedai explains it. No one is going to punish you over your lessons, not unless you try something you’ve been told not to. It is hard not to try, sometimes; you will find you want to channel as much as you want to breathe. But if you break too many dishes because you are daydreaming when you should be washing, if you’re disrespectful to an 허락받은 자, or leave the Tower without permission, or speak to an 에스 세다이 before she speaks to you, or. . . . The only thing to do is the best you can. There isn’t anything else *to* do.”

“It sounds almost as if they’re trying to make us want to leave,” 에그웨인 protested.

“They aren’t, but then again, they are. 에그웨인, there are only forty 수련생s in the Tower. Only forty, and no more than seven or eight will become 허락받은 자. That is not enough, 셰리암 Sedai says. She says there are not enough 에스 세다이 now to do what needs to be done. But the Tower will not . . . cannot . . . lower its standards. The 에스 세다이 cannot take a woman as a sister if she does not have the ability, and the strength, and the desire. They can’t give the ring and the shawl to one who cannot channel the Power well enough, or who will allow herself to be intimidated, or who will turn back when the road turns rough. Training and testing take care of the channeling, and for strength and desire. . . . Well, if you want to go, they will let you. Once you know enough that you won’t die of ignorance.”

“I suppose,” 에그웨인 said slowly, “셰리암 told us some of that. I never thought about there not being enough 에스 세다이, though.”

“She has a theory. She says we have culled humankind. You know about culling? Cutting out of the herd those animals that have traits you don’t like?” 에그웨인 nodded impatiently; no one could grow up around sheep without knowing about culling the flock. “셰리암 Sedai says that with the 적색 아자 hunting down men who could channel for three thousand years, we are culling the ability to channel out of us all. I would not mention this around any Reds, if I were you. 셰리암 Sedai has been in more than one shouting match over it, and we are only 수련생s.”

“I won’t.”

엘레인 paused, and then said, “Is 랜드 well?”

에그웨인 felt a sudden stab of jealousy—엘레인 was very pretty—but over it came a stronger stab of fear. She went over the little she knew of 랜드’s one meeting with the Daughter-Heir, reassuring herself: 엘레인 could not possibly know that 랜드 could channel.

“에그웨인?”

“He is as well as he can be.” *I hope he is, the wool-headed idiot.* “He was riding with some 시엔나르an soldiers the last I saw him.”

“시엔나르ans! He told me he was a shepherd.” She shook her head. “I find myself thinking of him at the oddest times. 엘라이더 thinks he is important in some way. She didn’t come right out and say so, but she ordered a search for him, and she was in a fury when she learned he had left Caemlyn.”

“엘라이더?”

“엘라이더 Sedai. My mother’s councilor. She is 적색 아자, but Mother seems to like her despite that.”

에그웨인’s mouth felt dry. *적색 아자, and interested in 랜드.* “I—I don’t know where he is, now. He left 시엔나르, and I don’t think he was going back.”

엘레인 gave her a level look. “I would not tell 엘라이더 where to find him if I knew, 에그웨인. He has done no wrong that I know, and I fear she wants to use him in some manner. Anyway, I’ve not seen her since the day we arrived, with 백의단 dogging our trail. They are still camped on the 용산 side.” Abruptly she bounded to her feet. “Let us talk of happier things. There are two others here who know 랜드, and I would like you to meet one of them.” She took 에그웨인’s hand and pulled her out of the room.

“Two girls? 랜드 seems to meet a lot of girls.”

“Ummm?” Still drawing 에그웨인 down the corridor, 엘레인 studied her. “Yes. Well. One of them is a lazy chit named Else Grinwell. I don’t think she will be here long. She shirks her chores, and she is always sneaking off to watch the 감시자s practice their swords. She says 랜드 came to her father’s farm, with a friend of his. 맷. It seems they put notions of the world beyond the next village into her head, and she ran away to come be an 에스 세다이.”

“Men,” 에그웨인 muttered. “I dance a few dances with a nice boy, and 랜드 goes around looking like a dog with a sore tooth, but he—” She cut off as a man stepped into the hall ahead of them. Beside her, 엘레인 stopped, too, and her hand tightened on 에그웨인’s.

There was nothing alarming about him, aside from the suddenness of his appearance. He was tall and handsome, short of middle years, with long, dark curling hair, but his shoulders sagged, and there was sadness in his eyes. He made no move toward 에그웨인 and 엘레인, only stood looking at them until one of the 허락받은 자 appeared at his shoulder.

“You should not be in here,” she said to him, not unkindly.

“I wanted to walk.” His voice was deep, and as sad as his eyes.

“You can walk out in the garden, where you are supposed to be. The sunshine will be good for you.”

The man rumbled a bitter laugh. “With two or three of you watching my every move? You’re just afraid I’ll find a knife.” At the look in the 허락받은 자’s eyes, he laughed again. “For myself, woman. For myself. Lead me to your garden, and your watching eyes.”

The 허락받은 자 touched his arm lightly, and led him away.

“로가인,” 엘레인 said when he was gone.

“The false Dragon!”

“He has been gentled, 에그웨인. He is no more dangerous than any other man, now. But I remember seeing him before, when it took six 에스 세다이 to keep him from wielding the Power and destroying us all.” She shivered.

에그웨인 did, too. That was what the 적색 아자 would do to 랜드.

“Do they always have to be gentled?” she asked. 엘레인 stared at her, mouth agape, and she quickly added, “It is just that I’d think the 에스 세다이 would find some other way to deal with them. Anaiya and 모이라인 both said the greatest feats of the 전설의 시대 required men and women working together with the Power. I just thought they’d try to find a way.”

“Well, do not let any Red sister hear you thinking it aloud. 에그웨인, they did try. For three hundred years after the 백색 탑 was built, they tried. They gave up because there was nothing to find. Come on. I want you to meet 민. Not in the garden where 로가인 is going, thank the Light.”

The name sounded vaguely familiar to 에그웨인, and when she saw the young woman, she knew why. There was a narrow stream in the garden, with a low stone bridge over it, and 민 sat cross-legged on the wall of the bridge. She wore a man’s tight breeches and baggy shirt, and with her dark hair cut short she could almost pass for a boy, though an uncommonly pretty one. A gray coat lay beside her on the coping.

“I know you,” 에그웨인 said. “You worked at the inn in Baerlon.” A light breeze riffled the water beneath the bridge, and graywings warbled in the trees of the garden.

민 smiled. “And you were one of those who brought the 어둠의 친구들 down on us to burn it down. No, don’t worry. The messenger who came to fetch me brought enough gold that Master Fitch is building it back again twice as big. Good morning, 엘레인. Not slaving over your lessons? Or over some pots?” It was said in a bantering tone, as between friends, as 엘레인’s answering grin proved.

“I see 셰리암 has not yet managed to get you into a dress.”

민’s laugh was wicked. “I’m no 수련생.” She made her voice squeaky. “Yes, 에스 세다이. No, 에스 세다이. May I sweep another floor, 에스 세다이? I,” she said, resuming her own low voice, “clothe myself the way I want.” She turned to 에그웨인. “Is 랜드 well?”

에그웨인’s mouth tightened. *He should wear ram’s horns like a 트롤록*, she thought angrily. “I was sorry when your inn caught fire, and I am glad Master Fitch was able to rebuild. Why have you come to 타르 발론? It’s clear you do not mean to be an 에스 세다이.” 민 arched an eyebrow in what 에그웨인 was sure was amusement.

“She likes him,” 엘레인 explained.

“I know.” 민 glanced at 에그웨인, and for an instant 에그웨인 thought she saw sadness—or regret?—in her eyes. “I am here,” 민 said carefully, “because I was sent for, and was given the choice between riding and coming tied in a sack.”

“You always exaggerate it,” 엘레인 said. “셰리암 Sedai saw the letter, and she says it was a request. 민 sees things, 에그웨인. That’s why she’s here; so the 에스 세다이 can study how she does it. It isn’t the Power.”

“Request,” 민 snorted. “When an 에스 세다이 requests your presence, it’s like a command from a queen with a hundred soldiers to back it up.”

“Everybody sees things,” 에그웨인 said.

엘레인 shook her head. “Not like 민. She sees—auras—around people. And images.”

“Not all the time,” 민 put in. “Not around everybody.”

“And she can read things about you from them, though I’m not sure she always tells the truth. She said I’d have to share my husband with two other women, and I’d never put up with that. She just laughs, and says it was never her idea of how to run things, either. But she said I would be a queen before she knew who I was; she said she saw a crown, and it was the Rose Crown of 안도르.”

Despite herself, 에그웨인 asked, “What do you see when you look at me?”

민 glanced at her. “A white flame, and. . . . Oh, all sorts of things. Idon’t know what it means.”

“She says that a great deal,” 엘레인 said dryly. “One of the things she said she saw looking at me was a severed hand. Not mine, she says. She claims she does not know what it means, either.”

“Because I don’t,” 민 said. “I don’t know what half of it means.”

The crunch of boots on the walk brought them around to look at two young men with their shirts and coats across their arms, leaving sweaty chests bare, and scabbarded swords in their hands. 에그웨인 found herself staring at the most handsome man she had ever seen. Tall and slim, but hard, he moved with a cat-like grace. She suddenly realized he was bowing over her hand—she had not even felt him take it in his—and fumbled in her mind for the name she had heard.

“갈라드,” she murmured. His dark eyes stared back into hers. He was older than she. Older than 랜드. At the thought of 랜드, she gave a start and came to herself.

“And I am 가윈”—the other young man grinned—“since I don’t think you heard the first time.” 민 was grinning, too, and only 엘레인 wore a frown.

에그웨인 abruptly remembered her hand, still held by 갈라드, and freed it.

“If your duties allow,” 갈라드 said, “I would like to see you again, 에그웨인. We could walk, or if you obtain permission to leave the Tower, we could picnic outside the city.”

“That—that would be nice.” She was uncomfortably aware of the others, 민 and 가윈 still with their amused grins, 엘레인 still with her scowl. She tried to settle herself, to think of 랜드. *He’s so . . . beautiful.* She gave a jump, half afraid she had spoken aloud.

“Until then.” Finally taking his eyes from hers, 갈라드 bowed to 엘레인. “Sister.” Lithe as a blade, he strolled on across the bridge.

“That one,” 민 murmured, peering after him, “will always do what is right. No matter who it hurts.”

“Sister?” 에그웨인 said. 엘레인’s scowl had lessened only slightly. “I thought he was your. . . . I mean, the way you’re frowning. . . .” She had thought 엘레인 was jealous, and she still was not sure.

“I am not his sister,” 엘레인 said firmly. “I refuse to be.”

“Our father was his father,” 가윈 said dryly. “You cannot deny that, unless you want to call Mother a liar, and that, I think, would take more nerve than we have between us.”

For the first time 에그웨인 realized that he had the same reddish gold hair as 엘레인, though darkened and curled by sweat.

“민 is right,” 엘레인 said. “갈라드 has not the smallest part of humanity in him. He takes right above mercy, or pity, or. . . . He is no more human than a 트롤록.”

가윈’s grin came back. “I do not know about that. Not from the way he was looking at 에그웨인, here.” He caught her look, and his sister’s, and held up his hands as if to fend them off with his sheathed sword. “Besides, he has the best hand with a sword I’ve ever seen. The 감시자s only need show him something once, and he’s learned it. They sweat me nearly to death to learn half what 갈라드 does without trying.”

“And being good with a sword is enough?” 엘레인 sniffed. “Men! 에그웨인, as you may have guessed, this disgracefully unclothed lummox is my brother. 가윈, 에그웨인 knows 랜드 al’Thor. She is from the same village.”

“Is she? Was he really born in the 두 강, 에그웨인?”

에그웨인 made herself nod calmly. *What does he know?* “Of course, he was. I grew up with him.”

“Of course,” 가윈 said slowly. “Such a strange fellow. A shepherd, he said, though he never looked or acted like any shepherd I ever saw. Strange. I have met all sorts of people, and they’ve met 랜드 al’Thor. Some do not even know his name, but the description could not be anyone else, and he’s shifted every one of their lives. There was an old farmer who came to Caemlyn just to see 로가인, when 로가인 was brought through on his way here; yet the farmer stayed to stand for Mother when the riots started. Because of a young man off to see the world, who made him think there was more to life than his farm. 랜드 al’Thor. You could almost think he was *ta’veren.* 엘라이더 is certainly interested in him. I wonder if meeting him will shift our lives in the Pattern?”

에그웨인 looked at 엘레인 and 민. She was sure they could not have a clue that 랜드 really was *ta’veren.* She had never really thought about that part of it before; he was 랜드, and he had been cursed with the ability to channel. But *ta’veren* did move people, whether they wanted to be moved or not. “I really do like you,” she said abruptly, including both girls in her gesture. “I want to be your friend.”

“And I want to be yours,” 엘레인 said.

Impulsively, 에그웨인 hugged her, and then 민 jumped down, and the three of them stood there on the bridge hugging one another all together.

“We three *are* tied together,” 민 said, “and we cannot let any man get in the way of that. Not even him.”

“Would one of you mind telling me what this is all about?” 가윈 inquired gently.

“You would not understand,” his sister said, and the three girls all caught a fit of the giggles.

가윈 scratched his head, then shook it. “Well, if it has anything to do with 랜드 al’Thor, be sure you don’t let 엘라이더 hear of it. She has been at me like a Whitecloak Questioner three times since we arrived. I do not think she means him any—” He gave a start; there was a woman crossing the garden, a woman in a red-fringed shawl. “ ‘Name the 어둠의 존재,’ ” he quoted, “ ‘and he appears.’ I do not need another lecture about wearing my shirt when I’m out of the practice yards. Good morning to you all.”

엘라이더 spared a glance for the departing 가윈 as she came up the bridge. She was a handsome woman rather than beautiful, 에그웨인 thought, but that ageless look marked her as surely as her shawl; only the newest-made sisters lacked it. When her gaze swept over 에그웨인, pausing only a moment, 에그웨인 suddenly saw a hardness in the 에스 세다이. She had always thought of 모이라인 as strong, steel under silk, but 엘라이더 dispensed with the silk.

“엘라이더,” 엘레인 said, “this is 에그웨인. She was born with the seed in her, too. And she has already had some lessons, so she is as far along as I am. 엘라이더?”

The 에스 세다이’s face was blank and unreadable. “In Caemlyn, child, I am councilor to the Queen your mother, but this is the 백색 탑, and you, a 수련생.” 민 made as if to go, but 엘라이더 stopped her with a sharp, “Stay, girl. I would speak with you.”

“I’ve known you all my life, 엘라이더,” 엘레인 said incredulously. “You watched me grow up, and made the gardens bloom in winter so I could play.”

“Child, there you were the Daughter-Heir. Here you are a 수련생. You must learn that. You will be great one day, but you must learn!”

“Yes, 에스 세다이.”

에그웨인 was astounded. If someone had snubbed her so before others, she would have been in a fury.

“Now, off with both of you.” A gong began to toll, deep and sonorous, and 엘라이더 tilted her head. The sun stood halfway to its pinnacle. “High,” 엘라이더 said. “You must hurry, if you do not want further admonishment. And 엘레인? See the 수련생 감독관 in her study after your chores. A 수련생 does not speak to 에스 세다이 unless bidden to. Run, both of you. You will be late. Run!”

They ran, holding their skirts up. 에그웨인 looked at 엘레인. 엘레인 had two spots of color in her cheeks and a determined look on her face.

“I will be 에스 세다이,” 엘레인 said softly, but it sounded like a promise.

Behind them, 에그웨인 heard the 에스 세다이 begin, “I am given to understand, girl, that you were brought here by 모이라인 Sedai.”

She wanted to stay and listen, to hear if 엘라이더 asked about 랜드, but High rang through the 백색 탑, and she was summoned to chores. She ran as she had been commanded to run.

“I will be 에스 세다이,” she growled. 엘레인 flashed a quick smile of understanding, and they ran faster.

민’s shirt clung to her when she finally left the bridge. Not sweat from the sun, but from the heat of 엘라이더’s questions. She looked over her shoulder to make sure the 에스 세다이 was not following her, but 엘라이더 was nowhere in sight.

How did 엘라이더 know that 모이라인 had summoned her? 민 had been sure that was a secret known only to her, 모이라인, and 셰리암. And all those questions about 랜드. It had not been easy keeping a smooth face and a steady eye while telling an 에스 세다이 to her face that she had never heard of him and knew nothing of him. *What does* she *want with him? Light, what does 모이라인 want with him? What is he? Light, I don’t want to fall in love with a man I’ve only met once, and a farmboy at that.*

“모이라인, the Light blind you,” she muttered, “whatever you brought me here for, come out from wherever you’re hiding and tell me so I can go!”

The only answer was the sweet song of the graywings. With a grimace she went in search of a place to cool off.

CHAPTER 25

![](images/00529.jpg)

*케렌*

The city of 케렌 lay across hills against the River Alguenya, and 랜드’s first sight of it came from the hills to the north, by the light of the midday sun. Elricain Tavolin and the fifty 케렌인 soldiers still seemed like guards to him—the more since crossing the bridge at the Gaelin; they became more stiff the further south they rode—but 로이알 and Hurin did not appear to mind, so he tried not to. He studied the city, as large as any he had seen. Fat ships and broad barges filled the river, and tall granaries sprawled along the far bank, but 케렌 seemed to be laid out in a precise grid behind its high, gray walls. Those walls themselves made a perfect square, with one side hard along the river. In just as exact a pattern, towers rose within the walls, soaring as much as twenty times the height of the wall, yet even from the hills 랜드 could see that each one ended in a jagged top.
Outside the city walls, surrounding them from riverbank to riverbank, lay a warren of streets, crisscrossing at all angles and teeming with people. Foregate, 랜드 knew it was called, from Hurin; once there had been a market village for every city gate, but over the years they had all grown into one, a hodgepodge of streets and alleys growing up every which way.

As 랜드 and the others rode into those dirt streets, Tavolin put some of his soldiers to clearing a path through the throng, shouting and urging their horses forward as if to trample any who did not get out of the way quickly. People moved aside with no more than a glance, as if it were an everyday occurrence. 랜드 found himself smiling, though.

The Foregate people’s clothes were shabby more often than not, yet much of it was colorful, and there was a raucous bustle of life to the place. Hawkers cried their wares, and shopkeepers called for people to examine the goods displayed on tables before their shops. Barbers, fruit-peddlers, knife-sharpeners, men and women offering a dozen services and a hundred things for sale, wandered through the crowds. Music drifted through the babble from more than one structure; at first 랜드 thought they were inns, but the signs out front all showed men playing flutes or harps, tumbling or juggling, and large as they were, they had no windows. Most of the buildings in Foregate seemed to be wood, however big they were, and a good many looked new, if poorly made. 랜드 gaped at several that stood seven stories or more; they swayed slightly, though the people hurrying in and out did not seem to notice.

“Peasants,” Tavolin muttered, staring straight ahead in disgust. “Look at them, corrupted by outland ways. They should not be here.”

“Where should they be?” 랜드 asked. The 케렌인 officer glared at him and spurred his horse forward, flogging at the crowd with his quirt.

Hurin touched 랜드’s arm. “It was the 아일 War, Lord 랜드.” He looked to make sure none of the soldiers were close enough to hear. “Many of the farmers were afraid to go back to their lands near the 세계의 척추, and they all came here, near enough. That’s why Galldrian has the river full of grain barges up from 안도르 and 티어. There’s no crops coming from farms in the east because there aren’t any farms anymore. Best not to mention it to a 케렌인 though, my Lord. They like to pretend the war never happened, or at least that they won it.”

Despite Tavolin’s quirt, they were forced to halt while a strange procession crossed their path. Half a dozen men, beating tambours and dancing, led the way for a string of huge puppets, each half again as tall as the men who worked them with long poles. Giant crowned figures of men and women in long, ornate robes bowed to the crowd amid the shapes of fanciful beasts. A lion with wings. A goat, walking on its hind legs, with two heads, both of which were apparently meant to be breathing fire, from the crimson streamers hanging from the two mouths. Something that seemed to be half cat and half eagle, and another with a bear’s head on a man’s body, which 랜드 took to be a 트롤록. The crowd cheered and laughed as they pranced by.

“Man who made that never saw a 트롤록,” Hurin grumbled. “Head’s too big, and it’s too skinny. Likely didn’t believe in them, either, my Lord, any more than in those other things. The only monsters these Foregate folk believe in are 아일.”

“Are they having a festival?” 랜드 asked. He did not see any sign of it other than the procession, but he thought that there must be a reason for that. Tavolin ordered his soldiers forward again.

“No more than every day, 랜드,” 로이알 said. Walking alongside his horse, the blanket-wrapped chest still strapped to his saddle, the 오지어 drew as many looks as the puppets had. Some even laughed and clapped as they had for the puppets. “I fear Galldrian keeps his people quiet by entertaining them. He gives gleemen and musicians the King’s Gift, a bounty in silver, to perform here in the Foregate, and he sponsors horse races down by the river every day. There are 불꽃놀이 many nights, too.” He sounded disgusted. “장로 하만 says Galldrian is a disgrace.” He blinked, realizing what he had said, and looked around hurriedly to see if any of the soldiers had heard. None seemed to have.

“Fireworks,” Hurin said, nodding. “The Illuminators have built a chapter house here, I’ve heard, the same as in Tanchico. I didn’t half mind seeing the 불꽃놀이, when I was here before.”

랜드 shook his head. He had never seen 불꽃놀이 elaborate enough to require even one Illuminator. He had heard they only left Tanchico to put on displays for rulers. It was a strange place he was coming to.

At the tall, square archway of the city gate, Tavolin ordered a halt and dismounted by a squat stone building just inside the walls. It had arrow-slits instead of windows, and a heavy, iron-bound door.

“A moment, my Lord 랜드,” the officer said. Tossing his reins to one of the soldiers, he disappeared inside.

With a wary look at the soldiers—they sat their horses rigidly in two long files; 랜드 wondered what they would do if he and 로이알 and Hurin tried to leave—he took the opportunity to study the city that lay before him.

케렌 proper was a sharp contrast to the chaotic bustle of the Foregate. Broad, paved streets, wide enough to make the people in them seem fewer than they were, crossed each other at right angles. Just as in Tremonsien, the hills had been carved and terraced to straight lines. Closed sedan chairs, some with small pennants bearing the sigil of a House, moved with deliberateness, and carriages rolled down the streets slowly. People went silently in dark clothes, with no bright colors except here and there slashes across the breast of coat or dress. The more slashes, the more proudly the wearer moved, but no one laughed, or even smiled. The buildings on their terraces were all of stone, and the ornamentation was straight-lined and sharp-angled. There were no hawkers or peddlers in the streets, and even the shops seemed subdued, with only small signs and no wares displayed outside.

He could see the great towers more clearly, now. Scaffolds of lashed poles surrounded them, and workmen swarmed on the scaffolding, laying new stones to push the towers higher still.

“The Topless Towers of 케렌,” 로이알 murmured sadly. “Well, they were tall enough to warrant the name, once. When the 아일 took 케렌, about the time you were born, the towers burned, and cracked, and fell. I don’t see any 오지어 among the stonemasons. No 오지어 could like working here—the 케렌인 want what they want, without embellishment—but there were 오지어 when I was here before.”

Tavolin came out, trailing another officer and two clerks, one carrying a large, wood-bound ledger and the other a tray with writing implements. The front of the officer’s head was shaven like Tavolin’s, though advancing baldness seemed to have taken more hair than the razor. Both officers looked from 랜드 to the chest hidden by 로이알’s striped blanket and back again. Neither asked what was under the blanket. Tavolin had looked at it often on the way from Tremonsien, but he had never asked, either. The balding man looked at 랜드’s sword, too, and pursed his lips for an instant.

Tavolin gave the other officer’s name as Asan Sandair, and announced loudly, “Lord 랜드 of House al’Thor, in 안도르, and his man, called Hurin, with 로이알, an 오지어 of 스테딩 Shangtai.” The clerk with the ledger opened it across his two arms, and Sandair wrote the names in a round hand.

“You must return to this guardhouse by this same hour tomorrow, my Lord,” Sandair said, leaving the sanding to the second clerk, “and give the name of the inn where you are staying.”

랜드 looked at the staid streets of 케렌, then back at the liveliness of the Foregate. “Can you tell me the name of a good inn out there?” He nodded to the Foregate.

Hurin made a frantic *hsst* and leaned close. “It would not be proper, Lord 랜드,” he whispered. “If you stay in the Foregate, being a lord and all, they’ll be sure you are up to something.”

랜드 could see the sniffer was right. Sandair’s mouth had dropped open and Tavolin’s brows had risen at his question, and they were both still watching him intently. He wanted to tell them he was not playing their Great Game, but instead he said, “We will take rooms in the city. We can go now?”

“Of course, my Lord 랜드.” Sandair made a bow. “But . . . the inn?”

“I will let you know when we find one.” 랜드 turned Red, then paused. Selene’s note crackled in his pocket. “I need to find a young woman from 케렌. The Lady Selene. She is my age, and beautiful. I don’t know her House.”

Sandair and Tavolin exchanged looks, then Sandair said, “I will make inquiries, my Lord. Perhaps I will be able to tell you something when you come tomorrow.”

랜드 nodded and led 로이알 and Hurin into the city. They attracted little notice, though there were few riders. Even 로이알 attracted almost none. The people seemed nearly ostentatious about minding their own business.

“Will they take it the wrong way,” 랜드 asked Hurin, “my asking after Selene?”

“Who can say with 케렌인, Lord 랜드? They seem to think everything has to do with *Daes Dae’mar.*”

랜드 shrugged. He felt as if people were looking at him. He could not wait to get a good, plain coat again, and stop pretending to be what he was not.

Hurin knew several inns in the city, though his time in 케렌 had been spent mainly in the Foregate. The sniffer led them to one called The Defender of the Dragonwall, the sign bearing a crowned man with his foot on another man’s chest and his sword at the man’s throat. The fellow on his back had red hair.

A hostler came to take their horses, darting quick looks at 랜드 and at 로이알 when he thought he was not observed. 랜드 told himself to stop having fancies; not everyone in the city could be playing this Game of theirs. And if they were, he was no part of it.

The common room was neat, with the tables laid out as strictly as the city, and only a few people at them. They glanced up at the newcomers, then back to their wine immediately; 랜드 had the feeling they were still watching, though, and listening. A small fire burned in the big fireplace, though the day was warming.

The innkeeper was a plump, unctuous man with a single stripe of green across his dark gray coat. He gave a start at his first sight of them, and 랜드 was not surprised. 로이알, with the chest in his arms under its striped blanket, had to duck his head to make it in through the door, Hurin was burdened with all their saddlebags and bundles, and his own red coat was a sharp contrast to the somber colors the people at the tables wore.

The innkeeper took in 랜드’s coat and his sword, and his oily smile came back. He bowed, washing his smooth hands. “Forgive me, my Lord. It was just that for a moment I took you for—Forgive me. My brain is not what it was. You wish rooms, my Lord?” He added another, lesser bow for 로이알. “I am called Cuale, my Lord.”

*He thought I was 아일*, 랜드 thought sourly. He wanted to be gone from 케렌. But it was the one place Ingtar might find them. And Selene had said she would wait for him in 케렌.

It took a little time for their rooms to be readied, Cuale explaining with too many smiles and bows that it was necessary to move a bed for 로이알. 랜드 wanted them all to share a room again, but between the innkeeper’s scandalized looks and Hurin’s insistence—“We have to show these 케렌인 we know what’s right as well as they do, Lord 랜드”—they ended with two, one for him alone, with a connecting door.

The rooms were much the same except that theirs had two beds, one sized for an 오지어, while his had only one bed, and that almost as big as the other two, with massive square posts that nearly reached the ceiling. His tall-backed, padded chair and the washstand were square and massive, too, and the wardrobe standing against his wall was carved in a heavy, rigid style that made the thing look ready enough to fall over on him. A pair of windows siding his bed looked out on the street, two floors below.

As soon as the innkeeper left, 랜드 opened the door and admitted 로이알 and Hurin into his room. “This place gnaws at me,” he told them. “Everybody looks at you as if they think you’re doing something. I’m going back to the Foregate, for an hour anyway. At least the people laugh, there. Which of you is willing to take the first watch on the Horn?”

“I will stay,” 로이알 said quickly. “I’d like a chance to do a little reading. Just because I didn’t see any 오지어 does not mean there are no stonemasons down from 스테딩 Tsofu. It is not far from the city.”

“I’d think you would want to meet them.”

“Ah . . . no, 랜드. They asked enough questions the last time about why I was outside alone as it was. If they’ve had word from 스테딩 Shangtai. . . . Well, I will just rest here and read, I think.”

랜드 shook his head. He often forgot that 로이알 had run away from home, in effect, to see the world. “What about you, Hurin? There’s music in the Foregate, and people laughing. I’ll wager no one is playing *Daes Dae’mar* there.”

“I would not be so certain of that myself, Lord 랜드. In any case, I thank you for the invitation, but I think not. There’s so many fights—and killings, too—in Foregate, that it stinks, if you know what I mean. Not that they’re likely to bother a lord, of course; the soldiers would be down on them if they did. But if it pleases you, I would like to have a drink in the common room.”

“Hurin, you don’t need my permission for anything. You know that.”

“As you say, my Lord.” The sniffer gave a suggestion of a bow.

랜드 took a deep breath. If they did not leave 케렌 soon, Hurin would be bowing and scraping left and right. And if 맷 and 페린 saw that, they would never let him forget it. “I hope nothing delays Ingtar. If he doesn’t come quickly, we’ll have to take the Horn back to 팔 다라 ourselves.” He touched Selene’s note through his coat. “We will have to. 로이알, I’ll come back so you can see some of the city.”

“I’d rather not risk it,” 로이알 said.

Hurin accompanied 랜드 downstairs. As soon as they reached the common room, Cuale was bowing in front of 랜드, pushing a tray at him. Three folded and sealed parchments lay on the tray. 랜드 took them, since that was what the innkeeper seemed to intend. They were a fine grade of parchment, soft and smooth to his touch. Expensive.

“What are these?” he asked.

Cuale bowed again. “Invitations, of course, my Lord. From three of the noble Houses.” He bowed himself away.

“Who would send me invitations?” 랜드 turned them over in his hand. None of the men at the tables looked up, but he had the feeling they were watching just the same. He did not recognize the seals. None was the crescent moon and stars Selene had used. “Who would know I was here?”

“Everyone by now, Lord 랜드,” Hurin said quietly. He seemed to feel eyes watching, too. “The guards at the gate would not keep their mouths closed about an outland lord coming to 케렌. The hostler, the innkeeper . . . everybody tells what they know where they think it will do them the most good, my Lord.”

With a grimace, 랜드 took two steps and hurled the invitations into the fire. They caught immediately. “I am not playing *Daes Dae’mar*,” he said, loudly enough for everyone to hear. Not even Cuale looked at him. “I’ve nothing to do with your Great Game. I am just here to wait for some friends.”

Hurin caught his arm. “Please, Lord 랜드.” His voice was an urgent whisper. “Please don’t do that again.”

“Again? You really think I’ll receive more?”

“I’m certain. Light, but you mind me of the time Teva got so mad at a hornet buzzing round his ears, he kicked the nest. You’ve likely just convinced everyone in the room you are in some deep part of the Game. It must be deep, as they’ll see it, if you deny playing at all. *Every* lord and lady in 케렌 plays it.” The sniffer glanced at the invitations, curling blackly in the fire, and winced. “And you have surely made enemies of three Houses. Not great Houses, or they’d not have moved so quickly, but still noble. You must answer any more invitations you receive, my Lord. Decline if you will—though they’ll read things into whose invitations you do decline. And into whose you accept. Of course, if you decline them all, or accept them all—”

“I’ll have no part of it,” 랜드 said quietly. “We are leaving 케렌 as soon as we can.” He thrust his fists into his coat pockets, and felt Selene’s note crumple. Pulling it out, he smoothed it on his coat front. “As soon as we can,” he muttered, putting it back in his pocket again. “Have your drink, Hurin.”

He stalked out angrily, not sure whether he was angry with himself, or with 케렌 and its Great Game, or Selene for vanishing, or 모이라인. She had started it all, stealing his coats and giving him a lord’s clothes instead. Even now that he called himself free of them, an 에스 세다이 still managed to interfere in his life, and without even being there.

He went back through the same gate by which he had entered the city, since that was the way he knew. A man standing in front of the guardhouse took note of him—his bright coat marked him out, as well as his height among the 케렌인—and hurried inside, but 랜드 did not notice. The laughter and music of the Foregate were pulling him on.

If his gold-embroidered red coat made him stand out inside the walls, it fit right into the Foregate. Many of the men milling through the crowded streets were dressed just as darkly as those in the city, but just as many wore coats of red, or blue, or green, or gold—some bright enough to be a Tinker’s clothes—and even more of the women had embroidered dresses and colored scarves or shawls. Most of the finery was tattered and ill-fitting, as if made for someone else originally, but if some of those who wore it eyed his fine coat, none seemed to take it amiss.

He was making his way through the throng, wondering what to see next, when a deep voice, accompanied by the plucking of a harp, drifted out from a doorway with the sign of a juggler over it.

“. . . cold blows the wind down Shara Pass; cold lies the grave unmarked. Yet every year at Sunday, upon those piled stones appears a single rose, one crystal teardrop like dew upon the petals, laid by the fair hand of Dunsinin, for she keeps fast to the bargain made by Rogosh Eagle-eye.”

The voice drew 랜드 like a rope. He pushed through the doorway as applause rose within.

“Two coppers, my good Lord,” said a rat-faced man who could have been twin to the other. “Two coppers to see—”

랜드 dug out some coins and thrust them at the man. He walked on in a daze, staring at the man bowing on the dais to the clapping of his listeners, cradling his harp in one arm and with the other spreading his patch-covered cloak as if to trap all the sound they made. He was a tall man, lanky and not young, with long mustaches as white as the hair on his head. And when he straightened and saw 랜드, the eyes that widened were sharp and blue.

“톰.” 랜드’s whisper was lost in the noise of the crowd.

Holding 랜드’s eye, 톰 Merrilin nodded slightly toward a small door beside the dais. Then he was bowing again, smiling and basking in the applause.

랜드 made his way to the door and through it. It was only a small hallway, with three steps leading up to the dais. In the other direction from the dais 랜드 could see a juggler practicing with colored balls, and six tumblers limbering themselves.

“Bigger fool if you had, boy. That 페이드”—he looked around; there was no one close enough to hear, but he lowered his voice anyway—“had no interest in me. It left me a little present of a stiff leg and ran off after you and 맷. All you could have done was die.” He paused, looking thoughtful. “모이라인 said I was still alive, did she? 랜드 shook his head. To his surprise, 톰 seemed disappointed.

“Too bad, in a way. She’s a fine woman, even if she is. . . .” He left it unsaid. “So it was 맷 or 페린 she was after. I won’t ask which. “For a time, boy, I thought you were the one 모이라인 wanted, and I even thought I knew why. You know, no man chooses to channel the Power. It is something that happens to him, like a disease. You cannot blame a man for falling sick, even if it might kill you, too.”

“Your nephew could channel, couldn’t he? You told me that was why you helped us, because your nephew had had trouble with the 백색 탑 and there was nobody to help him. There’s only one kind of trouble men can have with 에스 세다이.”

톰 studied the tabletop, pursing his lips. “I don’t suppose there is any use in denying it. You understand, it is not the kind of thing a man talks about, having a male relative who could channel. Aaagh! The 적색 아자 never gave Owyn a chance. They gentled him, and then he died. He just gave up wanting to live. . . .” He exhaled sadly.

랜드 shivered. *Why didn’t 모이라인 do that to me?* “A chance, 톰? Do you mean there was some way he could have dealt with it? Not gone mad? Not died?”

“Owyn held it off almost three years. He never hurt anyone. He didn’t use the Power unless he had to, and then only to help his village. He. . . .” 톰 threw up his hands. “I suppose there was no choice. The people where he lived told me he was acting strange that whole last year. They did not much want to talk about it, and they nearly stoned me when they found out I was his uncle. I suppose he *was* going mad. But he was my blood, boy. I can’t love the 에스 세다이 for what they did to him, even if they had to. If 모이라인’s let you go, then you are well out of it.”

For a moment 랜드 was silent. *Fool! Of course there’s no way to deal with it. You’re going to go mad and die whatever you do. But Ba’alzamon said—* “No!” He colored under 톰’s scrutiny. “I mean . . . I am out of it, 톰. But I still have the 발레르의 뿔. Think of it, 톰. 발레르의 뿔. Other gleemen might tell tales about it, but you could say you had it in your hands.” He realized he sounded like Selene, but all that did was make him wonder where she was. “There’s nobody I’d rather have with us than you, 톰.”

톰 frowned as if considering it, but in the end he shook his head firmly. “Boy, I like you well enough, but you know as well as I do that I only helped before because there was an 에스 세다이 mixed in it. Seaghan doesn’t try to cheat me more than I expect, and with the King’s Gift added in, I could never earn as much in the villages. To my very great surprise, Dena seems to love me, and—as much a surprise—I return the feeling. Now, why should I leave that to go be chased by 트롤록s and 어둠의 친구들? 발레르의 뿔? Oh, it is a temptation, I’ll admit, but no. No, I will not get mixed up in it again.”

He leaned over to pick up one of the wooden instrument cases, long and narrow. When he opened it, a flute lay inside, plainly made but mounted with silver. He closed it again and slid it across the table. “You might need to earn your supper again someday, boy.”

“I might at that,” 랜드 said. “At least we can talk. I will be in—”

The gleeman was shaking his head. “A clean break is best, boy. If you’re always coming around, even if you never mention it, I won’t be able to get the Horn out of my head. And I won’t be tangled in it. I won’t.”

After 랜드 left, 톰 threw his cloak on the bed and sat with his elbows on the table. *발레르의 뿔. How did that farmboy find*. . . . He shut off that line of thought. Think about the Horn too long, and he would find himself running off with 랜드 to carry it to 시엔나르. *That* would *make a story, carrying the 발레르의 뿔 to the 국경지대 with 트롤록s and 어둠의 친구들 pursuing.* Scowling, he reminded himself of Dena. Even if she had not loved him, talent such as hers was not to be found every day. And she did love, even if he could not begin to imagine why.

“Old fool,” he muttered.

“Aye, an old fool,” Zera said from the door. He gave a start; he had been so absorbed in his thoughts that he had not heard the door open. He had known Zera for years, off and on in his wanderings, and she always took full advantage of the friendship to speak her mind. “An old fool who’s playing the Game of Houses again. Unless my ears are failing, that young lord has the sound of 안도르 on his tongue. He’s no 케렌인, that’s for certain sure. *Daes Dae’mar* is dangerous enough without letting an outland lord mix you in his schemes.”

톰 blinked, then considered the way 랜드 had looked. That coat had surely been fine enough for a lord. He was growing old, letting things like that slip by him. Ruefully, he realized he was considering whether to tell Zera the truth or let her continue thinking as she did. *All it takes is to think about the Great Game, and I start playing it.* “The boy is a shepherd, Zera, from the 두 강.”

She laughed scornfully. “And I’m the Queen of 게알단. I tell you, the Game has grown dangerous in 케렌 the last few years. Nothing like what you knew in Caemlyn. There are murders done, now. You’ll have your throat cut for you, if you don’t watch out.”

“I tell you, I am not in the Great Game any longer. That’s all twenty years in the past, near enough.”

“Aye.” She did not sound as if she believed it. “But be that as it may, and young outland lords aside, you’ve begun performing at the lords’ manors.”

“They pay well.”

“And they’ll pull you into their plots as soon as they see how. They see a man, and think how to use him, as naturally as breathing. This young lord of yours won’t help you; they will eat him alive.”

He gave up on trying to convince her he was out of it. “Is that what you came up to say, Zera?”

“Aye. Forget playing the Great Game, 톰. Marry Dena. She’ll take you, the more fool her, bony and white-haired as you are. Marry her, and forget this young lord and *Daes Dae’mar.*”

“I thank you for the advice,” he said dryly. *Marry her? Burden her with an old husband. She’ll never be a bard with my past hanging around her neck.* “If you don’t mind, Zera, I want to be alone for a while. I perform for Lady Arilyn and her guests tonight, and I need to prepare.”

She gave him a snort and a shake of her head and banged the door shut behind her.

톰 drummed his fingers on the table. Coat or no coat, 랜드 was still only a shepherd. If he had been more, if he had been what 톰 once suspected—a man who could channel—neither 모이라인 nor any other 에스 세다이 would ever have let him walk away ungentled. Horn or no Horn, the boy was only a shepherd.

“He is out of it,” he said aloud, “and so am I.”

CHAPTER 27

![](images/00407.jpg)

*그림자 in the Night*

“I do not understand it,” 로이알 said. “I was winning, most of the time. And then Dena came in and joined the game, and she won it all right back. Every toss. She called it a little lesson. What did she mean by that?”

랜드 and the 오지어 were making their way through the Foregate, The Bunch of Grapes behind them. The sun sat low in the west, a red ball half below the horizon, throwing long shadows behind them. The street was empty save for one of the big puppets, a goat-horned 트롤록 with a sword at its belt, coming toward them with five men working the poles, but sounds of merriment drifted still from other parts of the Foregate, where the halls of entertainment and the taverns stood. Here, doors were already barred and windows shuttered.

랜드 stopped fingering the wooden flute case and slung it on his back. *I suppose I couldn’t expect him to throw over everything and come with me, but at least he could talk to me. Light, I wish Ingtar would show up.* He stuffed his hands in his pockets and felt Selene’s note.

“You don’t suppose she. . . .” 로이알 paused uncomfortably. “You don’t suppose she cheated, do you? Everybody was grinning as if she were doing something clever.”

랜드 shrugged at his cloak. *I have to take the Horn and go. If we wait for Ingtar, anything can happen. Fain will come sooner or later. I have to stay ahead of him.* The men with the puppet were almost to them.

“랜드,” 로이알 said suddenly, “I don’t think that’s a—”

Abruptly the men let their poles clatter to the packed dirt street; instead of collapsing, the 트롤록 leaped for 랜드 with outstretched hands.

There was no time to think. Instinct brought the sword out of its sheath in a flashing arc. The Moon Rises Over the Lakes. The 트롤록 staggered back with a bubbling cry, snarling even as it fell.

For an instant everyone stood frozen. Then the men—the 어둠의 친구들, they had to be—looked from the 트롤록 lying in the street to 랜드, with the sword in his hands and 로이알 at his side. They turned and ran.
랜드 was staring at the 트롤록, too. The void had surrounded him before his hand touched hilt; *세이딘* shone in his mind, beckoning, sickening. With an effort, he made the void vanish, and licked his lips. Without the emptiness, fear crawled on his skin.

“로이알, we have to get back to the inn. Hurin’s alone, and they—” He grunted as he was lifted into the air by a thick arm long enough to pin both of his to his chest. A hairy hand grabbed his throat. He caught sight of a tusked snout just over his head. A rank smell filled his nose, equal parts sour sweat and pigsty.

As quickly as it had seized him, the hand at his throat was torn away. Stunned, 랜드 stared at it, at the thick 오지어 fingers clutching the 트롤록’s wrist.

“Hold on, 랜드.” 로이알’s voice sounded strained. The 오지어’s other hand came around and took hold of the arm still holding 랜드 above the ground. “Hold on.”

랜드 was shaken from side to side as 오지어 and 트롤록 struggled. Abruptly he fell free. Staggering, he took two steps to get clear and turned back with sword raised.

Standing behind the boar-snouted 트롤록, 로이알 had it by wrist and forearm, holding its arms spread wide, breathing hard with the effort. The 트롤록 snarled gutturally in the harsh 트롤록 tongue, throwing its head back in efforts to catch 로이알 with a tusk. Their boots scuffled across the dirt of the street.

랜드 tried to find a place to put his blade in the 트롤록 without hurting 로이알, but 오지어 and 트롤록 spun in their rough dance so much that he could find no opening.

With a grunt, the 트롤록 pulled its left arm free, but before it could loose itself completely, 로이알 snapped his own arm around its neck, hugging the creature close. The 트롤록 clawed at its sword; the scythe-like blade hung on the wrong side for left-handed use, but inch by inch the dark steel began sliding out of the scabbard. And still they thrashed about so that 랜드 could not strike without risking 로이알.

*The Power.* That could do it. How, he did not know, but he knew nothing else to try. The 트롤록 had its sword half unsheathed. When the curved blade was bare, it would kill 로이알.

Reluctantly, 랜드 formed the void. *Saidin* shone at him, pulled at him. Dimly, he seemed to recall a time when it had sung to him, but now it only drew him, a flower’s perfume drawing a bee, a midden’s stench drawing a fly. He opened himself up, reached for it. There was nothing there. He could as well have been reaching for light in truth. The taint slid off onto him, soiling him, but there was no flow of light inside him. Driven by a distant desperation, he tried again and again. And again and again there was only the taint.

With a sudden heave, 로이알 threw the 트롤록 aside, so hard that the thing cartwheeled against the side of a building. It struck, headfirst, with a loud crack, and slid down the wall to lie with its neck twisted at an impossible angle. 로이알 stood staring at it, his chest heaving.

랜드 looked out of the emptiness for a moment before he realized what had happened. As soon as he did, though, he let void and tainted light go, and hurried to 로이알’s side.

“I never . . . killed before, 랜드.” 로이알 drew a shuddering breath.

“It would have killed you if you hadn’t,” 랜드 told him. Anxiously, he looked at the alleys and shuttered windows and barred doors. Where there were two 트롤록s, there had to be more. “I’m sorry you had to do it, 로이알, but it would have killed both of us, or worse.”

“I know. But I cannot like it. Even a 트롤록.” Pointing toward the setting sun, the 오지어 seized 랜드’s arm. “There’s another of them.”

Against the sun, 랜드 could not make out details, but it appeared to be another group of men with a huge puppet, coming toward 로이알 and him. Except that now he knew what to look for, the “puppet” moved its legs too naturally, and the snouted head rose to sniff the air without anyone lifting a pole. He did not think the 트롤록 and 어둠의 친구들 could see him among the evening shadows, or what lay in the street around him; they moved too slowly for that. Yet it was plain they were hunting, and coming closer.

“Fain knows I am out here somewhere,” he said, hastily wiping his blade on a dead 트롤록’s coat. “He’s set them to find me. He is afraid of the 트롤록s being seen, though, or he wouldn’t have them disguised. If we can reach a street where there are people, we’ll be safe. We have to get back to Hurin. If Fain finds him, alone with the Horn. . . .”

He pulled 로이알 along to the next corner and turned toward the nearest sounds of laughter and music, but long before they reached it, another group of men appeared ahead of them in the otherwise empty street with a puppet that was no puppet. 랜드 and 로이알 took the next turning. It led east.

Every time 랜드 tried to reach the music and laughter, there was a 트롤록 in the way, often sniffing the air for a scent. Some 트롤록s hunted by scent. Sometimes, here where there were no eyes to see, a 트롤록 stalked alone. More than once he was sure it was one he had seen before. They were closing in, and making sure he and 로이알 did not leave the deserted streets with their shuttered windows. Slowly the two of them were forced east, away from the city and Hurin, away from other people, along narrow, slowly darkening streets that ran in all directions, uphill and down. 랜드 eyed the houses they passed, the tall buildings closed up tight for the night, with more than a little regret. Even if he pounded on a door until someone opened it, even if they took 로이알 and him in, none of the doors he saw would stop a 트롤록. All that would do would be to offer up more victims with 로이알 and himself.

“랜드,” 로이알 said finally, “there is nowhere else to go.”

They had reached the eastern edge of the Foregate; the tall buildings to either side of them were the last. Lights in windows on the upper stories mocked him, but the lower floors were all shut tight. Ahead lay the hills, cloaked in first twilight and bare of so much as a farmhouse. Not entirely empty, though. He could just make out pale walls surrounding one of the larger hills, perhaps a mile away, and buildings inside.

“Once they push us out there,” 로이알 said, “they won’t have to worry who sees them.”

랜드 gestured to the walls around the hill. “Those should stop a 트롤록. It must be a lord’s manner. Maybe they’ll let us in. An 오지어, and an outland lord? This coat has to be good for something sooner or later.” He looked back down the street. No 트롤록s in sight yet, but he drew 로이알 around the side of the building anyway.

“I think that is the Illuminators’ chapter house, 랜드. Illuminators guard their secrets tightly. I don’t think they would let Galldrian himself inside there.”

“What trouble have you gotten yourself into now?” said a familiar woman’s voice. There was suddenly a spicy perfume in the air.

랜드 stared: Selene stepped around the corner they had just rounded, her white dress bright in the dimness. “How did you get here? What are you doing here? You have to leave immediately. Run! There are 트롤록s after us.”

“So I saw.” Her voice was dry, yet cool and composed. “I came to find you, and I find you allowing 트롤록s to herd you like sheep. Can the man who possesses the 발레르의 뿔 let himself be treated so?”

“I don’t have it with me,” he snapped, “and I don’t know how it could help if I did. The dead heroes are not supposed to come back to save me from 트롤록s. Selene, you have to get away. Now!” He peered around the corner.

Not more than a hundred paces away, a 트롤록 was sticking its horned head cautiously into the street, smelling the night. A large shadow by its side had to be another 트롤록, and there were smaller shadows, too. 어둠의 친구들.

“Too late,” 랜드 muttered. He shifted the flute case to pull off his cloak and wrap it around her. It was long enough to hide her white dress entirely, and trail on the ground besides. “You’ll have to hold that up to run,” he told her. “로이알, if they won’t let us in, we will have to find a way to sneak in.”

“But, 랜드—”

“Would you rather wait for the 트롤록s?” He gave 로이알 a push to start him, and took Selene’s hand to follow at a trot. “Find us a path that won’t break our necks, 로이알.”

“You’re letting yourself become flustered,” Selene said. She seemed to have less trouble following 로이알 in the failing light than 랜드 did. “Seek the Oneness, and be calm. One who would be great must always be calm.”

“The 트롤록s might hear you,” he told her. “I don’t want greatness.” He thought he heard an irritated grunt from her.

Stones sometimes turned underfoot, but the way across the hills was not hard despite the twilight shadows. Trees, and even brush, had long since been cleared from the hills for firewood. Nothing grew except knee-high grass that rustled softly around their legs. A night breeze came up softly. 랜드 worried that it might carry their scent to the 트롤록s.

로이알 stopped when they reached the wall; it stood twice as high as the 오지어, the stones covered with a whitish plaster. 랜드 peered back toward the Foregate. Bands of lighted windows reached out like spokes of a wheel from the city walls.

“로이알,” he said softly, “can you see them? Are they following us?”

The 오지어 looked in the direction of the Foregate, and nodded unhappily. “I only see some of the 트롤록s, but they are coming this way. Running. 랜드, I really don’t think—”

Selene cut him off. “If he wants to go in, *alantin*, he needs a door. Such as that one.” She pointed to a dark patch a little down the wall. Even with her telling him, 랜드 was not certain it *was* a door, but when she strode to it and pulled, it opened.

“랜드,” 로이알 began.

랜드 pushed him to the door. “Later, 로이알. And softly. We’re hiding, remember?” He got them inside and closed the door behind them. There were brackets for a bar, but no bar to be seen. It would not stop anyone, but maybe the 트롤록s would hesitate to come inside the walls.

They were in an alleyway leading up the hill between two long, low windowless buildings. At first he thought they were stone, too, but then he realized the white plaster had been laid over wood. It was dark enough now for the moon reflecting from the walls to give a semblance of light.

“Better to be arrested by the Illuminators than taken by 트롤록s,” he murmured, starting up the hill.

“But that is what I was trying to tell you,” 로이알 protested. “I’ve heard the Illuminators kill intruders. They keep their secrets hard and fast, 랜드.”

랜드 stopped dead and stared back at the door. The 트롤록s were still out there. At the worst, humans had to be better to deal with than 트롤록s. He might be able to talk the Illuminators into letting them go; 트롤록s did not listen before they killed. “I’m sorry I got you into this, Selene.”

“Danger adds a certain something,” she said softly. “And so far, you handle it well. Shall we see what we find?” She brushed past him up the alleyway. 랜드 followed, the spicy smell of her filling his nostrils.

Atop the hill, the alleyway opened onto a wide expanse of smoothly flattened clay, almost as pale as the plaster and nearly surrounded by more white, windowless buildings with the shadows of narrow alleys between, but to 랜드’s right stood one building with windows, light falling onto the pale clay. He pulled back into the shadows of the alley as a man and a woman appeared, walking slowly across the open space.

Their clothes were certainly not 케렌인. The man wore breeches as baggy as his shirt sleeves, both in a soft yellow, with embroidery on the legs of his breeches and across the chest of his shirt. The woman’s dress, worked elaborately across the breast, seemed a pale green, and her hair was done in a multitude of short braids.

“All is in readiness, you say?” the woman demanded. “You are certain, Tammuz? All?”

The man spread his hands. “Always you check behind me, 알루드라. All is in readiness. The display, it could be given this very moment.”

“The gates and doors, they are all barred? All of the . . . ?” Her voice faded as they moved on to the far end of the lighted building.

랜드 studied the open area, recognizing almost nothing. In the middle of it, several dozen upright tubes, each nearly as tall as he and a foot or more across, sat on large wooden bases. From each tube, a dark, twisted cord ran across the ground and behind a low wall, perhaps three paces long, on the far side. All around the open space stood a welter of wooden racks with troughs and tubes and forked sticks and a score of other things.

All the 불꽃놀이 he had ever seen could be held in one hand, and that was as much as he knew, except that they burst with a great roar, or whizzed along the ground in spirals of sparks, or sometimes shot into the air. They always came with warnings from the Illuminators that opening one could cause it to go off. In any case, 불꽃놀이 were too expensive for the Village Council to have allowed anybody unskilled to open one. He could well remember the time when 맷 had tried to do just that; it was nearly a week before anyone but 맷’s own mother would speak to him. The only thing that 랜드 found familiar at all was the cords—the fuses. That, he knew, was where you set the fire.

With a glance back at the unbarred door, he motioned the others to follow and started around the tubes. If they were going to find a place to hide, he wanted to be as far from that door as he could.

It meant making their way between the racks, and 랜드 held his breath every time he brushed against one. The things in them shifted with the slightest touch, rattling. All of them seemed to be made of wood, without a piece of metal. He could imagine the racket if one were knocked over. He eyed the tall tubes warily, remembering the bang made by one the size of his finger. If those were 불꽃놀이, he did not want to be this close to them.

로이알 muttered to himself continually, especially when he bumped one of the racks, then started back so fast that he bumped another. The 오지어 crept along in a cloud of clatters and muttering.

Selene was no less unnerving. She strode as casually as if they were on a city street. She did not bump anything, did not make a sound, but she also made no effort to keep the cloak closed. The white of her dress seemed brighter than all the walls together. He peered at the lighted windows, waiting for someone to appear. All it would take was one; Selene could not fail to be seen, the alarm given.

The windows remained empty, though. 랜드 was just breathing a sigh of relief as they approached the low wall—and the alleys and buildings behind it—when 로이알 brushed against another rack, standing right beside the wall. It held ten soft-looking sticks, as long as 랜드’s arm, with thin streams of smoke rising from their tips. The rack made hardly a sound when it fell, the smoldering sticks sprawling across one of the fuses. With a crackling hiss, the fuse burst into flame, and the flame raced toward one of the tall tubes.

랜드 goggled for an instant, then he tried to whisper a shout. “Behind the wall!”

Selene made an angry noise when he bore her to the ground behind the wall, but he did not care. He tried to spread himself over her protectively as 로이알 crowded beside them. Waiting for the tube to burst, he wondered if there would be anything left of the wall. There was a hollow thump that he felt through the ground as much as heard. Cautiously, he lifted himself off of Selene enough to peer around the edge of the wall. She fisted him in the ribs, hard, and wriggled out from under him with an oath in a language he did recognize, but he was beyond noticing.

A trickle of smoke was leaking from the top of one of the tubes. That was all. He shook his head wonderingly. *If that’s all there is to it. . . .*

With a crash like thunder, a huge flower of red and white bloomed high in the now dark sky, then slowly began drifting away in sparkles.

As he goggled at it, the lighted building erupted with noise. Shouting men and women filled the windows, staring and pointing.

랜드 longingly eyed the dark alleyway, only a dozen steps away. And the first step would be in full view of the people at the windows. Pounding feet poured from the building.

He pressed 로이알 and Selene back against the wall, hoping they looked like just another shadow. “Be still and be silent,” he whispered. “It’s our only hope.”

“Sometimes,” Selene said quietly, “if you are very still, no one can see you at all.” She did not sound the least bit worried.

Boots thumped back and forth on the other side of the wall, and voices were raised in anger. Especially the one 랜드 recognized as 알루드라.

“You great buffoon, Tammuz! You great pig, you! Your mother, she was a goat, Tammuz! One day you will kill us all.”

“I am not to blame for this, 알루드라,” the man protested. “I have been sure to put everything where it belonged, and the punks, they were—”

“You will not speak to me, Tammuz! A great pig does not deserve to speak like a human!” 알루드라’s voice changed in answer to another man’s question. “There is no time to prepare another. Galldrian, he must be satisfied with the rest for tonight. And one early. And you, Tammuz! You will set everything right, and tomorrow you will leave with the carts to buy the manure. Does anything else go wrong this night, I will not trust you again even with so much as the manure!”

Footsteps faded back toward the building to the accompaniment of 알루드라’s muttering. Tammuz remained, growling under his breath about the unfairness of it all.

랜드 stopped breathing as the man came over to right the toppled stand. Pressed back in the shadows against the wall, he could see Tammuz’s back and shoulder. All the man had to do was turn his head, and he could not miss seeing 랜드 and the others. Still complaining to himself, Tammuz arranged the smoldering sticks in the stand, then stalked off toward the building where everyone else had gone.

Letting his breath go, 랜드 took a quick look after the man, then pulled back into the shadows. A few people still stood at the windows. “We can’t expect any more luck tonight,” he whispered.

“It is said great men make their own luck,” Selene said softly.

“Will you stop that,” he told her wearily. He wished the smell of her did not fill his head so; it made it hard to think clearly. He could remember the feel of her body when he pushed her down—softness and firmness in a disturbing blend—and that did not help either.

“랜드?” 로이알 was peering around the end of the wall away from the lighted building. “I think we need some more luck, 랜드.”

랜드 shifted to look over the 오지어’s shoulder. Beyond open space, in the alleyway that led to the barless door, three 트롤록s were peering cautiously out of the shadows toward the lighted windows. One woman was standing at a window; she did not seem to see the 트롤록s.

“So,” Selene said quietly. “It becomes a trap. These people may kill you if they take you. The 트롤록s surely will. But perhaps you can slay the 트롤록s too quickly for them to make any outcry. Perhaps you can stop the people from killing you to preserve their little secrets. You may not want greatness, but it will take a great man to do these things.”

“You don’t have to sound happy about it,” 랜드 said. He tried to stop thinking about how she smelled, how she felt, and the void almost surrounded him. He shook it away. The 트롤록s did not seem to have located them, yet. He settled back, staring at the nearest dark alleyway. Once they made a move toward it, the 트롤록s would surely see, and so would the woman at the window. It would be a race as to whether 트롤록s or Illuminators reached them first.

“Your greatness will make me happy.” Despite the words, Selene sounded angry. “Perhaps I should leave you to find your own way for a time. If you’ll not take greatness when it is in your grasp, perhaps you deserve to die.”

랜드 refused to look at her. “로이알, can you see if there’s another door down that alley?”

The 오지어 shook his head. “There is too much light here and too much dark there. If I were in the alley, yes.”

랜드 fingered the hilt of his sword. “Take Selene. As soon as you see a door—*if* you do—call out, and I’ll follow. If there isn’t a door at the end, you will have to lift her so she can reach the top of the wall and climb over.”

“All right, 랜드.” 로이알 sounded worried. “But when we move, those 트롤록s will come after us, no matter who is watching. Even if there is a door, they will be on our heels.”

“You let me worry about the 트롤록s.” *Three of them. I might do it, with the void.* The thought of *세이딘* decided him. Too many strange things had happened when he let the male half of the True Source come close. “I will follow as soon as I can. Go.” He turned to peer around the wall at the 트롤록s.

From the corner of his eye, he had an impression of 로이알’s bulk moving, of Selene’s white dress, half covered by his cloak. One of the 트롤록s beyond the tubes pointed to them excitedly, but still the three hesitated, glancing up at the window where the woman still watched. *Three of them. There has to be a way. Not the void. Not* 세이딘.

“There is a door!” came 로이알’s soft call. One of the 트롤록s took a step out of the shadows, and the others followed, gathering themselves. As from a distance, 랜드 heard the woman at the window cry out, and 로이알 shouted something.

Without thinking, 랜드 was on his feet. He had to stop the 트롤록s somehow, or they would run him down, and 로이알 and Selene. He snatched one of the smoldering sticks and hurled himself at the nearest tube. It tilted, started to fall over, and he caught the square wooden base; the tube pointed straight at the 트롤록s. They slowed uncertainly—the woman at the window screamed—and 랜드 touched the smoking end of the stick to the fuse right where it joined the tube.

The hollow thump came immediately, and the thick wooden base slammed against him, knocking him down. A roar like a thunderclap broke the night and a blinding burst of light tore away the dark.

Blinking, 랜드 staggered to his feet, coughing in thick, acrid smoke, ears ringing. He stared in amazement. Half the tubes and all of the racks lay on their sides, and one corner of the building beside which the 트롤록s had stood was simply gone, flames licking at ends of planks and rafters. Of the 트롤록s there was no sign.

Through the ringing in his ears, 랜드 heard shouts from the Illuminators in the building. He broke into a tottering run, lumbered into the alley. Halfway down it he stumbled over something and realized it was his cloak. He snatched it up without pausing. Behind him, the cries of the Illuminators filled the night.

로이알 was bouncing impatiently on his feet beside the open door. And he was alone.

“Where is Selene?” 랜드 demanded.

“She went back, 랜드. I tried to grab her, and she slipped right out of my hands.”

랜드 turned back toward the noise. Through the incessant sound in his ears, some of the shouts were barely distinguishable. There was light there, now, from the flames.

“The sand buckets! Fetch the sand buckets quickly!”

“This is disaster! Disaster!”

“Some of them went that way!”

로이알 grabbed 랜드’s shoulder. “You cannot help her, 랜드. Not by being taken yourself. We must go.” Someone appeared at the end of the alley, a shadow outlined by the glow of flames behind, and pointed toward them. “Come on, 랜드!”

랜드 let himself be pulled out of the door into the darkness. The fire faded behind them until it was only a glow in the night, and the lights of the Foregate came closer. 랜드 almost wished more 트롤록s would appear, something he could fight. But there was only the night breeze ruffling the grass.

“I tried to stop her,” 로이알 said. There was a long silence. “We really couldn’t have done anything. They would just have taken us, too.”

랜드 sighed. “I know, 로이알. You did what you could.” He walked backwards a few steps, staring at the glow. It seemed less; the Illuminators must be putting out the flames. “I have to help her somehow.” *How?* Saidin? *The Power?* He shivered. “I have to.”

They went through the Foregate by the lighted streets, wrapped in a silence that shut out the gaiety around them.

When they entered The Defender of the Dragonwall, the innkeeper held out his tray with a sealed parchment.

랜드 took it, and stared at the white seal. A crescent moon and stars. “Who left this? When?”

“An old woman, my Lord. Not a quarter of an hour gone. A servant, though she did not say from what House.” Cuale smiled as if inviting confidences.

“Thank you,” 랜드 said, still staring at the seal. The innkeeper watched them go upstairs with a thoughtful look.

Hurin took his pipe out of his mouth when 랜드 and 로이알 entered the room. Hurin had his short sword and sword-breaker on the table, wiping them with an oily rag. “You were long with the gleeman, my Lord. Is he well?”

랜드 gave a start. “What? 톰? Yes he’s. . . .” He broke open the seal with his thumb and read.

*When I think I know what you are going to do, you do something else. You are a dangerous man. Perhaps it will not be long before we are together again. Think of the Horn. Think of the glory. And think of me, for you are always mine.*

Again, it bore no signature but the flowing hand itself.

“Are all women crazy?” 랜드 demanded of the ceiling. Hurin shrugged. 랜드 threw himself into the other chair, the one sized for an 오지어; his feet dangled above the floor, but he did not care. He stared at the blanket-covered chest under the edge of 로이알’s bed. *Think of the glory.* “I wish Ingtar would come.”

CHAPTER 29
