CHAPTER 35

![](images/00413.jpg)

*스테딩 Tsofu*

The river hills on which the city of 케렌 stood gave way to flatter lands and forests when 랜드 and the others had ridden half a day, the 시엔나르ans still with their armor on the packhorses. There were no roads where they went, only a scattering of cart tracks, and few farms or villages. Verin pressed for speed, and Ingtar—grumbling constantly that they were letting themselves be tricked, that Fain would never have told them where he was really going, yet grumbling at the same time about riding in the opposite direction from Toman Head, as if part of him believed and Toman Head were not months away except by the way they took—Ingtar obliged her. The Gray Owl banner flew on the wind of their passage.

랜드 rode with grim determination, avoiding conversation with Verin. He had this thing to do—this duty, Ingtar would have called it—and then he could be free of 에스 세다이 once and for all. 페린 seemed to share something of his mood, staring straight ahead at nothing as they rode. When they finally stopped for the night at the edge of a forest, with full dark almost on them, 페린 asked 로이알 questions about the *stedding*. 트롤록s would not enter a *stedding;* would wolves? 로이알 replied shortly that it was only creatures of the Shadow that were reluctant to enter *stedding*. And 에스 세다이, of course, since they could not touch the True Source inside a *stedding*, or channel the 하나의 힘. The 오지어 himself appeared the most reluctant of all to go to 스테딩 Tsofu. 맷 was the only one who seemed eager, almost desperately so. His skin looked as if he had not seen the sun in a year, and his cheeks had begun to go hollow, though he said he felt ready to run a footrace. Verin put her hands on him for 치유 before he rolled into his blankets, and again before they mounted their horses in the morning, but it made no difference in how he looked. Even Hurin frowned when he looked at 맷.

The sun stood high on the second day when Verin suddenly sat up straight in her saddle and looked around. Beside her, Ingtar gave a start.

랜드 could not see anything different about the forest now surrounding them. The undergrowth was not too thick; they had found an easy way under the canopy of oak and hickory, blackgum and beech, pierced here and there by a tall pine or leatherleaf, or the white slash of a paperbark. But as he followed them, he suddenly felt a chill pass through him, as though he had leaped into a Waterwood pond in winter. It flashed through him and was gone, leaving behind a feeling of refreshment. And there was a dull and distant sense of loss, too, though he could not imagine of what.

Every rider, as he reached that point, gave a jerk or made some exclamation. Hurin’s mouth dropped open, and Uno whispered, “Bloody, flaming. . . .” Then he shook his head as if he could not think of anything else to say. There was a look of recognition in 페린’s yellow eyes.

로이알 took a deep, slow breath and let it out. “It feels . . . good . . . to be back in a *stedding*.”

Frowning, 랜드 looked around. He had expected a *stedding* to be somehow different, but except for that one chill, the forest was the same as what they had been riding through all day. There was the sudden sense of being rested, of course. Then an 오지어 stepped out from behind an oak.

She was shorter than 로이알—which meant she stood head and shoulders taller than 랜드—but with the same broad nose and big eyes, the same wide mouth and tufted ears. Her eyebrows were not so long as 로이알’s, though, and her features seemed delicate beside his, the tufts on her ears finer. She wore a long green dress and a green cloak embroidered with flowers, and carried a bunch of silverbell blossoms as if she had been gathering them. She looked at them calmly, waiting.

로이알 scrambled down from his tall horse and bowed hastily. 랜드 and the others did the same, if not so quickly as 로이알; even Verin inclined her head. 로이알 gave their names formally, but he did not mention the name of his *stedding*.

For a moment the 오지어 girl—랜드 was sure she was no older than 로이알—studied them, then smiled. “Be welcome to 스테딩 Tsofu.” Her voice was a lighter version of 로이알’s, too; the softer rumble of a smaller bumblebee. “I am 에리스, daughter of Iva daughter of Alar. Be welcome. We have had so few human visitors since the stonemasons left 케렌, and now so many at once. Why, we even had some of the 이동 People, though, of course, they left when the. . . . Oh, I talk too much. I will take you to the Elders. Only. . . .” She searched among them for the one in charge, and settled finally on Verin. “에스 세다이, you have so many men with you, and armed. Could you please leave some of them Outside? Forgive me, but it is always unsettling to have very many armed humans in the *stedding* at once.”

“Of course, 에리스,” Verin said. “Ingtar, will you see to it?”

Ingtar gave orders to Uno, and so it was that he and Hurin were the only 시엔나르ans to follow 에리스 deeper into the *stedding*.

Leading his horse like the others, 랜드 looked up as 로이알 came closer, with many glances at 에리스 up ahead with Verin and Ingtar. Hurin walked midway between, staring around in amazement, though 랜드 was not sure at what exactly. 로이알 bent to speak quietly. “Is she not beautiful, 랜드? And her voice sings.”

맷 snickered, but when 로이알 looked at him questioningly, he said, “Very pretty, 로이알. A little tall for my taste, you understand, but very pretty, I’m sure.”

로이알 frowned uncertainly, but nodded. “Yes, she is.” His expression lightened. “It does feel good to be back in a *stedding*. Not that the Longing was taking me, you understand.”

“The Longing?” 페린 said. “I do not understand, 로이알.”

“We 오지어 are bound to the *stedding*, 페린. It is said that before the 세계의 파멸, we could go where we wished for as long as we wished, like you humans, but that changed with the Breaking. 오지어 were scattered like every other people, and they could not find any of the *stedding* again. Everything was moved, everything changed. Mountains, rivers, even the seas.”

“Everybody knows about the Breaking,” 맷 said impatiently. “What does it have to do with this—this Longing?”

“It was during the Exile, while we wandered lost, that the Longing first came on us. The desire to know the *stedding* once more, to know our homes again. Many died of it.” 로이알 shook his head sadly. “More died than lived. When we finally began to find the *stedding* again, one at a time, in the years of the Covenant of the Ten Nations, it seemed we had defeated the Longing at last, but it had changed us, put seeds in us. Now, if an 오지어 is Outside too long, the Longing comes again; he begins to weaken, and he dies if he does not return.”

“Do you need to stay here awhile?” 랜드 asked anxiously. “There’s no need to kill yourself to go with us.”

“I will know it when it comes.” 로이알 laughed. “It will be long before it is strong enough to cause harm to me. Why, Dalar spent ten years among the Sea Folk without ever seeing a *stedding*, and she came safely home.”

An 오지어 woman appeared out of the trees, pausing a moment to speak with 에리스 and Verin. She looked Ingtar up and down and seemed to dismiss him, which made him blink. Her eyes swept across 로이알, flicked over Hurin and the Emond’s Fielders, before she went off into the forest again; 로이알 seemed to be trying to hide behind his horse. “Besides,” he said, peering cautiously across his saddle after her, “it is a dull life in the *stedding* compared to traveling with three *ta’veren*.”

“If you are going to start that again,” 맷 muttered, and 로이알 spoke up quickly. “Three friends, then. You are my friends, I hope.”

“I am,” 랜드 said simply, and 페린 nodded.

맷 laughed. “How could I not be friends with somebody who dices so badly?” He threw up his hands when 랜드 and 페린 looked at him. “Oh, all right. I like you, 로이알. You’re my friend. Just don’t go on about. . . . Aaah! Sometimes you’re as bad to be around as 랜드.” His voice sank to a mutter. “At least we’re safe here in a *stedding*.”

랜드 grimaced. He knew what 맷 meant. *Here in a* stedding, *where I can’t channel*.

페린 punched 맷’s shoulder, but looked sorry that he had when 맷 grimaced at him with that gaunt face.

It was the music 랜드 became aware of first, unseen flutes and fiddles in a jolly tune that floated through the trees, and deep voices singing and laughing.

> “Clear the field, smooth it low.

> Let no weed or stubble stand.

> Here we labor, here we toil,

> here the towering trees will grow.”

Almost at the same moment he realized that the huge shape he was seeing through the trees was itself a tree, with a ridged, buttressed trunk that must have been twenty paces thick. Gaping, he followed it up with his eyes, up through the forest canopy, to branches spreading like the top of a gigantic mushroom a good hundred paces above the ground. And beyond it were taller still.

“Burn me,” 맷 breathed. “You could build ten houses from just one of those. Fifty houses.”

“Cut down a Great Tree?” 로이알 sounded scandalized, and more than a little angry. His ears were stiff and still, his long eyebrows down on his cheeks. “We never cut down one of the Great Trees, not unless it dies, and they almost never do. Few survived the Breaking, but some of the largest were seedlings during the 전설의 시대.”

“I’m sorry,” 맷 said. “I was just saying how big they are. I won’t hurt your trees.” 로이알 nodded, seeming mollified.

More 오지어 appeared now, walking among the trees. Most seemed intent on whatever they were about; though all looked at the newcomers, and even gave a friendly nod or a small bow, none stopped or spoke. They had a curious way of moving, in some manner blending a careful deliberateness with an almost childlike carefree joyfulness. They knew and liked who and what they were and where they were, and they seemed at peace with themselves and everything around them. 랜드 found himself envying them.

Few of the 오지어 men were any taller than 로이알, but it was easy to pick out the older men; one and all they wore mustaches as long as their dangling eyebrows and narrow beards under their chins. All of the younger were smooth-shaven, like 로이알. Many of the men were in their shirtsleeves, and carried shovels and mattocks or saws and buckets of pitch; the others wore plain coats that buttoned to the neck and flared about their knees like kilts. The women seemed to favor embroidered flowers, and many wore flowers in their hair, too. The embroidery was limited to the cloaks of the younger women; the older women’s dresses were embroidered, as well, and some women with gray hair had flowers and vines from neck to hem. A handful of the 오지어, women and girls for the most part, did seem to take special notice of 로이알; he walked staring straight ahead, ears twitching more wildly the further they went.

랜드 was startled to see an 오지어 apparently walking up out of the ground, out of one of the grassy, wildflower-covered mounds that lay scattered all among the trees here. Then he saw windows in the mounds, and an 오지어 woman standing at one apparently rolling a piecrust, and realized he was looking at 오지어 houses. The window frames were stone, but they not only seemed natural formations, they appeared to have been sculpted by wind and water over generations.

The Great Trees, with their massive trunks and spreading roots as thick as horses, needed a great deal of room between them, but several grew right in the town. Dirt ramps took the paths over the roots. In fact, aside from the pathways, the only way to tell town from forest at a glance was a large open space in the center of the town, around what could only be the stump of one of the Great Trees. Nearly a hundred paces across, its surface was polished as smooth as any floor, and there were steps built up to it at several places. 랜드 was imagining how tall that tree had been when 에리스 spoke loudly enough for them all to hear.

“Here come our other guests.”

Three human women came walking around the side of the huge stump. The youngest was carrying a wooden bowl.

“아일,” Ingtar said. “창의 처녀들. As well I *did* leave Masema with the others.” Yet he stepped away from Verin and 에리스, and reached over his shoulder to loosen his sword in its scabbard.

랜드 studied the 아일 with an uneasy curiosity. They were what too many people had tried to tell him he was. Two of the women were mature, the other little more than a girl, but all three were tall for women. Their short-cut hair ranged from a reddish brown to almost golden, with a narrow, shoulder-length tail left long at the back. They wore loose breeches tucked into soft boots, and all their clothes were some shade of brown or gray or green; he thought the garments would fade into rock or woods almost as well as a 감시자’s cloak. Short bows poked over their shoulders, quivers and long knives hung at their belts, and each carried a small, round shield of hide and a cluster of spears with short shafts and long points. Even the youngest moved with a grace that suggested she knew how to use the weapons she carried.

Abruptly the women became aware of the other humans; they seemed as startled at being startled as they did at the sight of 랜드 and the others, but they moved like lightning. The youngest one shouted, “시엔나르ans!” and turned to set the bowl carefully behind her. The other two quickly lifted brown cloths from around their shoulders, wrapping them around their heads instead. The older women were raising black veils across their faces, hiding everything but their eyes, and the youngest straightened to imitate them. Crouching low, they advanced at a deliberate pace, shields held forward with their clusters of spears, except for the one each woman held ready in her other hand.

Ingtar’s sword came out of its sheath. “Stand clear, 에스 세다이. 에리스, stand clear.” Hurin snatched out his sword-breaker, wavered between cudgel and sword for his other hand; after another glance at the 아일’s spears, he chose the sword.

“You must not,” the 오지어 girl protested. Wringing her hands, she turned from Ingtar to the 아일 and back. “You must not.”

랜드 realized the heron-mark blade was in his hands. 페린 had his axe half out of the loop at his belt and was hesitating, shaking his head.

“Are you two crazy?” 맷 demanded. His bow still slanted across his back. “I don’t care if they are 아일, they’re women.”

“Stop this!” Verin demanded. “Stop this immediately!” The 아일 never broke stride, and the 에스 세다이 clenched her fists in frustration.

맷 moved back to put a foot in his stirrup. “I’m leaving,” he announced. “You hear me? I’m not staying to let them stick those things in me, and I am not going to shoot a woman!”

“The Pact!” 로이알 was shouting. “Remember the Pact!” It had no more effect than the continued pleas from Verin and 에리스.

랜드 noticed that both the 에스 세다이 and the 오지어 girl were keeping well out of the 아일’s way. He wondered if 맷 had the right idea. He was not sure he could hurt a woman even if she *was* trying to kill him. What decided him was the thought that even if he did manage to reach Red’s saddle, the 아일 were now no more than thirty paces away. He suspected those short spears could be thrown that far. As the women came closer, still crouching, spears ready, he stopped worrying about not hurting them and began worrying about how to stop them from hurting him.

Nervously, he sought the void, and it came. And the distant thought floated outside it that it was only the void. The glow of *세이딘* was not there. The emptiness was more empty than he ever remembered, vaster, like a hunger great enough to consume him. A hunger for more; there was *supposed* to be something more.

Abruptly an 오지어 strode in between the two groups, his narrow beard quivering. “What is the meaning of this? Put up your weapons.” He sounded scandalized. “For you”—his glare took in Ingtar and Hurin, 랜드 and 페린, and did not spare 맷 for all his empty hands—“there is some excuse, but for you—” He rounded on the 아일 women, who had stopped their advance. “Have you forgotten the Pact?”

The women uncovered their heads and faces so hastily that it seemed they were trying to pretend they had never been covered. The girl’s face was bright red, and the other women looked abashed. One of the older women, the one with the reddish hair, said, “Forgive us, Treebrother. We remember the Pact, and we would not have bared steel, but we are in the land of the Treekillers, where every hand is against us, and we saw armed men.” Her eyes were gray, 랜드 saw, like his own.

“You are in a *stedding*, Rhian,” the 오지어 said gently. “Everyone is safe in the *stedding*, little sister. There is no fighting here, and no hand raised against another.” She nodded, ashamed, and the 오지어 looked at Ingtar and the others.

Ingtar sheathed his sword, and 랜드 did the same, though not so quickly as Hurin, who looked almost as embarrassed as the 아일. 페린 had never gotten his axe all the way out. As he took hand from hilt, 랜드 let the void go, too, and shivered. The void went, but it left behind a slowly fading echo of the emptiness all through him, and a desire for something to fill it.

The 오지어 turned to Verin and bowed. “에스 세다이, I am Juin, son of Lacel son of Laud. I have come to take you to the Elders. They would know why an 에스 세다이 comes among us, with armed men and one of our own youths.” 로이알 hunched his shoulders as if trying to disappear.

Verin gave the 아일 a regretful look, as if she wanted to talk with them, then motioned Juin to lead, and he took her away without another word or even the first look at 로이알.

For a few moments, 랜드 and the others stood facing the three 아일 women uneasily. At least, 랜드 knew he was uneasy. Ingtar seemed steady as a stone, with no more expression than one. The 아일 might have unveiled their faces, but they still had spears in their hands, and they studied the four men as though trying to see inside them. 랜드 in particular received increasingly angry looks. He heard the youngest woman mutter, “He is wearing a sword,” in tones of mingled horror and contempt. Then the three were leaving, stopping to retrieve the wooden bowl and looking over their shoulders at 랜드 and the others until they vanished among the trees.

“창의 처녀들,” Ingtar muttered. “I never thought they’d stop once they veiled their faces. Certainly not for a few words.” He looked at 랜드 and his two friends. “You should see a charge by Red Shields, or Stone Dogs. As easy to stop as an avalanche.”

“They would not break the Pact once it was recalled to them,” 에리스 said, smiling. “They came for sung wood.” A note of pride entered her voice. “We have two Treesingers in 스테딩 Tsofu. They are rare, now. I have heard that 스테딩 Shangtai has a young Treesinger who is very talented, but we have two.” 로이알 blushed, but she did not appear to notice. “If you will come with me, I will show you where you may wait until the Elders have spoken.”

As they followed her, 페린 murmured, “Sung wood, my left foot. Those 아일 are searching for He Who Comes With the Dawn.”

And 맷 added dryly, “They’re looking for you, 랜드.”

“For me! That is crazy. What makes you think—”

He cut off as 에리스 showed them down the steps of a wildflower-covered house apparently set aside for human guests. The rooms were twenty paces from stone wall to stone wall, with painted ceilings a good two spans above the floor, but the 오지어 had done their best making something that would be comfortable for humans. Even so, the furniture was a little too large for comfort, the chairs tall enough to lift a man’s heels off the floor, the table higher than 랜드’s waist. Hurin, at least, could have walked erect into the stone fireplace, which seemed to have been worn by water rather than made by hands. 에리스 eyed 로이알 doubtfully, but he waved away her concern and pulled one of the chairs into the corner least easily seen from the door.

As soon as the 오지어 girl left, 랜드 got 맷 and 페린 over to one side. “What do you mean they’re looking for me? Why? For what reason? They looked right at me, and went away.”

“They looked at you,” 맷 said with a grin, “like you hadn’t bathed in a month, and had doused yourself with sheepdip besides.” His grin faded. “But they could be looking for you. We met another 아일.”

랜드 listened in growing amazement to their tale of the meeting in 동족 살해자’s Dagger. 맷 told most of it, with 페린 putting in a correcting word now and again when he embellished too much. 맷 made a great show of how dangerous the 아일man had been, and how close the meeting had come to a fight.

“And since you’re the only 아일 we know,” he finished, “well, it could be you. Ingtar says 아일 never live outside the 황무지, so you must be the only one.”

“I don’t think that’s funny, 맷,” 랜드 growled. “I am not an 아일.” *The Amyrlin said you are. Ingtar thinks you are. Tam said. . . . He was sick, fevered*. They had severed the roots he had thought he had, the 에스 세다이 and Tam between them, though Tam had been too sick to know what he was saying. They had cut him loose to tumble before the wind, then offered him something new to hold on to. False Dragon. 아일. He could not claim those for roots. He would not. “Maybe I don’t belong to anyone. But the 두 강 is the only home I know.”
“I didn’t mean anything,” 맷 protested. “It’s just. . . . Burn me, Ingtar says you are. Masema says you are. Urien could have been your cousin, and if Rhian put on a dress and said she was your aunt, you’d believe it yourself. Oh, all right. Don’t look at me like that, 페린. If he wants to say he isn’t, all right. What difference does it make, anyway?” 페린 shook his head.

오지어 girls brought water and towels for washing faces and hands, and cheese and fruit and wine, with pewter goblets a little too large to be comfortable in the hand. Other 오지어 women came, too, their dresses all embroidered. One by one they appeared, a dozen of them all told, to ask if the humans were comfortable, if they needed anything. Each turned her attentions to 로이알 just before she left. He gave his answers respectfully but in as few words as 랜드 had ever heard him use, standing with an 오지어-sized, wood-bound book clutched to his chest like a shield, and when they went, he huddled in his chair with the book held up in front of his face. The books in the house were one thing not sized for humans.

“Just smell this air, Lord 랜드,” Hurin said, filling his lungs with a smile. His feet dangled from one of the chairs at the table; he swung them like a boy. “I never thought most places smelled bad, but this. . . . Lord 랜드, I don’t think there’s *ever* been any killing here. Not even any hurting, except by accident.”

“The *stedding* are supposed to be safe for everyone,” 랜드 said. He was watching 로이알. “That’s what the stories say, anyway.” He swallowed a last bit of white cheese and went over to the 오지어. 맷 followed with a goblet in his hand. “What’s the matter, 로이알?” 랜드 said. “You’ve been as nervous as a cat in a dogyard ever since we came here.”

“It is nothing,” 로이알 said, giving the door an uneasy glance from the corner of his eye.

“Are you afraid they’ll find out you left 스테딩 Shangtai without permission from your Elders?”

로이알 looked around wildly, the tufts on his ears vibrating. “Don’t say that,” he hissed. “Not where anyone can hear. If they found out. . . .” With a heavy sigh, he slumped back, looking from 랜드 to 맷. “I don’t know how humans do it, but among 오지어. . . . If a girl sees a boy she likes, she goes to her mother. Or sometimes the mother sees someone she thinks is suitable. In any case, if they agree, the girl’s mother goes to the boy’s mother, and the next thing the boy knows, his marriage is all arranged.”

“Doesn’t the boy have any say in it?” 맷 asked incredulously.

“None. The women always say we would spend our lives married to the trees if it was left to us.” 로이알 shifted, grimacing. “Half of our marriages take place between *stedding;* groups of young 오지어 visit from *stedding* to *stedding* so they can see, and be seen. If they discover I’m Outside without permission, the Elders will almost certainly decide I need a wife to settle me down. Before I know it, they’ll have sent a message to 스테딩 Shangtai, to my mother, and she will come here and have me married before she washes off the dust of her journey. She’s always said I am too hasty and need a wife. I think she was looking when I left. Whatever wife she chooses for me . . . well, any wife at all won’t let me go back Outside until I have gray in my beard. Wives always say no man should be allowed Outside until he’s settled enough to control his temper.”

맷 gave a guffaw loud enough to draw every head, but at 로이알’s frantic gesture he spoke softly. “Among us, men do the choosing, and no wife can stop a man doing what he wants.”

랜드 frowned, remembering how 에그웨인 had begun following him around when they were both little. It was then that Mistress al’Vere had begun taking a special interest in him, more than in any of the other boys. Later, some girls would dance with him on feastdays and some would not, and those who would were always 에그웨인’s friends, while those who would not were girls 에그웨인 did not like. He also seemed to remember Mistress al’Vere taking Tam aside—*And she was muttering about Tam not having a wife for her to talk to!*—and after that, Tam and everyone else had acted as if he and 에그웨인 were promised, even though they had not knelt before the Women’s Circle to say the words. He had never thought about it this way before; things between 에그웨인 and him had always just seemed to be the way they were, and that was that.

“I think we do it the same way,” he muttered, and when 맷 laughed, he added, “Do you remember your father ever doing anything your mother really didn’t want him to?” 맷 opened his mouth with a grin, then frowned thoughtfully and closed it again.

Juin came down the steps from outside. “If you please, will all of you come with me? The Elders would see you.” He did not look at 로이알, but 로이알 still almost dropped the book.

“If the Elders try to make you stay,” 랜드 said, “we’ll say we need you to go with us.”

“I’ll bet it isn’t about you at all,” 맷 said. “I’ll bet they are just going to say we can use the Waygate.” He shook himself, and his voice fell even lower. “We really have to do it, don’t we.” It was not a question.

“Stay and get married, or travel the Ways.” 로이알 grimaced ruefully. “Life is very unsettling with *ta’veren* for friends.”

CHAPTER 36

![](images/00371.jpg)

*Among the Elders*

As Juin took them through the 오지어 town, 랜드 saw that 로이알 was growing more and more anxious. 로이알’s ears were as stiff as his back; his eyes grew bigger every time he saw another 오지어 looking at him, especially the women and girls, and a large number of them did seem to take notice of him. He looked as if he expected his own execution.

*What Might Be*

It was so easy, now. The flame consumed fear and passion and was gone almost before he thought to form it. Gone, leaving only emptiness, and shining *세이딘*, sickening, tantalizing, stomach-turning, seductive. He . . . reached for it . . . and it filled him, made him alive. He did not move a muscle, but he felt as if he were quivering with the rush of the 하나의 힘 into him. The symbol formed itself, an arrow piercing a circle, floating just beyond the void, as hard as the stuff it was carved on. He let the 하나의 힘 flow through him to the symbol.

The symbol shimmered, flickered.

“Something is happening,” Verin said. “Something . . .”

The world flickered.

The iron lock spun across the farmhouse floor, and 랜드 dropped the hot teakettle as a huge figure with ram’s horns on its head loomed in the doorway with the darkness of Winternight behind it.

“Run!” Tam shouted. His sword flashed, and the 트롤록 toppled, but it grappled with Tam as it fell, pulling him down.

More crowded in at the door, black-mailed shapes with human faces distorted with muzzles and beaks and horns, oddly curved swords stabbing at Tam as he tried to struggle to his feet, spiked axes swinging, red blood on steel.

“Father!” 랜드 screamed. Clawing his belt knife from its sheath, he threw himself over the table to help his father, and screamed again as the first sword ran through his chest.

Blood bubbled up into his mouth, and a voice whispered inside his head, *I have won again, 르웨어스 테린*.

*Flicker*.

랜드 struggled to hold the symbol, dimly aware of Verin’s voice. “. . . is not . . .”

The Power flooded.

*Flicker*.

랜드 was happy after he married 에그웨인, and tried to not let the moods take him, the times when he thought there should have been something more, something different. News of the world outside came into the 두 강 with peddlers, and merchants come to buy wool and tabac, always news of fresh troubles, of wars and false 용 everywhere. There was a year when neither merchants nor peddlers came, and when they returned the next they brought word that 아투르 호크윙’s armies had come back, or their descendants, at least. The old nations were broken, it was said, and the world’s new masters, who used chained 에스 세다이 in their battles, had torn down the 백색 탑 and salted the ground where 타르 발론 had stood. There were no more 에스 세다이.

It all made little difference in the 두 강. Crops still had to be planted, sheep sheared, lambs tended. Tam had grandsons and granddaughters to dandle on his knee before he was laid to rest beside his wife, and the old farmhouse grew new rooms. 에그웨인 became Wisdom, and most thought she was even better than the old Wisdom, 니나브 al’Maera, had been. It was as well she was, for her cures that worked so miraculously on others were only just able to keep 랜드 alive from the sickness that constantly seemed to threaten him. His moods grew worse, blacker, and he raged that this was not what was meant to be. 에그웨인 grew frightened when the moods were on him, for strange things sometimes happened when he was at his bleakest—lightning storms she had not heard listening to the wind, wildfires in the forest—but she loved him and cared for him and kept him sane, though some muttered that 랜드 al’Thor was crazy and dangerous.

When she died, he sat alone for long hours by her grave, tears soaking his gray-flecked beard. His sickness came back, and he wasted; he lost the last two fingers on his right hand and one on his left, his ears looked like scars, and men muttered that he smelled of decay. His blackness deepened.

Yet when the dire news came, none refused to accept him at their side. 트롤록s and 페이드s and things undreamed of had burst out of the 황무지, and the world’s new masters were being thrown back, for all the powers they wielded. So 랜드 took up the bow he had just fingers enough left to shoot and limped with those who marched north to the River Taren, men from every village, farm, and corner of the 두 강, with their bows, and axes, and boarspears, and swords that had lain rusting in attics. 랜드 wore a sword, too, with a heron on the blade, that he had found after Tam died, though he knew nothing of how to use it. Women came, too, shouldering what weapons they could find, marching alongside the men. Some laughed, saying that they had the strange feeling they had done this before.

And at the Taren the people of the 두 강 met the invaders, endless ranks of 트롤록s led by nightmare 페이드s beneath a dead black banner that seemed to eat the light. 랜드 saw that banner and thought the madness had taken him again, for it seemed that this was what he had been born for, to fight that banner. He sent every arrow at it, straight as his skill and the void would serve, never worrying about the 트롤록s forcing their way across the river, or the men and women dying to either side of him. It was one of those 트롤록s that ran him through, before it loped howling for blood deeper into the 두 강. And as he lay on the bank of the Taren, watching the sky seem to grow dark at noon, breath coming ever slower, he heard a voice say, *I have won again, 르웨어스 테린*.

*Flicker*.

The arrow-and-circle contorted into parallel wavy lines, and he fought it back again.

Verin’s voice. “. . . right. Something . . .”

The Power raged.

*Flicker*.

Tam tried to console 랜드 when 에그웨인 took sick and died just a week before their wedding. 니나브 tried, too, but she was shaken herself, since for all her skill she had no idea what it was that had killed the girl. 랜드 had sat outside 에그웨인’s house while she died, and there seemed to be nowhere in Emond’s Field he could go that he did not still hear her screaming. He knew he could not stay. Tam gave him a sword with a heron-mark blade, and though he explained little of how a shepherd in the 두 강 had come by such a thing, he taught 랜드 how to use it. On the day 랜드 left, Tam gave him a letter he said might get 랜드 taken into the army of 일리안, and hugged him, and said, “I’ve never had another son, or wanted another. Come back with a wife like I did, if you can, boy, but come back in any case.”

랜드 had his money stolen in Baerlon, though, and his letter of introduction, and almost his sword, and he met a woman called 민 who told him such crazy things about himself that he finally left the city to get away from her. Eventually his wanderings brought him to Caemlyn, and there his skill with the sword earned him a place in the Queen’s Guards. Sometimes he found himself looking at the Daughter-Heir, 엘레인, and at such times he was filled with odd thoughts that this was not the way things were supposed to be, that there should be something more to his life. 엘레인 did not look at him, of course; she married a 타이런 prince, though she did not seem happy in it. 랜드 was just a soldier, once a shepherd from a small village so far toward the western border that only lines on a map any longer truly connected it to 안도르. Besides, he had a dark reputation, as a man of violent moods.

Some said he was mad, and in ordinary times perhaps not even his skill with the sword would have kept him in the Guard, but these were not ordinary times. False 용 sprang up like weeds. Every time one was taken down, two more proclaimed themselves, or three, till every nation was torn by war. And 랜드’s star rose, for he had learned the secret of his madness, a secret he knew he had to keep and did. He could channel. There were always places, times, in a battle when a little channeling, not big enough to be noticed in the confusion, could make luck. Sometimes it worked, this channeling, and sometimes not, but it worked often enough. He knew he was mad, and did not care. A wasting sickness came on him, and he did not care about that, either, and neither did anyone else, for word had come that 아투르 호크윙’s armies had returned to reclaim the land.

랜드 led a thousand men when the Queen’s Guards crossed the Mountains of Mist—he never thought of turning aside to visit the 두 강; he seldom thought of the 두 강 at all, anymore—and he commanded the Guard when the shattered remnants retreated back across the mountains. The length of 안도르 he fought and fell back, amid hordes of fleeing refugees, until at last he came to Caemlyn. Many of the people of Caemlyn had fled already, and many counseled the army to retreat further, but 엘레인 was Queen, now, and vowed she would not leave Caemlyn. She would not look at his ruined face, scarred by his sickness, but he could not leave her, and so what was left of the Queen’s Guards prepared to defend the Queen while her people ran.

The Power came to him during the battle for Caemlyn, and he hurled lightning and fire among the invaders, and split the earth under their feet, yet the feeling came again, too, that he had been born for something else. For all he did, there were too many of the enemy to stop, and they also had those who could channel. At last, a lightning bolt hurled 랜드 from the Palace wall, broken, bleeding, and burned, and as his last breath rattled in his throat, he heard a voice whisper, *I have won again, 르웨어스 테린*.

*Flicker*.

랜드 struggled to hold the void as it quivered under the hammer blows of the world flickering, to hold the one symbol as a thousand of them darted along the surface of the void. He struggled to hold on to any one symbol.

“. . . is wrong!” Verin screamed.

The Power was everything.

*Flicker. Flicker. Flicker. Flicker. Flicker. Flicker*.

He was a soldier. He was a shepherd. He was a beggar, and a king. He was farmer, gleeman, sailor, carpenter. He was born, lived, and died an 아일. He died mad, he died rotting, he died of sickness, accident, age. He was executed, and multitudes cheered his death. He proclaimed himself the 용의 환생 and flung his banner across the sky; he ran from the Power and hid; he lived and died never knowing. He held off the madness and the sickness for years; he succumbed between two winters. Sometimes 모이라인 came and took him away from the 두 강, alone or with those of his friends who had survived Winternight; sometimes she did not. Sometimes other 에스 세다이 came for him. Sometimes the 적색 아자. 에그웨인 married him; 에그웨인, stern-faced in the stole of the 아미를린 석좌, led the 에스 세다이 who gentled him; 에그웨인, with tears in her eyes, plunged a dagger into his heart, and he thanked her as he died. He loved other women, married other women. 엘레인, and 민, and a fair-haired farmer’s daughter met on the road to Caemlyn, and women he had never seen before he lived those lives. A hundred lives. More. So many he could not count them. And at the end of every life, as he lay dying, as he drew his final breath, a voice whispered in his ear. *I have won again, 르웨어스 테린. Flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker flicker*.

The void vanished, contact with *세이딘* fled, and 랜드 fell with a thud that would have knocked the breath out of him if he had not already been half numb. He felt rough stone under his cheek, and his hands. It was cold.

He was aware of Verin, struggling from her back to hands and knees. He heard someone vomit roughly, and raised his head. Uno was kneeling on the ground, scrubbing the back of his hand across his mouth. Everyone was down, and the horses stood stiff-legged and quivering, eyes wild and rolling. Ingtar had his sword out, gripping the hilt so hard the blade shook, staring at nothing. 로이알 sat sprawled, wide-eyed and stunned. 맷 was huddled in a ball with his arms wrapped around his head, and 페린 had his fingers dug into his face as if he wanted to rip away whatever he had seen, or perhaps rip out the eyes that had seen it. None of the soldiers were any better. Masema wept openly, tears streaming down his face, and Hurin was looking around as if for a place to run.

“What . . . ?” 랜드 stopped to swallow. He was lying on rough, weathered stone half buried in the dirt. “What happened?”

“A surge of the 하나의 힘.” The 에스 세다이 tottered to her feet and pulled her cloak tight with a shiver. “It was as if we were being forced . . . pushed. . . . It seemed to come out of nowhere. You must learn to control it. You must! That much of the Power could burn you to a cinder.”

“Verin, I. . . . I lived. . . . I was. . . .” He realized the stone under him was rounded. The Portal Stone. Hastily, shakily, he pushed himself to his feet. “Verin, I lived and died, I don’t know how many times. Every time it was different, but it was me. It was me.”

“The Lines that join the Worlds That Might Be, laid by those who knew the Numbers of Chaos.” Verin shuddered; she seemed to be talking to herself. “I’ve never heard it, but there is no reason we would not be born in those worlds, yet the lives we lived would be different lives. Of course. Different lives for the different ways things might have happened.”

“Is that what happened? I . . . we . . . saw how our lives could have been?” *I have won again, 르웨어스 테린. No! I am 랜드 al’Thor!*

Verin gave herself a shake and looked at him. “Does it surprise you that your life might go differently if you made different choices, or different things happened to you? Though I never thought I—Well. The important thing is, we are here. Though not as we hoped.”

“Where is here?” he demanded. The woods of 스테딩 Tsofu were gone, replaced by rolling land. There seemed to be forest not far to the west, and a few hills. It had been high in the day when they gathered around the Stone in the *stedding* but here the sun stood low toward afternoon in a gray sky. The handful of trees nearby were bare branched, or else held a few leaves bright with color. A cold wind gusted from the east, sending leaves scurrying across the ground.

“Toman Head,” Verin said. “This is the Stone I visited. You should not have tried to bring us directly here. I don’t know what went wrong—I don’t suppose I ever will—but from the trees, I would say it is well into late autumn. 랜드, we haven’t gained any time by it. We’ve lost time. I would say we have easily spent four months in coming here.”

“But I didn’t—”

“You must let me guide you in these things. I cannot teach you, it’s true, but perhaps I can at least keep you from killing yourself—and the rest of us—by overreaching. Even if you do not kill yourself, if the 용의 환생 burns himself out like a guttering candle, who will face the 어둠의 존재 then?” She did not wait for him to renew his protests, but went to Ingtar instead.

The 시엔나르an gave a start when she touched his arm, and looked at her with frantic eyes. “I walk in the Light,” he said hoarsely. “I will find the 발레르의 뿔 and pull down 세이올 굴’s power. I will!”

“Of course you will,” she said soothingly. She took his face in her hands, and he drew a sudden breath, abruptly recovering from whatever had held him. Except that memory still lay in his eyes. “There,” she said. “That will do for you. I will see how I can help the rest. We may still recover the Horn, but our path has not grown smoother.”

As she started around among the others, stopping briefly by each, 랜드 went to his friends. When he tried to straighten 맷, 맷 jerked and stared at him, then grabbed 랜드’s coat with both hands. “랜드, I’d never tell anyone about—about you. I wouldn’t betray you. You have to believe that!” He looked worse than ever, but 랜드 thought it was mostly fright.

“I do,” 랜드 said. He wondered what lives 맷 had lived, and what he had done. *He must have told someone, or he wouldn’t be so anxious about it.* He could not hold it against him. Those had been other 맷s, not this one. Besides, after some of the alternatives he had seen for himself. . . . “I believe you. 페린?”

The curly-haired youth dropped his hands from his face with a sigh. Red marks scored his forehead and cheeks where his nails had dug in. His yellow eyes hid his thoughts. “We don’t have many choices really, do we, 랜드? Whatever happens, whatever we do, some things are almost always the same.” He let out another long breath. “Where are we? Is this one of those worlds you and Hurin were talking about?”

“It’s Toman Head,” 랜드 told him. “In our world. Or so Verin says. And it is autumn.”

맷 looked worried. “How could—? No, I don’t want to know how it happened. But how are we going to find Fain and the dagger now? He could be anywhere by this time.”

“He’s here,” 랜드 assured him. He hoped he was right. Fain had had time to take ship for anyplace he wanted to go. Time to ride to Emond’s Field. Or 타르 발론. *Please, Light, he didn’t get tired of waiting. If he’s hurt 에그웨인, or anybody in Emond’s Field, I’ll. . . . Light burn me, I tried to come in time.*

“The larger towns on Toman Head are all west of here,” Verin announced loudly enough for all to hear. Everyone was on their feet again, except for 랜드 and his two friends; she came and put her hands on 맷 as she spoke. “Not that there are many villages large enough to call towns. If we are to find any trace of the 어둠의 친구들, to the west is the place to begin. And I think we should not waste the daylight sitting here.”

When 맷 blinked and stood up—he still looked ill, but he moved spryly—she put her hands on 페린. 랜드 backed away when she reached for him.

“Don’t be foolish,” she told him.

“I don’t want your help,” he said quietly. “Or any 에스 세다이 help.”

Her lips twitched. “As you wish.”

They mounted immediately and rode west, leaving the Portal Stone behind. No one protested, 랜드 least of all. *Light, let me not be too late.*

*Practice*

Sitting cross-legged on her bed in her white dress, 에그웨인 made three tiny balls of light weave patterns above her hands. She was not supposed to do this without at least one of the 허락받은 자 to supervise, but 니나브, glaring and striding up and down in front of the small fireplace, did after all wear the Serpent ring given to the 허락받은 자, and her white dress had the colored rings encircling the hem, even if she was not allowed to try to teach anyone yet. And 에그웨인 had found over these last thirteen weeks that she could not resist. She knew how easy it was to touch *세다르* now. She could always feel it there, waiting for her, like the smell of perfume or the feel of silk, drawing her, drawing her. And once she did touch it, she could rarely stop from channeling, or at least trying to. She failed almost as often as she succeeded, but that was only another spur to keep on.

It often frightened her. How much she wanted to channel frightened her, and how drab and dreary she felt when she was not channeling, compared to when she was. She wanted to drink it all in, despite the cautions about burning herself out, and that wanting frightened her most of all. Sometimes she wished she had never come to 타르 발론. But the fright could not make her stop for long, any more than the fear of being caught by an 에스 세다이 or by any of the 허락받은 자 beside 니나브.

It was safe enough here, though, in her own room. 민 was there, sitting on the three-legged stool watching her, but she knew 민 well enough now to know 민 would never report her. She thought she was lucky to have made two good friends since coming to 타르 발론.
It was a little, windowless room, as all 수련생s’ rooms were. Three short paces took 니나브 from wall to white-plastered wall; 니나브’s own room was much larger, but since she had made no friends among the other 허락받은 자, she came to 에그웨인’s room when she needed someone to talk to, even as now when she did not talk at all. The tiny fire on the narrow hearth handily kept the first chill of approaching autumn at bay, though 에그웨인 was sure it would not serve so well when winter came. A small table for study completed the furnishings, and her belongings hung neatly on a row of pegs on the wall or sat on the short shelf above the table. Novices were usually kept too busy to spend time in their rooms, but today was a freeday, only the third since she and 니나브 had come to the 백색 탑.

“Else was making calf’s eyes at 갈라드 today while he was working with the 감시자s,” 민 said, rocking the stool on two legs.

The small balls faltered for an instant above 에그웨인’s hands. “She can look at whoever she wants,” 에그웨인 said casually. “I can’t imagine why I would be interested.”

“No reason, I suppose. He is awfully handsome, if you don’t mind him being so rigid. Very nice to look at, especially with his shirt off.”

The balls spun furiously. “I certainly have no desire to look at 갈라드, with or without his shirt.”

“I shouldn’t tease you,” 민 said contritely. “I’m sorry for that. But you do like to look at him—don’t grimace at me like that—and so does nearly every woman in the 백색 탑 who isn’t a Red. I’ve seen 에스 세다이 down at the practice yards when he’s working forms, especially Greens. Checking on their 감시자s, they say, but I don’t see so many when 갈라드 isn’t there. Even the cooks and maids come out to watch him.”

The balls stopped dead, and for a moment 에그웨인 stared at them. They vanished. Suddenly she giggled. “He *is* good-looking, isn’t he? Even when he walks he looks as if he’s dancing.” The color in her cheeks deepened. “I know I shouldn’t stare at him, but I can’t help myself.”

“I can’t either,” 민 said, “and I can see what he is like.”

“But if he is good—?”

“에그웨인, 갈라드 is so good he’d make you tear your hair out. He’d hurt a person because he had to serve a greater good. He wouldn’t even notice who was hurt, because he’d be so intent on the other, but if he did, he would expect them to understand and think it was all well and right.”

“I suppose you know,” 에그웨인 said. She had seen 민’s ability to look at people and read all sorts of things about them; 민 did not tell everything she saw, and she did not always see anything, but there had been enough for 에그웨인 to believe. She glanced at 니나브—the other woman was still pacing, muttering to herself—then reached for *세다르* again and resumed her juggling in a desultory fashion.

민 shrugged. “I guess I might as well tell you. He didn’t even notice what Else was doing. He asked her if she knew whether you might be walking the South Garden after supper, since today is a freeday. I felt sorry for her.”

“Poor Else,” 에그웨인 murmured, and the balls of light became more lively above her hands. 민 laughed.

The door banged open, caught by the wind. 에그웨인 gave a yelp and let the balls vanish before she saw it was only 엘레인.

The golden-haired Daughter-Heir of 안도르 pushed the door shut and hung up her cloak on a peg. “I just heard,” she said. “The rumors are true. King Galldrian is dead. That makes it a war of succession.”

민 snorted. “Civil war. War of succession. A lot of silly names for the same thing. Do you mind if we don’t talk about it? That’s all we hear. War in 케렌. War on Toman Head. They may have caught the false Dragon in 살다에아, but there’s still war in 티어. Most of it is rumors, anyway. Yesterday, I heard one of the cooks saying she’d heard 아투르 호크윙 was marching on Tanchico. 아투르 호크윙!”

“I thought you did not want to talk about it,” 에그웨인 said.

“I saw 로가인,” 엘레인 said. “He was sitting on a bench in the Inner Court, crying. He ran when he saw me. I cannot help feeling sorry for him.”

“Better he cries than the rest of us, 엘레인,” 민 said.

“I know what he is,” 엘레인 said calmly. “Or rather, what he was. He isn’t anymore, and I can feel sorry for him.”

에그웨인 slumped back against the wall. *랜드.* 로가인 always made her think of 랜드. She had not dreamed about him in months, now, not the kind of dreams she had had on the *River Queen.* Anaiya still made her write down everything she dreamed, and the 에스 세다이 checked them for signs, or connections to events, but there was never anything about 랜드 except dreams that, Anaiya said, meant she missed him. Oddly, she felt almost as if he were not there any longer, as if he had ceased to exist, along with her dreams, a few weeks after reaching the 백색 탑. *And I sit thinking about how nicely 갈라드 walks,* she thought bitterly. *랜드 has to be all right. If he’d been caught and gentled, I’d have heard something.*

That sent a chill through her, as it never failed to do, the thought of 랜드 being gentled, 랜드 weeping and wanting to die as 로가인 did.

엘레인 sat down beside her on the bed, tucking her feet up under her. “If you are mooning over 갈라드, 에그웨인, you will have no sympathy from me. I’ll have 니나브 dose you with one of those horrible concoctions she’s always talking about.” She frowned at 니나브, who had taken no notice of her entrance. “What is the matter with her? Don’t tell me she has started sighing after 갈라드, too!”

“I wouldn’t bother her.” 민 leaned toward the two of them and lowered her voice. “That skinny 허락받은 자 Irella told her she was as clumsy as a cow and had half the Talents, and 니나브 clouted her ear.” 엘레인 winced. “Exactly,” 민 murmured. “They had her up to 셰리암’s study before you could blink, and she hasn’t been fit to live with since.”

Apparently 민 had not dropped her voice enough, for there was a growl from 니나브. Suddenly the door whipped open once more, and a gale howled into the room. It did not ruffle the blankets on 에그웨인’s bed, but 민 and the stool toppled, to roll against the wall. Immediately the wind died, and 니나브 stood with a stricken look on her face.

에그웨인 hurried to the door and peeked out. The noonday sun was burning off the last reminders of last night’s rainstorm. The still-damp balcony around the Novices’ Court was empty, the long row of doors to 수련생s’ rooms all shut. The 수련생s who had taken advantage of the freeday to enjoy themselves in the gardens were no doubt catching up on their sleep. No one could have seen. She closed the door and took her place beside 엘레인 again as 니나브 helped 민 to her feet.

“I’m sorry, 민,” 니나브 said in a tight voice. “Sometimes my temper. . . . I can’t ask you to forgive me, not for this.” She took a deep breath. “If you want to report me to 셰리암, I will understand. I deserve it.”

에그웨인 wished she had not heard that admission; 니나브 could grow prickly over such things. Searching for something on which to focus, something 니나브 could believe she had had her attention on, she found herself touching *세다르* once more, and began juggling the balls of light again. 엘레인 quickly joined her; 에그웨인 saw the glow form around the Daughter-Heir even before three tiny balls appeared above her hands. They began to pass the little glowing spheres back and forth in increasingly intricate patterns. Sometimes one winked out as one girl or the other failed to maintain it as it came to her, then winked back a little altered in color or size.

The 하나의 힘 filled 에그웨인 with life. She smelled the faint rose aroma of soap from 엘레인’s morning bath. She could feel the rough plaster of the walls, the smooth stones of the floor, as well as she could the bed where she sat. She could hear 민 and 니나브 breathe, much less their quiet words.

“If it comes to forgiving,” 민 said, “maybe you should forgive me. You have a temper, and I have a big mouth. I will forgive you if you forgive me.” With murmurs of “forgiven” that sounded meant on both sides, the two women hugged. “But if you do it again,” 민 said with a laugh, “I might clout *your* ear.”

“Next time,” 니나브 replied, “I will throw something at you.” She was laughing, too, but her laughter ceased abruptly as her eye fell on 에그웨인 and 엘레인. “You two stop that, or there *will* be someone going to the 수련생 감독관. Two someones.”

“니나브, you wouldn’t!” 에그웨인 protested. When she saw the look in 니나브’s eyes, though, she hastily severed all contact with *세다르.* “Very well. I believe you. There’s no need to prove it.”

“We have to practice,” 엘레인 said. “They ask more and more of us. If we did not practice on our own, we would never keep up.” Her face showed calm composure, but she had let go of *세다르* as hastily as 에그웨인 herself had.

“And what happens when you draw too much,” 니나브 asked, “and there’s no one there to stop you? I wish you were more afraid. I am. Don’t you think I know what it is like for you? It’s always there, and you want to fill yourself with it. Sometimes it is all I can do to make myself stop; I want all of it. I know it would burn me to a crisp, and I want it anyway.” She shivered. “I just wish you were more afraid.”

“I am afraid,” 에그웨인 said with a sigh. “I’m terrified. But it doesn’t seem to help. What about you, 엘레인?”

“The only thing that terrifies me,” 엘레인 said airily, “is washing dishes. It seems as if I have to wash dishes every day.” 에그웨인 threw her pillow at her. 엘레인 pulled it off her head and threw it back, but then her shoulders slumped. “Oh, very well. I am so scared I don’t know why my teeth are not chattering. 엘라이더 told me I’d be so frightened that I would want to run away with the 이동 People, but I did not understand. A man who drove oxen as hard as they drive us would be shunned. I am tired all the time. I wake up tired and go to bed exhausted, and sometimes I’m so afraid that I will slip and channel more of the Power than I can handle that I. . . .” Peering into her lap, she let the words trail off.

에그웨인 knew what she had not spoken. Their rooms lay right next to each other, and as in many of the 수련생 rooms, a small hole had long ago been bored through the wall between, too small to be seen unless you knew where to look, but useful for talk after the lamps were extinguished, when the girls could not leave their rooms. 에그웨인 had heard 엘레인 crying herself to sleep more than once, and she had no doubt that 엘레인 had heard her own crying.

“The 이동 People are tempting,” 니나브 agreed, “but wherever you go, it will not change what you can do. You cannot run from *세다르.*” She did not sound as if she liked what she was saying.

“What do you see, 민?” 엘레인 said. “Are we all going to be powerful 에스 세다이, or will we spend the rest of our lives washing dishes as 수련생s, or. . . .” She shrugged uncomfortably as if she did not want to voice the third alternative that came to mind. Sent home. Put out of the Tower. Two 수련생s had been put out since 에그웨인 came, and everyone spoke of them in whispers, as if they were dead.

민 shifted on her stool. “I don’t like reading friends,” she muttered. “Friendship gets in the way of the reading. It makes me try to put the best face on what I see. That’s why I don’t do it for you three anymore. Anyway, nothing has changed about you that I can. . . .” She squinted at them, and suddenly frowned. “That’s new,” she breathed.

“What?” 니나브 asked sharply.

민 hesitated before answering. “Danger. You are all in some kind of danger. Or you will be, very soon. I can’t make it out, but it is danger.”

“You see,” 니나브 said to the two girls sitting on the bed. “You must take care. We all must. You must both promise not to channel again without someone to guide you.”

“I don’t want to talk about it anymore,” 에그웨인 said.

엘레인 nodded eagerly. “Yes. Let’s talk about something else. 민, if you put on a dress, I’ll wager 가윈 would ask you to go walking with him. You know he’s been looking at you, but I think the breeches and the man’s coat put him off.”

“I dress the way I like, and I won’t change for a lord, even if he is your brother.” 민 spoke absently, still squinting at them and frowning; it was a conversation they had had before. “Sometimes it is useful to pass as a boy.”

“No one who looks twice believes you are a boy.” 엘레인 smiled.

에그웨인 was uncomfortable. 엘레인 was forcing a semblance of gaiety, 민 was hardly paying attention, and 니나브 looked as if she wanted to warn them again.

When the door swung open once more, 에그웨인 bounded to her feet to close it, grateful for something to do besides watch the others pretend. Before she reached it, though, a dark-eyed 에스 세다이 with her blond hair done in a multitude of braids stepped into the room. 에그웨인 blinked in surprise, as much at it being any 에스 세다이 as at Liandrin. She had not heard that Liandrin had returned to the 백색 탑, but beyond that, 수련생s were sent for if an 에스 세다이 wanted them; it could mean no good, a sister coming herself.

The room was crowded with five women in it. Liandrin paused to adjust her red-fringed shawl, eyeing them. 민 did not move, but 엘레인 rose, and the three standing curtsied, though 니나브 barely flexed her knee. 에그웨인 did not think 니나브 would ever grow used to having others in authority over her.

Liandrin’s eyes settled on 니나브. “And why are you here, in the 수련생s’ quarters, child?” Her tone was ice.

“I am visiting with friends,” 니나브 said in a tight voice. After a moment she added a belated, “Liandrin Sedai.”

“The 허락받은 자, they can have no friends among the 수련생s. This you should have learned by this time, child. But it is as well that I find you here. You and you”—her finger stabbed at 엘레인 and 민—“will go.”

“I will return later.” 민 rose casually, making a great show of being in no hurry to obey, and strolled by Liandrin with a grin, of which Liandrin took no notice at all. 엘레인 gave 에그웨인 and 니나브 a worried look before she dropped a curtsy and left.

After 엘레인 closed the door behind her, Liandrin stood studying 에그웨인 and 니나브. 에그웨인 began to fidget under the scrutiny, but 니나브 held herself straight, with only a little heightening of her color.

“You two are from the same village as the boys who traveled with 모이라인. Is it not so?” Liandrin said suddenly.

“Do you have some word of 랜드?” 에그웨인 asked eagerly. Liandrin arched an eyebrow at her. “Forgive me, 에스 세다이. I forget myself.”

“Have you word of them?” 니나브 said, just short of a demand. The 허락받은 자 had no rule about not speaking to an 에스 세다이 until spoken to.

“You have concern for them. That is good. They are in danger, and you might be able to help them.”

“How do you know they’re in trouble?” There was no doubt about the demand in 니나브’s voice this time.

Liandrin’s rosebud mouth tightened, but her tone did not change. “Though you are not aware of it, 모이라인 has sent letters to the 백색 탑 concerning you. 모이라인 Sedai, she worries about you, and about your young . . . friends. These boys, they are in danger. Do you wish to help them, or leave them to their fate?”

“Yes,” 에그웨인 said, at the same time that 니나브 said, “What kind of trouble? Why do *you* care about helping them?” 니나브 glanced at the red fringe on Liandrin’s shawl. “And I thought you didn’t like 모이라인.”

“Do not presume too much, child,” Liandrin said sharply. “To be 허락받은 자 is not to be a sister. 허락받은 자 and 수련생s alike listen when a sister speaks, and do as they are told.” She drew a breath and went on; her tone was coldy serene again, but angry white spots marred her cheeks. “Someday, I am sure, you will serve a cause, and you will learn then that to serve it you must work even with those whom you dislike. I tell you I have worked with many with whom I would not share a room if it were left to me alone. Would you not work alongside the one you hated worst, if it would save your friends?”

니나브 nodded reluctantly. “But you still haven’t told us what kind of danger they’re in. Liandrin Sedai.”

“The danger comes from 세이올 굴. They are hunted, as I understand they once before were. If you will come with me, some dangers, at least, may be eliminated. Do not ask how, for I cannot tell you, but I tell you flatly it is so.”

“We will come, Liandrin Sedai,” 에그웨인 said.

“Come where?” 니나브 said. 에그웨인 shot her an exasperated look.

“Toman Head.”

에그웨인’s mouth fell open, and 니나브 muttered, “There’s a war on Toman Head. Does this danger have something to do with 아투르 호크윙’s armies?”

“You believe rumors, child? But even if they were true, is that enough to stop you? I thought you called these men friends.” A twist to Liandrin’s words said she would never do the same.

“We will come,” 에그웨인 said. 니나브 opened her mouth again, but 에그웨인 went right on. “We will go, 니나브. If 랜드 needs our help—and 맷, and 페린—we have to give it.”

“I know that,” 니나브 said, “but what I want to know is, why us? What can we do that 모이라인—or you, Liandrin—cannot?”

The white grew in Liandrin’s cheeks—에그웨인 realized 니나브 had forgotten the honorific in addressing her—but what she said was, “You two come from their village. In some way I do not entirely understand, you are connected to them. Beyond that, I cannot say. And no more of your foolish questions will I answer. Will you come with me for their sake?” She paused for their assent; a visible tension left her when they nodded. “Good. You will meet me at the northernmost edge of the 오지어 grove one hour before sunset with your horses and whatever you will need for the journey. Tell no one of this.”

“We are not supposed to leave the Tower grounds without permission,” 니나브 said slowly.

“You have my permission. Tell no one. No one at all. The 흑색 아자 walks the halls of the 백색 탑.”

에그웨인 gasped, and heard an echoed gasp from 니나브, but 니나브 recovered quickly. “I thought all 에스 세다이 denied the existence of—of that.”

Liandrin’s mouth tightened into a sneer. “Many do, but Tarmon Gai’don approaches, and the time leaves when denials can be made. The 흑색 아자, it is the opposite of everything for which the Tower stands, but it exists, child. It is everywhere, any woman could belong to it, and it serves the 어둠의 존재. If your friends are pursued by the Shadow, do you think the 흑색 아자 will leave you alive and free to help them? Tell no one—no one!—or you may not live to reach Toman Head. One hour before sunset. Do not fail me.” With that, she was gone, the door closing firmly behind her.

에그웨인 collapsed onto her bed with her hands on her knees. “니나브, she’s 적색 아자. She can’t know about 랜드. If she did. . . .”

“She cannot know,” 니나브 agreed. “I wish I knew why a Red wanted to help. Or why she’s willing to work with 모이라인. I’d have sworn neither of them would give the other water if she were dying of thirst.”

“You think she’s lying?”

“She is 에스 세다이,” 니나브 said dryly. “I’ll wager my best silver pin against a blueberry that every word she said was true. But I wonder if we heard what we thought we did.”

“The 흑색 아자.” 에그웨인 shivered. “There was no mistaking what she said about that, the Light help us.”

“No mistaking,” 니나브 said. “And she’s forestalled us asking anyone for advice, because after that, who can we trust? 빛 help us indeed.”

민 and 엘레인 came bustling in, slamming the door behind them. “Are you really going?” 민 asked, and 엘레인 gestured toward the tiny hole in the wall above 에그웨인’s bed, saying, “We listened from my room. We heard everything.”

에그웨인 exchanged glances with 니나브, wondering how much they had overheard, and saw the same concern on 니나브’s face. *If they manage to cipher out about 랜드. . . .*

“You have to keep this to yourselves,” 니나브 cautioned them. “I suppose Liandrin has arranged permission from 셰리암 for us to go, but even if she hasn’t, even if they start searching the Tower from top to bottom for us tomorrow, you mustn’t say a word.”

“Keep it to myself?” 민 said. “No fear on that. I’m going with you. All I do all day is try to explain to one Brown sister or another something I don’t understand myself. I can’t even go for a walk without the Amyrlin herself popping out and asking me to read whoever we see. When that woman asks you to do something, there doesn’t seem to be any way out of it. I must have read half the 백색 탑 for her, but she always wants another demonstration. All I needed was an excuse to leave, and this is it.” Her face wore a look of determination that allowed no argument.

에그웨인 wondered why 민 was so determined to go with them rather than simply leaving on her own, but before she had time to do more than wonder, 엘레인 said, “I am going, too.”

“엘레인,” 니나브 said gently, “에그웨인 and I are the boys’ kith from Emond’s Field. You are the Daughter-Heir of 안도르. If you disappear from the 백색 탑, why, it—it could start a war.”

“Mother wouldn’t start a war with 타르 발론 if they dried and salted me, which they may be trying to do. If you three can go off and have an adventure, you needn’t think I am going to stay here and wash dishes, and scrub floors, and have some 허락받은 자 berating me because I didn’t make the fire the exact shade of blue she wanted. 가윈 will die from envy when he finds out.” 엘레인 grinned and reached over to tug playfully at 에그웨인’s hair. “Besides, if you leave 랜드 lying about loose, I might have a chance to pick him up.”

“I don’t think either of us is going to have him,” 에그웨인 said sadly.

“Then we’ll find whoever he does choose and make her life miserable. But he couldn’t be fool enough to choose someone else when he could have one of us. Oh, please smile, 에그웨인. I know he’s yours. I just feel”—she hesitated, searching for the word—“free. I’ve never had an adventure. I’ll bet we won’t either of us cry ourselves to sleep on an adventure. And if we do, we will make sure the gleemen leave that part out.”

“This is foolishness,” 니나브 said. “We are going to Toman Head. You’ve heard the news, and the rumors. It will be dangerous. You must stay here.”

“I heard what Liandrin Sedai said about the—the 흑색 아자, too.” 엘레인’s voice dropped almost to a whisper at that name. “How safe will I be here, if *they* are here? If Mother even suspected the 흑색 아자 really existed, she would pitch me into the middle of a battle to get me away from them.”

“But, 엘레인—”

“There is only one way for you to stop me coming. That is to tell the 수련생 감독관. We will make a pretty picture, all three of us lined up in her study. All four of us. I don’t think 민 would escape from something like this. So since you are not going to tell 셰리암 Sedai, I am coming, too.”

니나브 threw up her hands. “Perhaps you can say something to convince her,” she told 민.

민 had been leaning against the door, squinting at 엘레인, and now she shook her head. “I think she has to come as much as the rest of you. The rest of us. I can see the danger around all of you more clearly, now. Not clearly enough to make it out, but I think it has something to do with you deciding to go. That’s why it is clearer; because it is more certain.”

“That’s no reason for her to come,” 니나브 said, but 민 shook her head again.

“She is linked to—to those boys as much as you, or 에그웨인, or me. She’s part of it, 니나브, whatever it is. Part of the Pattern, I suppose an 에스 세다이 would say.”

엘레인 seemed taken aback, and interested, too. “I am? What part, 민?”

“I can’t see it clearly.” 민 looked at the floor. “Sometimes I wish I couldn’t read people at all. Most people aren’t satisfied with what I see anyway.”

“If we are all going,” 니나브 said, “then we had best be about making plans.” However much she might argue beforehand, once a course of action had been decided, 니나브 always went right to the practicalities: what they had to take with them, and how cold it would be by the time they reached Toman Head, and how they could get their horses from the stables without being stopped.

Listening to her, 에그웨인 could not help wondering what the danger was that 민 saw for them, and what danger threatened 랜드. She knew of only one danger that could threaten him, and it made her cold to think of it. *Hold on, 랜드. Hold on, you wool-headed idiot. I’ll help you somehow.*
