I swore I would never even hold a fan again!* But there were other 살다에안 customs. She was surprised to see the knife in her hand; she had been taught not to draw a knife unless she meant to use it. “Farm girls in 살다에아 have a way of dealing with women who poach others’ men. Berelain stood smiling, tapping the blade of 파일’s knife on her palm. “A custom of Mayene. The 타이런s do like to use assassins, and the guards cannot always be close at hand. Finally managing to draw a breath, 파일 struggled to her feet, pulling a second knife. “I will drag you to him, after I cut off those clothes you are almost wearing, and make you tell him you are nothing but a sow!” *Light help me, I* am *behaving like a farmgirl, and talking like one!* The worst part was that she meant it.

Berelain set herself warily. She meant to use her hands, obviously, not the knife. She held it like a fan. 파일 advanced on the balls of her feet.

파일 gaped at him. With no warning, she pivoted, driving her fist toward Rhuarc’s short ribs. The toughest man would feel it there.

He seemed to move without looking at her, caught her hand, forced her arm straight to her side, twisted. Abruptly she was standing very straight and hoping he did not push her arm right up out of her shoulder.

As if nothing had happened, he addressed Berelain. “You will go to your room, and you will not come out until the sun is above the horizon. I will see that no breakfast is brought to you. A little hunger will remind you that there is a time and place for fighting.”

Berelain drew herself up indignantly. “I am the First of Mayene. I will not be ordered about like—”

Berelain’s face went white and red by turns. “Very well,” she said stiffly. “If you insist, I will perhaps—”

파일 stared after her in amazement. It was almost worth having her arm nearly disjointed. Rhuarc was watching Berelain go, too, a small appreciative smile on his lips.

She glared at him, but she suspected he meant just what he said. Those knives had been made for her by a man who knew what he was doing; the balance was just right. “What ‘first talk’ did you have with her? Why did she run like that?”

“That is between her and me. You will not go near her again, 파일. I do not believe she started this; that one’s weapons are not knives. If either of you makes trouble again, I will put both of you to carrying offal. Some of the 타이런s thought they could keep on fighting their duels after I had declared peace on this place, but the smell of the refuse carts soon taught them their mistake. She waited until he had gone before nursing her shoulder. He reminded her of her father. She could not help laughing aloud. “You will take him from me, you silly peahen? By the time you see him again, if you ever do, he’ll be mine once more.” Chuckling to herself, and occasionally rubbing her shoulder, she walked on with a light heart.

CHAPTER 15

![](images/00648.jpg)

*Into the Doorway*

Holding the glass-mantled lamp high, 맷 peered down the narrow corridor, deep in the belly of the Stone. *Not unless my life depended on it. That’s what I promised. Well, burn me if it doesn’t!* Before doubt could seize him again, he hurried on, past doors dry-rotted and hanging aslant, past others only shreds of wood clinging to rusted hinges. The floor had been swept recently, but the air still smelled of old dust and mold. Something skittered in the darkness, and he had a knife out before he realized it was just a rat, running from him, no doubt running toward some escape hole it knew.

“Show me the way out,” he whispered after it, “and I’ll come with you.” *Why am I whispering? There’s nobody down here to hear me*. It seemed a place for quiet, though. He could feel the whole weight of the Stone over his head, pressing down.

The last door, she had said. That one hung askew, too. He kicked it open, and it fell apart. The room was littered with dim shapes, with crates and barrels and things stacked high against the walls and out into the floor. Dust, too. *The Great Hold! It looks like the basement of an abandoned farmhouse, only worse*. He was surprised that 에그웨인 and 니나브 had not dusted and tidied while they were down here. Women were always dusting and straightening, even things that did not need it. Footprints crisscrossed the floor, some of them from boots, but no doubt they had had men to shift the heavier items about for them. 니나브 liked finding ways to make a man work; likely she had deliberately hunted out some fellows enjoying themselves.

What he sought stood out among the jumble. A tall redstone doorframe, looming oddly in the shadows cast by his lamp. When he came closer, it still looked odd. Twisted, somehow. His eye did not want to follow it around; the corners did not join right. The tall hollow rectangle seemed likely to fall over at a breath, but when he gave it an experimental push, it stood steady. He pushed a bit harder, not sure he did not want to heave the thing over, and that side of it scraped through the dust. Goose bumps ran down his arms. There might as well have been a wire fastened to the top, suspending it from the ceiling. He held the lamp up to see. There was no wire. *At least it won’t topple while I’m inside. Light, I am going inside, aren’t I?*

A clutter of figurines and small things wrapped in rotting cloth occupied the top of a tall, upended barrel near him. He pushed the jumble to one side so he could set the lamp there, and studied the doorway. The *ter’angreal*. If 에그웨인 knew what she was talking about. She probably did; no doubt she had learned all sorts of strange things in the Tower, however much she denied. *She would deny things, wouldn’t she now. Learning to be 에스 세다이. She didn’t deny this though, now did she?* If he squinted, it just looked like a stone doorframe, dully polished and the duller for dust. Just a plain doorframe. Well, not entirely plain. Three sinuous lines carved deep in the stone ran down each upright from top to bottom. He had seen fancier on farmhouses. He would probably step through and find himself still in this dusty room.

*Won’t know till I try, will I? Luck!* Taking a deep breath—and coughing from the dust—he put his foot through.

He seemed to be stepping through a sheet of brilliant white light, infinitely bright, infinitely thick. For a moment that lasted forever, he was blind; a roaring filled his ears, all the sounds of the world gathered together at once. For just the length of one measureless step.

Stumbling another pace, he stared around in amazement. The *ter’angreal* was still there, but this was certainly not where he had started. The twisted stone doorframe stood in the center of a round hall with a ceiling so high it was lost in shadows, surrounded by strange spiraled yellow columns snaking up into the gloom, like huge vines twining ’round poles that had been taken away. A soft light came from glowing spheres atop coiled stands of some white metal. Not silver; the shine was too dull for that. And no hint of what made the glow; it did not look like flame; the spheres simply shone. The floor tiles spiraled out in white and yellow stripes from the *ter’angreal*. There was a heavy scent in the air, sharp and dry and not particularly pleasant. He almost turned around and went back on the spot.

“A long time.”

He jumped, a knife coming into his hand, and peered among the columns for the source of the breathy voice that pronounced those words so harshly.

“A long time, yet the seekers come again for answers. The questioners come once more.” A shape moved, back among the columns; a man, 맷 thought. “Good. You have brought no lamps, no torches, as the agreement was, and is, and ever will be. You have no iron? No instruments of music?”

The figure stepped out, tall, barefoot, arms and legs and body wound about in layers of yellow cloth, and 맷 was suddenly not so sure if it was a man. Or human. It looked human, at first glance, though perhaps too graceful, but it seemed far too thin for its height, with a narrow, elongated face. Its skin, and even its straight black hair, caught the pale light in a way that reminded him of a snake’s scales. And those eyes, the pupils just black, vertical slits. No, not human.

“Iron. Instruments of music. You have none?”

맷 wondered what it thought the knife was; it certainly did not seem concerned over it. Well, the blade was good steel, not iron. “No. No iron, and no instruments of—Why—?” He cut off sharply. Three questions, 에그웨인 had said. He was not about to waste one on “iron” or “instruments of music.” *Why should he care if I have a dozen musicians in my pocket and a smithy on my back?* “I have come here for true answers. If you are not the one to give them, take me to who can.”

The man—it was male at least, 맷 decided—smiled slightly. He did not show any teeth. “According to the agreement. Come.” He beckoned with one long-fingered hand. “Follow.”

맷 made the knife disappear up his sleeve. “Lead, and I will follow.” *Just you keep ahead of me and in plain sight. This place makes my skin crawl*.

There was not a straight line to be seen anywhere except for the floor itself, as he trailed the strange man. Even the ceiling was always arched, and the walls bowed out. The halls were continuously curved, the doorways rounded, the windows perfect circles. Tilework made spirals and sinuous lines, and what seemed to be bronze metalwork set in the ceiling at intervals was all complicated scrolls. There were no pictures of anything, no wall hangings or paintings. Only patterns, and always curves.

He saw no one except his silent guide; he could have believed the place empty except for the two of them. From somewhere he had a dim memory of walking halls that had not known a human foot in hundreds of years, and this felt the same. Yet sometimes he caught a flicker of motion out of the corner of his eye. Only, however quickly he turned, there was never anyone there. He pretended to rub his forearms, checking the knives up his coatsleeves for reassurance.

What he saw through those round windows was even worse. Tall wispy trees with only a drooping umbrella of branches at the top, and others like huge fans of lacy leaves, a tangle of growth equal to the heart of any briar-choked thicket, all under a dim, overcast light, though there did not seem to be a cloud in the sky. There were always windows, always along just one side of the curving corridor, but sometimes the side changed, and what surely should have been looking into courtyard or rooms instead gave out into that forest. He never caught as much as a glimpse of any other part of this palace, or whatever it was, through those windows, or any other building, except. . . .

Through one circular window he saw three tall silvery spires, curving in toward each other so their points all aimed at the same spot. They were not visible from the next window, three paces away, but a few minutes later, after he and his guide had rounded enough curves that he had to be looking in another direction, he saw them again. He tried telling himself these were three different spires, but between them and him was one of those fan-shaped trees with a dangling broken branch, a tree that had been in the same spot the first time. After his third sight of the spires and the strange tree with the broken branch, this time ten paces farther on but on the other side of the hallway, he tried to stop looking at what lay outside at all.

The walk seemed interminable.

“When—? Are—?” 맷 ground his teeth. Three questions. It was hard to learn anything without asking questions. “I hope you are taking me to those who can answer my questions. Burn my bones, I do. For my sake and yours, the Light know it true.”

“Here,” the peculiar, yellow-wrapped fellow said, gesturing with one of those thin hands to a rounded doorway twice as large as any 맷 had seen before. His strange eyes studied 맷 intently. His mouth gaped open, and he inhaled, long and slow. 맷 frowned at him, and the stranger gave a writhing hitch of his shoulders. “Here your answers may be found. Enter. Enter and ask.”

맷 drew a deep breath of his own, then grimaced and scrubbed at his nose. That sharp, heavy smell was a rank nuisance. He took a hesitant step toward the tall doorway, and looked around for his guide again. The fellow was gone. *Light! I don’t know why anything in this place surprises me now. Well, I will be burned if I’ll turn back now*. Trying not to think of whether he could find the *ter’angreal* again on his own, he went in.

It was another round room, with spiraling floor tiles in red and white under a domed ceiling. It had no columns, or furnishings of any kind, except for three thick, coiled pedestals around the heart of the floor’s spirals. 맷 could see no way to reach the top of them except by climbing the twists, yet a man like his guide sat cross-legged atop each, only wrapped in layers of red. Not all men, he decided at a second look; two of those long faces with the odd eyes had a definite feminine cast. They stared at him, intense penetrating stares, and breathed deeply, almost panting. He wondered if he made them nervous in some way. *Not much bloody chance of that. But they’re certainly getting under my coat*.

“It has been long,” the woman on the right said.

“Very long,” the woman on the left added.

The man nodded. “Yet they come again.”

All three had the breathy voice of the guide—almost indistinguishable from it, in fact—and the harsh way of pronouncing words. They spoke in unison, and the words might as well have come from one mouth. “Enter and ask, according to the agreement of old.”

If 맷 had thought his skin crawled before, now he was sure it was writhing. He made himself go closer. Carefully—careful to say nothing that even sounded like a question—he laid the situation before them. The 백의단, certainly in his home village, surely hunting friends of his, maybe hunting him. One of his friends going to face the 백의단, another not. His family, not likely in danger, but with the bloody Children of the bloody Light around. . . . A *ta’veren* pulling at him so he could hardly move. He saw no reason to give names, or mention that 랜드 was the 용의 환생. His first question—and the other two, for that matter—he had worked out before going down to the Great Hold. “Should I go home to help my people?” he asked finally.

Three sets of slitted eyes lifted from him—reluctantly, it seemed—and studied the air above his head. Finally the woman on the left said, “You must go to Rhuidean.”
As soon as she spoke their eyes all dropped to him again, and they leaned forward, breathing deeply again, but at that moment a bell tolled, a sonorous brazen sound that rolled through the room. They swayed upright, staring at one another, then at the air over 맷’s head again.

“He is another,” the woman on the left whispered. “The strain. The strain.”

“The savor,” the man said. “It has been long.”

“There is yet time,” the other woman told them. She sounded calm—they all did—but there was a sharpness to her voice when she turned back to 맷. “Ask. Ask.”

맷 glared up at them furiously. *Rhuidean? Light!* That was somewhere out in the 황무지, the Light and the 아일 knew where. That was about as much as he knew. In the 황무지! Anger drove questions about how to get away from 에스 세다이 and how to recover the lost parts of his memory right out his head. “Rhuidean!” he barked. “빛 burn my bones to ash if I want to go Rhuidean! And my blood on the ground if I will! Why should I? You are not answering my questions. You are supposed to answer, not hand me riddles!”

“If you do not go to Rhuidean,” the woman on the right said, “you will die.”

The bell tolled again, louder this time; 맷 felt its tremor through his boots. The looks the three shared were plainly anxious. He opened his mouth, but they were only concerned with each other.

“The strain,” one of the women said hurriedly. “It is too great.”

“The savor of him,” the other woman said on her heels. “It has been so very long.”

Before she was done the man spoke. “The strain is too great. Too great. Ask. Ask!”

“Burn your soul for a craven heart,” 맷 growled, “I will that! Why will I die if I do not go to Rhuidean? I very likely will die if I try. It makes no—”

The man cut him off and spoke hurriedly. “You will have sidestepped the thread of fate, left your fate to drift on the winds of time, and you will be killed by those who do not want that fate fulfilled. Now, go. You must go! Quickly!”

The yellow-clad guide was suddenly there at 맷’s side, tugging at his sleeve with those too-long hands.

맷 shook him off. “No! I will not go! You have led me from the questions I wanted to ask and given me senseless answers. You will not leave it there. What fate are you talking about? I will have one clear answer out of you, at least!”

A third time the bell sounded mournfully, and the entire room trembled.

“Go!” the man shouted. “You have had your answers. You must go before it is too late!”

Abruptly a dozen of the yellow-clad men were around 맷, seeming to appear out of the air, trying to pull him toward the door. He fought with fists, elbows, knees. “What fate? Burn your hearts, what fate?” It was the room itself that pealed, the walls and floor quivering, nearly taking 맷 and his attackers off their feet. “What fate?”

The three were on their feet atop the pedestals, and he could not tell which shrieked which answer.

“To marry the Daughter of the Nine Moons!”

“To die and live again, and live once more a part of what was!”

“To give up half the light of the world to save the world!”

Together they howled like steam escaping under pressure. “Go to Rhuidean, son of battles! Go to Rhuidean, trickster! Go, gambler! Go!”

맷’s assailants snatched him into the air by his arms and legs and ran, holding him over their heads. “Unhand me, you white-livered sons of goats!” he shouted, struggling. “Burn your eyes! 그림자 take your souls, loose me! I will have your guts for a saddle girth!” But writhe and curse as he would, those long fingers gripped like iron.

Twice more the bell tolled, or the palace did. Everything shook as in an earthquake; the walls rang with deafening reverberations, each louder than the last. 맷’s captors stumbled on, nearly falling but never stopping their pell-mell race. He did not even see where they were taking him until they suddenly stopped short, heaving him into the air. Then he saw the twisted doorway, the *ter’angreal*, as he flew toward it.

White light blinded him; the roar filled his head till it drove thought away.

He fell heavily onto a dusty floor in dim light and rolled up against the barrel holding his lamp in the Great Hold. The barrel rocked, packets and figurines toppling to the floor in a crash of breaking stone and ivory and porcelain. Bounding to his feet, he threw himself back at the stone doorframe. “Burn you, you can’t throw me—!”

He hurtled through—and stumbled against the crates and barrels on the other side. Without a pause, he turned and leaped at it again. With the same result. This time he caught himself on the barrel holding his lamp, which nearly fell onto the already shattered things littering the floor under his boots. He grabbed it in time, burning his hand, and fumbled it back to a steadier perch.

*Burn me if I want to be down here in the dark*, he thought, sucking his fingers. *Light, the way my luck is running, it probably would have started a fire and I’d have burned to death!*

He glared at the *ter’angreal*. Why was it not working? Maybe the folk on the other side had shut it off somehow. He understood practically nothing of what had happened. That bell, and their panic. You would have thought they were afraid the roof would come down on their heads. Come to think of it, it very nearly had. And Rhuidean, and all the rest of it. The 황무지 was bad enough, but they said he was fated to marry somebody called the Daughter of the Nine Moons. Marry! And to a noblewoman, by the sound of it. He would sooner marry a pig than a noblewoman. And that business about dying and living again. *Nice of them to add the last bit!* If some black-veiled 아일man killed him on the way to Rhuidean, he would find out how true it was. It was all nonsense, and he did not believe a word of it. Only. . . . The bloody doorway *had* taken him somewhere, and they had only wanted to answer three questions, just the way 에그웨인 had said.

“I won’t marry any bloody noblewoman!” he told the *ter’angreal*. “I’ll marry when I’m too old to have any fun, that’s what! Rhuidean my bloody—!”

A boot appeared, backing out of the twisted stone doorway, followed by the rest of 랜드, with that fiery sword in his hands. The blade vanished as he stepped clear, and he heaved a sigh of relief. Even in the dim light, 맷 could see he was troubled, though. He gave a start when he saw 맷. “Just poking around, 맷? Or did you go through, too?”

맷 eyed him warily for a moment. At least that sword was gone. He did not seem to be channeling—though how was anybody to tell?—and he did not look particularly like a madman. In fact, he looked very much as 맷 remembered. He had to remind himself they were not back home any longer, and 랜드 was *not* what he remembered. “Oh, I went through, all right. A bunch of bloody liars, if you ask me! What are they? Made me think of snakes.”

“Not liars, I think.” 랜드 sounded as if he wished they were. “No, not that. They were afraid of me, right from the first. And when that tolling started. . . . The sword kept them back; they wouldn’t even look at it. Shied away. Hid their eyes. Did you get your answers?”

“Nothing that makes sense,” 맷 muttered. “What about you?”

Suddenly 모이라인 appeared from the *ter’angreal*, seeming to step gracefully out of thin air, flowing out. She would be a fine one to dance with if she were not 에스 세다이. Her mouth tightened at the sight of them.

“You! You were both in there. That is why . . . !” She made a vexed hiss. “One of you would have been bad enough, but two *ta’veren* at once—you might have torn the connection entirely and been trapped there. Wretched boys playing with things you do not know the danger of. 페린! Is 페린 in there, too? Did he share your . . . *exploit*?”

“The last I saw of 페린,” 맷 said, “he was getting ready to go bed.” Maybe 페린 would give him the lie by being the next to step out of the thing, but he might as well deflect the 에스 세다이’s anger if he could. No need for 페린 to face it, too. *Maybe he’ll make it clear of her, at least, if he gets away before she knows what he’s doing. Bloody woman! I’ll wager* she *was noble born*.

That Moraine was angry there was no doubt. The blood had drained out of her cheeks, and her eyes were dark augers boring into 랜드. “At least you escaped with your lives. Who told you of this? Which one of them? I will make her wish I had peeled off her hide like a glove.”

“A book told me,” 랜드 said calmly. He sat down back on the edge of a crate that creaked alarmingly under his weight and crossed his arms. All very cool; 맷 wished he could emulate it. “A pair of books, in fact. *Treasures of the Stone* and *Dealings with the Territory of Mayene*. Surprising what you can dig out of books if you read long enough, isn’t it?”

“And you?” She shifted that drilling gaze to 맷. “Did you read it in a book, too? You?”

“I do read sometimes,” he said dryly. He would not have been averse to a little hide-peeling for 에그웨인 and 니나브 after what they had done to make him tell where he had hidden the Amyrlin’s letter—tying him up with the Power was bad enough, but the rest!—yet it was more fun to tweak 모이라인’s nose. “*Treasures. Dealings*. Lots of things in books.” Luckily, she did not insist that he repeat the titles; he had not paid attention once 랜드 brought up books.

Instead she swung back to 랜드. “And your answers?”

“Are mine,” 랜드 replied, then frowned. “It wasn’t easy, though. They brought a . . . woman . . . to interpret, but she talked like an old book. I could hardly understand some of the words. I never considered they might speak another language.”

“The 고대어,” 모이라인 told him. “They use the 고대어—a rather harsh dialect of it—for their dealings with men. And you, 맷? Was your interpreter easily understood?”

He had to work moisture back into his mouth. “The 고대어? Is that what it was? They didn’t give me one. In fact, I never got to ask any questions. That bell started shaking the walls down, and they hustled me out like I was tracking cow manure on the rugs.” She was still staring, her eyes still digging into his head. She knew about the 고대어 slipping out of him, sometimes. “I . . . almost understood a word here and there, but not to know it. You and 랜드 got answers. What do they get out of it? The snakes with legs. We aren’t going upstairs to find ten years gone, are we, like Bili in the story?”

“Sensations,” 모이라인 replied with a grimace. “Sensations, emotions, experiences. They rummage through them; you can feel them doing it, making your skin crawl. Perhaps they feed on them in some manner. The 에스 세다이 who studied this *ter’angreal* when it was in Mayene wrote of a strong desire to bathe afterward. I certainly intend to.”

“But their answers are true?” 랜드 said as she started to turn away. “You are sure of it? The books implied as much, but can they really give true answers about the future?”

“The answers are true,” 모이라인 said slowly, “so long as they are in regard to your own future. That much is certain.” She watched 랜드, and himself, weighing the effect of her words. “As to how, though, there is only speculation. That world is . . . folded . . . in strange ways. I cannot be clearer. It may be that that allows them to read the thread of a human life, read the various ways it may yet be woven into the Pattern. Or perhaps it is a talent of the people. The answers are often obscure, however. If you need help working out what yours mean, I offer my services.” Her eyes flickered from one of them to the other, and 맷 nearly swore. She did not believe him about no answers. Unless it was simply general 에스 세다이 suspicion.

랜드 gave her a slow smile. “And will you tell me what you asked, and what they answered?”

For answer, she returned a level, searching look, then started for the door. A small ball of light, as bright as a lantern, was suddenly floating ahead of her, illuminating her way.

맷 knew he should leave it alone, now. Just let her go and hope she forgot he had ever been down here. But a knot of anger still burned inside him. All those ridiculous things they had said. Well, maybe they were true, if 모이라인 said so, but he wanted to grab those fellows by the collar, or whatever passed for a collar in those wrappings, and make them explain a few things.

“Why can’t you go there twice, 모이라인?” he called after her. “Why not?” He very nearly asked why they worried about iron and musical instruments, too, and bit his tongue. He could not know about those if he had not understood what they were saying.

She paused at the door to the hall, and it was impossible to see if she was looking at the *ter’angreal* or at 랜드. “If I knew everything, 매트림, I would not need to ask questions.” She peered into the room a moment longer—she *was* staring at 랜드—then glided away without another word.

For a time 맷 and 랜드 looked at each other in silence.

“*Did* you find out what you wanted?” 랜드 asked finally.

“Did you?”

A bright flame leaped into existence, balanced above 랜드’s palm. Not the smooth glowing sphere of the 에스 세다이, but a rough blaze like a torch. As 랜드 moved to leave, 맷 added another question. “Are you really going to just let the 백의단 do whatever they want back home? You know they’re heading for Emond’s Field. If they are not there already. Yellow eyes, the bloody 용의 환생. It’s too much, otherwise.”

“페린 will do . . . what he has to do to save Emond’s Field,” 랜드 replied in a pained voice. “And I must do what I have to, or more than Emond’s Field will fall, and to worse than 백의단.”

맷 stood watching the light of that flame fade away down the hall, until he remembered where he was. Then he snatched up his lamp and hurried out. *Rhuidean! Light, what am I going to do?*

*Leavetakings*

Lying on sweat-soaked sheets, staring at the ceiling, 페린 realized that the darkness was turning to gray. Soon the sun would be edging above the horizon. Morning. A time for new hopes; a time to be up and doing. New hopes. He almost laughed. How long had he been awake? An hour or more, surely, this time. Scratching his curly beard, he winced. His bruised shoulder had stiffened, and he sat up slowly; sweat popped out on his face as he worked the arm. He kept at it methodically, though, suppressing groans and now and again biting back a curse, until he could move the arm freely, if not comfortably.

Such sleep as he had managed had been broken and fitful. When he was awake he had seen 파일’s face, her dark eyes accusing him, the hurt he had put there making him cringe inside. When he slept, he dreamed of mounting a gallows, and 파일 watching, or worse, trying to stop it, trying to fight 백의단 with their lances and swords, and he was screaming while they fitted the noose around his neck, screaming because the 백의단 were killing 파일. Sometimes she watched them hang him with a smile of angry satisfaction. Small wonder such dreams wakened him with a jerk. Once he had dreamed of wolves running out of the forest to save both 파일 and him—only to be spitted on Whitecloak lances, shot down by their arrows. It had not been a restful night. Washing and dressing as hurriedly as he could, he left the room as if hoping to leave memories of his dreams behind.

Little outward evidence remained of the night’s attack, here a sword-slashed tapestry, there a chest with a corner splintered by an axe or a lighter patch on the stone-tiled floor where a bloodstained rug had been removed. The majhere had her liveried army of servants out in force, though many wore bandages, sweeping, mopping, clearing away and replacing. She limped about leaning on a stick, a broad woman with her gray hair pushed up like a round cap by the dressing wound around her head, calling her orders in a firm voice, with the clear intention of removing every sign of the Stone’s second violation. She saw 페린 and gave him an infinitesimal curtsy. Even the High Lords did not get much more from her, even when she was well. Despite all the cleaning and scrubbing, under the smell of waxes and polishes and cleaning fluids 페린 could still catch the faint scent of blood, sharply metallic human blood, fetid 트롤록 blood, acrid 미르드랄 blood with its stink that burned his nostrils. He would be glad to be away from here.

The door to 로이알’s room was a span across and more than two spans high, with an overlarge door handle in the shape of entwined vines level with 페린’s head. The Stone had a number of rarely used 오지어 guest rooms; the Stone of 티어 predated even the age of great 오지어 stoneworks, but it was a point of prestige to use 오지어 stonemasons, at least from time to time. 페린 knocked and at the call of “Come in,” in a voice like a slow avalanche, lifted the handle and complied.

The room was on a scale with the door in every dimension, yet 로이알, standing in the middle of the leaf-patterned carpet in his shirtsleeves, a long pipe in his teeth, reduced it all to seemingly normal size. The 오지어 stood taller than a 트롤록 in his wide-toed, thigh-high boots, if not so broad as one. His dark green coat, buttoned to the waist, then flaring to his boot tops like a kilt over baggy trousers, no longer looked odd to 페린, but one look was enough to tell this was not an ordinary man in an ordinary room. The 오지어’s nose was so broad as to seem a snout, and eyebrows like long mustaches dangled beside eyes the size of teacups. Tufted ears poked up through shaggy black hair that hung nearly to his shoulders. When he grinned around his pipestem at the sight of 페린, it split his face in half.

“Good morning, 페린,” he rumbled, removing the pipe. “You slept well? Not easy, after such a night as that. Myself, I have been up half the night, writing down what happened.” He had a pen in his other hand, and ink stains on his sausage-thick fingers.

Books lay everywhere, on 오지어-sized chairs and the huge bed and the table that stood as high as 페린’s chest. That was no surprise, but what was a little startling was the flowers. Flowers of every sort, in every color. Vases of flowers, baskets of them, posies tied with ribbon or even string, great woven banks of flowers standing about like lengths of garden wall. 페린 had certainly never seen the like inside a room. Their scent filled the air. Yet what really caught his eye was the swollen knot on 로이알’s head, the size of a man’s fist, and the heavy limp in 로이알’s walk. If 로이알 had been hurt too badly to travel. . . . He felt ashamed at thinking of it that way—the 오지어 was a friend—but he had to.

“You were injured, 로이알? 모이라인 could Heal you. I’m sure she will.”

“Oh, I can get around with no trouble. And there were so many who truly needed her help. I would not want to bother her. It certainly is not enough to hamper me in my work.” 로이알 glanced at the table where a large cloth-bound book—large for 페린, but it would fit in one of the 오지어’s coat pockets—lay open beside an uncorked ink bottle. “I hope I wrote it all down correctly. I did not see very much last night until it was done.”

“로이알,” 파일 said, standing up from behind one of the banks of flowers with a book in her hands, “is a hero.”

페린 jumped; the flowers had masked her scent completely. 로이알 made shushing noises, his ears twitching with embarrassment, and waved his big hands at her, but she went on, her voice cool but her eyes hot on 페린’s face.

“He gathered as many children as he could—and some of their mothers—into a large room, and held the door alone against 트롤록s and 미르드랄 through the entire fight. These flowers are from the women of the Stone, tokens to honor his steadfast courage, his faithfulness.” She made “steadfast” and “faithfulness” crack like whips.

페린 managed not to flinch, but only just. What he had done was right, but he could not expect her to see it. Even if she knew why, she would not see it. *It was the right thing. It was*. He only wished he felt better about the entire matter. It was hardly fair that he could be right and still feel in the wrong.

“It was nothing.” 로이알’s ears twitched wildly. “It is just that the children could not defend themselves. That’s all. Not a hero. No.”

“Nonsense.” 파일 marked her place in the book with a finger and moved closer to the 오지어. She did not come up to his chest. “There is not a woman in the Stone who would not marry you, if you were human, and some would anyway. 로이알 well named, for your nature is loyalty. Any woman could love that.”

The 오지어’s ears went stiff with shock, and 페린 grinned. She had obviously been feeding 로이알 honey and butter all morning in hope the 오지어 would agree to take her along no matter what 페린 wanted, but in trying to prick him she had just fed 로이알 a stone without knowing it. “Have you heard from your mother, 로이알?” he asked.

“No.” 로이알 managed to sound relieved and worried at the same time. “But I saw Laefar in the city yesterday. He was as surprised to see me as I to see him; we are not a common sight in 티어. He came from 스테딩 Shangtai to negotiate repairs on some 오지어 stonework in one of the palaces. I have no doubt the first words out of his mouth when he returns to the *stedding* will be ‘로이알 is in 티어.’ ”

“That is worrying,” 페린 said, and 로이알 nodded dejectedly.

“Laefar says the Elders have named me a runaway and my mother has promised to have me married and settled. She even has someone chosen. Laefar did not know who. At least, he said he did not. He thinks such things are funny. She could be here in a month’s time.”

파일’s face was a picture of confusion that almost made 페린 grin again. She thought she knew so much more than he did about the world—well, she did, in truth—but she did not know 로이알. 스테딩 Shangtai was 로이알’s home, in the 세계의 척추, and since he was barely past ninety, he was not old enough to have left on his own. 오지어 lived a very long time; by their standards, 로이알 was no older than 페린, maybe younger. But 로이알 had gone anyway, to see the world, and his greatest fear was that his mother would find him and drag back to the *stedding* to marry, never to leave again.

While 파일 was trying to figure out what was going on, 페린 stepped into the silence. “I need to go back to the 두 강, 로이알. Your mother won’t find you there.”

“Yes. That is true.” The 오지어 gave an uncomfortable shrug. “But my book. 랜드’s story. And yours, and 맷’s. I have so many notes already, but. . . .” He moved around behind the table, peering down at the open book, the pages filled with his neat script. “I will be the one to write the true story of the 용의 환생, 페린. The only book by someone who traveled with him, who actually saw it unfold. *The 용의 환생*, by 로이알, son of 아렌트 son of 할란, of 스테딩 Shangtai.” Frowning, he bent over the book, dipping his pen in the ink bottle. “That is not quite right. It was more—”

페린 put a hand on the page where 로이알 was going to write. “You’ll write no book if your mother finds you. Not about 랜드, at least. And I need you, 로이알.”

“Need, 페린? I do not understand.”

“There are 백의단 in the 두 강. Hunting me.”

“Hunting you? But why?” 로이알 looked almost as confused as 파일 had. 파일, on the other hand, had donned a complacent smugness that was worrisome. 페린 went on anyway.

“The reasons don’t matter. The fact is that they are. They may hurt people, my family, looking for me. Knowing 백의단, they will. I can stop it, if I can get there quickly, but it must be quickly. 빛 only knows what they’ve done already. I need you to take me there, 로이알, by the Ways. You told me once there was a Waygate here, and I know there was one at Manetheren. It must still be there, in the mountains above Emond’s Field. Nothing can destroy a Waygate, you said. I need you, 로이알.”

“Well, of course I will help,” 로이알 said. “The Ways.” He exhaled noisily, and his ears wilted a bit. “I want to write of adventures, not have them. But I suppose one more time will not hurt. 빛 send it so,” he finished fervently.

파일 cleared her throat delicately. “Are you not forgetting something, 로이알? You promised to take me into the Ways whenever I asked, and before you took anyone else.”

“I did promise you a look at a Waygate,” 로이알 said, “and what it is like inside. You can have that when 페린 and I go. You could come with us, I suppose, but the Ways are not traveled lightly, 파일. I would not enter them myself if 페린 did not have need.”

“파일 will not be coming,” 페린 said firmly. “Just you and me, 로이알.”

Ignoring him, 파일 smiled up at 로이알 as if he were teasing her. “You promised more than a look, 로이알. To take me wherever I wanted, whenever I wanted, and before anyone else. You swore to it.”

“I did,” 로이알 protested, “but only because you refused to believe I would show you. You said you would not believe unless I swore. I will do as I promised, but surely you do not want to step ahead of 페린’s need.”

“You swore,” 파일 said calmly. “By your mother, and your mother’s mother, and your mother’s mother’s mother.”

“Yes, I did, 파일, but 페린—”

“You swore, 로이알. Do you mean to break your oath?”

The 오지어 looked like misery stacked on misery. His shoulders slumped and his ears drooped, the corners of his wide mouth turned down and the ends of his long eyebrows draggled onto his cheeks.

“She tricked you, 로이알.” 페린 wondered if they could hear his teeth grinding. “She deliberately tricked you.”

Red stained 파일’s cheeks, but she still had the nerve to say, “Only because I had to, 로이알. Only because a fool man thinks he can order my life to suit himself. I’d not have done it, otherwise. You must believe that.”

“Doesn’t it make any difference that she tricked you?” 페린 demanded, and 로이알 shook his massive head sadly.

“오지어 *keep* their word,” 파일 said. “And 로이알 is going to take me to the 두 강. Or to the Waygate at Manetheren, at least. I have a wish to see the 두 강.”

로이알 stood up straight, “But that means I can help 페린 after all. 파일, why did you drag this out? Even Laefar would not think this funny.” There was a touch of anger in his voice; it took a good bit to make an 오지어 angry.

“If he asks,” she said determinedly. “That was part of it, 로이알. No one but you and me, unless they asked me. He has to ask me.”
“No,” 페린 told her while 로이알 was still opening his mouth. “No, I won’t ask. I will ride to Emond’s Field first. I’ll walk! So you might as well give up this foolishness. Tricking 로이알. Trying to force yourself in where . . . where you aren’t wanted.”

Her calm dropped away in anger. “And by the time you reach there, 로이알 and I will have done for the 백의단. It will all be over. Ask, you anvil-headed blacksmith. Just ask and you can come with us.”

페린 took hold of himself. There was no way to argue her around to his way of thinking, but he would not ask. She was right—he would need weeks to reach the 두 강 on his horse; they could be there in two days, perhaps, through the Ways—but he would not ask. *Not after she tricked 로이알 and tried to bully me!* “Then I’ll travel the Ways to Manetheren alone. I’ll follow you two. If I stay far enough back not to be part of your party, I won’t be breaking 로이알’s oath. You can’t stop me following.”

“That is dangerous, 페린,” 로이알 said worriedly. “The Ways are dark. If you miss a turning, or take the wrong bridge by accident, you could be lost forever. Or until *Machin Shin* catches you. Ask her, 페린. She said you can come if you do. Ask her.”

The 오지어’s deep voice trembled speaking the name of *Machin Shin*, and a shiver ran down 페린’s back, too. *Machin Shin*. The Black Wind. Not even 에스 세다이 knew whether it was 그림자태생 or something that had grown out of the Ways’ corruption. *Machin Shin* was why traveling the Ways meant risking death; that was what 에스 세다이 said. The Black Wind ate souls; that 페린 knew for truth. But he kept his voice steady and his face straight. *I’ll be burned if I let her think I am weakening*. “I can’t, 로이알. Or anyway, I won’t.”

“No. If he is too stiff-necked to ask, why should I? Why should I even care if he does get lost?” She turned to 페린. “You can travel close to us. As close as you need to, so long as it’s plain you are following. You will trail after me like a puppy until you ask. Why won’t you just ask?”

“I would like to leave today, 로이알,” 페린 said, not looking at 파일.

“Best to go quickly,” 로이알 agreed with a regretful look at the book on the table. “I can tidy my notes on the journey, I suppose. 빛 knows what I will miss, being away from 랜드.”

“Did you hear me, 페린?” 파일 demanded.

“I will get my horse and a few supplies, 로이알. We can be on our way by midmorning.”

로이알 eyed her worriedly. “페린, are you certain you could not—”

“No,” 페린 interrupted gently. “She is muleheaded, and she likes playing tricks. I won’t dance so she can laugh.” He ignored the sound coming from deep in 파일’s throat, like a cat staring at a strange dog and ready to attack. “I will let you know as soon as I am ready.” He started for the door, and she called after him furiously.

“ ‘When’ is my decision, 페린 Aybara. 민e and 로이알’s. Do you hear me? You had better be ready in two hours, or we’ll leave you behind. You can meet us at the Dragonwall Gate stable, if you’re coming. Do you hear me?”

He sensed her moving and shut the door behind him just as something thumped into it heavily. A book, he thought. 로이알 would give her fits about that. Better to hit 로이알 on the head than harm one of his books.

For a moment he leaned against the door, despairing. All he had done, all he had gone through, making her hate him, and she was going to be there to see him die anyway. The best thing he could say was that she might enjoy it now. *Stubborn, muleheaded woman!*

When he turned to go, one of the 아일 was approaching, a tall man with reddish hair and green eyes who could have been 랜드’s older cousin, or a young uncle. He knew the man, and liked him, if only because Gaul had never given even a flicker of notice to his yellow eyes. “May you find shade this morning, 페린. The majhere told me you had come this way, though I think she itched to put a broom in my hands. As hard as a Wise One, that woman.”

Gaul shook his head. “랜드 al’Thor took me aside and spoke to me, asking me to tell no one. I think he spoke to others, too, but I do not know how many will want to go with you. We have been on this side of the Dragonwall for a long time, and many ache for the Three-fold 란d.”

Gaul shook his head again. “He said only that you were going, and that there were men who might try to kill you. I mean to accompany you, though, if you will have me.”

“Will I?” 페린 almost laughed. “I will that. We will be into the Ways in a few hours.”

“The Ways?” Gaul’s expression did not change, but he blinked.

“Does that make a difference?”

“Death comes for all men, 페린.” It was hardly a comforting answer.

“I cannot believe 랜드 is that cruel,” 에그웨인 said, and 니나브 added, “At least he did not try to stop you.” Seated on 니나브’s bed, they were finishing the division of the gold 모이라인 had provided. Four fat purses apiece to be carried in pockets sewn under 엘레인’s and 니나브’s skirts, and another each, not so large as to attract unwanted attention, to carry at the belt. 에그웨인 had taken a lesser amount, there being less use for gold in the 황무지.

엘레인 frowned at the two neatly tied bundles and the leather scrip lying beside the door. They held all of her clothes and other things. Cased knife and fork, hairbrush and comb, needles, pins, thread, thimble, scissors. A tinder box and a second knife, smaller than the one at her belt. Soap and bath powder and. . . . It was ridiculous to go over the list again. 에그웨인’s stone ring was snug in her pouch. She was ready to go. There was nothing to hold her back.

“No, he did not.” 엘레인 was proud of how calm and collected she sounded. *He seemed almost relieved! Relieved! And I had to give him that letter, laying my heart open like a stone-blind fool. At least he won’t open it until I am gone*. She jumped at the touch of 니나브’s hand on her shoulder.

“Did you want him to ask you to stay? You know what your answer would have been. You do, don’t you?”

엘레인 compressed her lips. “Of course I do. But he did not have to look happy about it.” She had not meant to say that.

니나브 gave her an understanding look. “Men are difficult at the best.”

“I still cannot believe he would be so . . . so . . .” 에그웨인 began in an angry mutter. 엘레인 never learned what she meant to say, for at that moment the door crashed open so hard that it bounced off the wall.

엘레인 embraced *세다르* before she had stopped flinching, then felt a moment of embarrassment when the rebounding door slapped hard against 란’s outstretched hand. A moment more, and she decided to hold on to the Source a while longer. The 감시자 filled the doorway with his broad shoulders, his face a thunderhead; if his blue eyes could really have given off the thunderbolts they threatened, they would have blasted 니나브. The glow of *세다르* surrounded 에그웨인, too, and did not fade.

란 did not appear to see anyone but 니나브. “You let me believe you were returning to 타르 발론,” he rasped at her.

“You may have believed it,” she said calmly, “but I never said it.”

“Never said it? Never said it! You spoke of leaving today, and always linked your leaving with those 어둠의 친구들 being sent to 타르 발론. Always! What did you mean me to think?”

“But I never said—”

“Light, woman!” he roared. “Do not bandy words with me!”

엘레인 exchanged worried looks with 에그웨인. This man had an iron self-control, but he was at a breaking point now. 니나브 was one who often let her emotions rage, yet she faced him coolly, head high and eyes serene, hands still on her green silk skirts.

란 took hold of himself with an obvious effort. He appeared as stone-faced as ever, as much in control of himself—and 엘레인 was sure it was all on the surface. “I’d not have known where you were off to if I had not heard that you had ordered a carriage. To take you to a ship bound for Tanchico. I do not know why the Amyrlin allowed you to leave the Tower in the first place, or why 모이라인 involved you in questioning Black sisters, but you three are 허락받은 자. 허락받은 자, not 에스 세다이. Tanchico now is no place for anyone except a full 에스 세다이 with a 감시자 to watch her back. I’ll not let you go into that!”

“So,” 니나브 said lightly. “You question 모이라인’s decisions, and those of the 아미를린 석좌 as well. Perhaps I’ve misunderstood 감시자s all along. I thought you swore to accept and obey, among other things. 란, I do understand your concern, and I am grateful—more than grateful—but we all have tasks to perform. “Why? For the love of the Light, at least tell me why! Tanchico!”

“If 모이라인 has not told you,” 니나브 said gently, “perhaps she has her reasons. We must do our tasks, as you must do yours.”

란 trembled—actually trembled!—and clamped his jaw shut angrily. When he spoke, he was strangely hesitant. “You will need someone to help you in Tanchico. Someone to keep a 타라본er street thief from slipping a knife into your back for your purse. Tanchico was that sort of city before the war began, and everything I’ve heard says it is worse now. I could . . . I could protect you, 니나브.”

엘레인’s eyebrows shot up. He could not be suggesting. . . . He just could not be.

니나브 gave no sign that he had said anything out of the ordinary. “Your place is with 모이라인.”

“모이라인.” Sweat beaded on the 감시자’s hard face, and he struggled with the words. “I can . . . I must . . . 니나브, I . . . I. . . .”

“You *will* remain with 모이라인,” 니나브 said sharply, “until she releases you from your bond. You will do as I say.” Pulling a carefully folded paper from her pouch, she thrust it into his hands. He frowned, read, then blinked and read again.

엘레인 knew what it said.

> What the bearer does is done at my order and by my authority. Obey, and keep silent, at my command.

> *시우안 산체* *Watcher of the 봉인* *Flame of 타르 발론* *The 아미를린 석좌*

The other like it rested in 에그웨인’s pouch, though none of them were sure what good it would do where she was going.

“But this allows you to do anything you please,” 란 protested. “You can speak in the Amyrlin’s name. Why would she give this to an 허락받은 자?”

“Ask no questions I cannot answer,” 니나브 said, then added with a hint of a grin, “Just count yourself lucky I do not tell you to dance for me.”

엘레인 suppressed a smile of her own. 에그웨인 made a choking sound of swallowed laughter. It was what 니나브 had said when the Amyrlin first handed them the letters. *With this I could make a 감시자 dance*. Neither of them had had any doubt which 감시자 she had meant.

“Do you not? You dispose of me very neatly. My bond, and my oaths. This letter.” 란 had a dangerous gleam in his eye, which 니나브 seemed not to notice as she took back the letter and replaced it in the pouch on her belt.

“You are very full of yourself, al’란 Mandragoran. We do as we must, as you will.”

“Full of myself, 니나브 al’Meara? *I* am full of myself?” 란 moved so quickly toward 니나브 that 엘레인 very nearly wrapped him in flows of Air before she could think. One moment 니나브 was standing there, with just time to gape at the tall man sweeping toward her; the next her shoes were dangling a foot off the floor and she was being quite thoroughly kissed. At first she kicked his shins and hammered him with her fists and made sounds of frantic, furious protest, but her kicks slowed and stopped, and then she was holding on to his shoulders and not protesting at all.

에그웨인 dropped her eyes with embarrassment, but 엘레인 watched interestedly. Was that how she had looked when 랜드. . . . *No! I will not think about him*. She wondered if there was time to write him another letter, taking back everything she had said in the first, letting him know she was not to be trifled with. But did she want to?

After a while 란 set 니나브 back on her feet. She swayed a bit as she straightened her dress and patted her hair furiously. “You have no right . . .” she began in a breathless voice, then stopped to swallow. “I will not be *manhandled* in that fashion for the whole world to see. I will not!”

“Not the whole world,” he replied. “But if they can see, they can hear as well. You have made a place in my heart where I thought there was no room for anything else. You have made flowers grow where I cultivated dust and stones. Remember this, on this journey you insist on making. If you die, I will not survive you long.” He gave 니나브 one of his rare smiles. If it did not exactly soften his face, at least it made it less hard. “And remember also, I am not always so easily commanded, even with letters from the Amyrlin.” He made an elegant bow; for a moment 엘레인 thought he actually meant to kneel and kiss 니나브’s Great Serpent ring. “As you command,” he murmured, “so do I obey.” It was difficult to tell whether he meant to be mocking or not.

As soon as the door closed behind him, 니나브 sank onto the edge of her bed as if letting her knees give way at last. She stared at the door with a pensive frown.

“ ‘Poke the meekest dog too often,’ ” 엘레인 quoted, “ ‘and he will bite.’ Not that 란 is very meek.” She got a sharp look and a sniff from 니나브.

“He is insufferable,” 에그웨인 said. “Sometimes he is. 니나브, why did you do that? He was ready to go with you. I know you want nothing more than to break him free of 모이라인. Do not try to deny it.”

니나브 did not try. Instead she fussed with her dress, and smoothed the coverlet on the bed. “Not like that,” she said finally. “I mean him to be mine. All of him. I will not have him remembering a broken oath to 모이라인. I will not have that between us. For him, as well as myself.”

“But will it be any different if you bring him to ask 모이라인 to release him from his bond?” 에그웨인 asked. “란 is the kind of man who would see it as much the same thing. All that leaves is to somehow make her let him go of her own accord. How can you manage that?”

“I do not know.” 니나브 firmed her voice. “Yet what must be done, can be done. There is always a way. That is for another time. Work to be done, and we sit here fretting over men. Are you sure you have everything you need for the 황무지, 에그웨인?”

“아비엔다 is readying everything,” 에그웨인 said. “She still seems unhappy, but she says we can reach Rhuidean in little more than a month, if we are lucky. You will be in Tanchico by then.”

“Perhaps sooner,” 엘레인 told her, “if what they say about Sea Folk rakers is true. You will be careful, 에그웨인? Even with 아비엔다 for a guide, the 황무지 cannot be safe.”

“I will. You be careful. Both of you. Tanchico is not much safer than the 황무지 now.”

Abruptly they were all hugging one another, repeating cautions to take care, making sure they all remembered the schedule for meeting in *Tel’aran’rhiod*’s Stone.

엘레인 wiped tears from her cheeks. “As well 란 left.” She laughed tremulously. “He would think we were all being foolish.”

“No, he would not,” 니나브 said, pulling up her skirts to settle a purse of gold into its pocket. “He may be a man, but he is not a complete dolt.”

There had to be time between here and the carriage to locate paper and pen, 엘레인 decided. She would find time. 니나브 had the right of it. Men needed a firm hand. 랜드 would find he could not get away from her so easily. And he would not find it easy to worm his way back into her good graces.
