The dim yellow light flickered, making faint shadows dance on patched canvas walls that were a far cry from the grandeur of the Amyrlin’s study in the 백색 탑, but that did not upset her. Truth be known, she herself was some considerable distance short of the grandeur normally associated with the 아미를린 석좌. She knew very well that the seven-striped stole on her shoulders was the only reason any stranger would believe her Amyrlin. If they did not think it an extremely foolish joke. Odd things had happened in the 백색 탑’s history—시우안 had told her secret details of some of them—yet surely nothing so odd as her.

“Four or five days would be better,” 셰리암 mused, studying the sheaf of papers in her lap. Slightly plump, with high cheekbones and tilted green eyes, in her dark green riding dress she managed to look elegant and commanding despite her perch on one of the two precarious stools in front of the table. Exchange her narrow blue stole of the 연대기 수호자 for the Amyrlin’s, and anyone would think she wore it by right. Sometimes she certainly seemed to believe the striped stole rested on her own shoulders. “Or perhaps longer. It would not hurt to build our stores up once more.”

시우안, atop the other rickety stool, shook her head slightly, but 에그웨인 did not need the hint. “One day.” She might be just eighteen and well short of a true Amyrlin’s grandeur, but she was no fool. Too many of the sisters seized on any excuse for a halt—too many of the 의석자들, as well—and if they stopped too long, it might be impossible to start them moving again. 셰리암 opened her mouth.

“One, daughter,” 에그웨인 said firmly. Whatever 셰리암 thought, the fact was that 셰리암 Bayanar was the Keeper and 에그웨인 al’Vere the Amyrlin. If only 셰리암 could be brought to realize that. And the 탑의 회의실; they were worse. She wanted to snarl or snap or maybe throw something, but after close to a month and half, she already had a lifetime’s practice in keeping her face and voice smooth at far greater provocation than this. “Any longer, and we’ll begin to strip the countryside bare. I won’t leave people to starve. On the practical side, if we take too much from them, even paid for, they’ll give us a hundred problems in return.”

“Raids on the herds and flocks and thieves at the store-wagons,” 시우안 murmured. Studying her divided gray skirts, not looking at anyone, she seemed to be thinking aloud. “Men shooting at our guards at night, maybe setting fire to whatever they can reach. A bad business. Hungry people become desperate in a hurry.” Those were the same reasons Lord Bryne had given 에그웨인, in very nearly the same words.

The fiery-haired woman shot 시우안 a hard look. Many sisters had a difficult time with 시우안. Her face was probably the best known in the camp, young enough to have looked proper above an 허락받은 자’s dress, or a 수련생’s for that matter. That was a side effect of being stilled, though not many had known it; 시우안 could hardly walk a step without sisters staring at her, the once 아미를린 석좌, deposed and cut off from *세다르*, then Healed and restored to at least some ability, when everyone knew that was impossible. Many welcomed her back warmly as a sister once more, for herself and for the miracle that held out hope against whatevery 에스 세다이 feared beyond death, but just as many or more offered lukewarm toleration or condescension or both, blaming her for their present situation.

셰리암 was one of those who thought 시우안 should instruct the new young Amyrlin in protocol and the like, which everyone believed she hated, and keep her mouth closed unless she was called upon. She was less than she had been, no longer Amyrlin and no longer anywhere near so strong in the Power. It was not cruelty as 에스 세다이 saw it. The past was past; what was now, was, and must be accepted. Anything else only brought greater pain. By and large, 에스 세다이 admitted change slowly, but once they did, for most it was as if things had always been that way. “One day, Mother, as you say,” 셰리암 sighed at last, bowing her head slightly. Less in submission, 에그웨인 was sure, than to hide a grimace over her stubbornness. She would accept the grimace if the acquiescence came with it. For the time being, she had to.

시우안 bowed her head, too. To hide a smile. Any sister might be appointed to any post, but the social pecking order was quite rigid, and 시우안 stood a long way further down than she had. That was one reason.

The papers on 셰리암’s lap were duplicated on 시우안’s, and on the table in front of 에그웨인. Reports on everything from the number of candles and sacks of beans remaining in the camp to the state of the horses, and the same for Lord Bryne’s army. The army’s camp encircled the 에스 세다이’s, with a ring perhaps twenty steps wide between, but in many ways they might as well have been a mile apart. Surprisingly, Lord Bryne insisted on that as much as the sisters. The 에스 세다이 did not want soldiers wandering among their tents, a lot of unwashed, illiterate ruffians with light fingers often as not, and it seemed the soldiers did not want 에스 세다이 wandering among them either—though, perhaps wisely, they held their reasons close. They marched toward 타르 발론 to pull down a usurper to the 아미를린 석좌 and raise 에그웨인 in her place, yet few men were truly comfortable around 에스 세다이. Few enough women, either.

As Keeper, 셰리암 would have been all too happy to take these minor matters out of 에그웨인’s hands. She had said as much, explaining how minor they were, how the 아미를린 석좌 should not be burdened with day-to-day trifles. 시우안, on the other hand, said a good Amyrlin paid attention to just those, not trying to duplicate the work of dozens of sisters and clerks, yet checking on something different every day. That way she had a good idea of what was happening and what needed doing before someone came running to her with a crisis already breaking into shards. A feel for how the wind was blowing, 시우안 called it. Making sure these reports reached her had required weeks, and 에그웨인 was sure that once she let them pass to 셰리암’s control, she would never again learn anything until it was long dealt with. If then.

A silence stretched as they began reading the next paper in each stack.

They were not alone. Chesa, seated on cushions to one side of the tent, spoke. “Too little light is bad for the eyes,” she murmured almost to herself, holding up one of 에그웨인’s silk stockings that she was darning. “You’ll never catch me ruining my eyes over words in this little light.” Just short of stout, with a twinkle in her eyes and a merry smile, 에그웨인’s maid was always trying to slip advice to the Amyrlin as though talking about herself. She could have been in 에그웨인’s service twenty years instead of less than two months, and three times as old as 에그웨인 instead of barely twice. Tonight, 에그웨인 suspected that she talked to fill silences. There was a tension in the camp since 로가인 had escaped. A man who could channel, shielded and under close guard, yet he had slipped away like fog. Everyone walked on edge wondering how, wondering where he was, what he intended to do now. 에그웨인 wished harder than most that she could be sure she knew where 로가인 Ablar was.

Giving her papers a firm snap of her wrists, 셰리암 frowned at Chesa; she did not understand why 에그웨인 let her maid be present at these meetings, much less let her chatter away freely. It probably never occurred to her that Chesa’s presence and her unexpected chatter frequently unsettled her just enough to help 에그웨인 sidestep advice she did not want to take and postpone decisions she did not want to make, at least not the way 셰리암 wanted them made. Certainly the notion had never occurred to Chesa; she smiled apologetically and returned to her darning, occasionally murmuring to herself.

“If we continue, Mother,” 셰리암 said coolly, “we may finish before dawn.”

Staring at the next page, 에그웨인 rubbed her temples. Chesa might be right about the light. She had another headache coming on. Then again, it might be the page, detailing what money was left. The stories she had read never mentioned how much coin was required to keep an army. Pinned to the sheet were notes from two of the 의석자들, Romanda and Lelaine, suggesting the soldiers be paid less frequently, paid less in fact. More than suggesting, really, just as Romanda and Lelaine were more than simply two 의석자들 in the Hall. Other 의석자들 followed where they led, if not all by any means, while the only Sitter 에그웨인 could count on was Delana, and her not far. It was rare that Lelaine and Romanda agreed on anything, and they could hardly have chosen a worse. Some of the soldiers had sworn oaths, yet most were there for their pay, and maybe the hope of loot.

“The soldiers are to be paid as before,” 에그웨인 muttered, crumpling the two notes. She was not going to let her army melt away, any more than she would allow looting.

“As you command, Mother.” 셰리암’s eyes sparkled with pleasure. The difficulties must be clear to her—anyone who thought her less than very intelligent was in deep trouble—but she did have a blind spot. If Romanda or Lelaine said the sun was coming up, 셰리암 most likely would claim it was going down; she had had almost as much sway with the Hall as they did now, perhaps more, until they put a halt to it between them. The opposite was true, as well; those two would speak against anything 셰리암 wanted before they stopped to think. Which had its uses, all in all.

에그웨인’s fingers tapped on the tabletop, but she made them stop. The money had to be found—somewhere, somehow—but she did not have to let 셰리암 see her worry.

“That new woman will work out,” Chesa murmured over her sewing. “타이런s always carry their noses high, of course, but Selame does know what’s required of a lady’s maid. Meri and I will settle her down soon enough.” 셰리암 rolled her eyes irritably.

에그웨인 smiled to herself. 에그웨인 al’Vere with three maids waiting on her; as unbelievable as the stole itself. But the smile lasted only a heartbeat. Maids had to be paid, too. A tiny sum, balanced against thirty thousand soldiers, and the Amyrlin could hardly do her own laundry or mend her own shifts, but she could have managed splendidly with Chesa alone. And would have, had she any choice in it. Less than a week earlier Romanda had decided that the Amyrlin needed another servant and found Meri among the refugees who huddled in every village until they were chased away, and not to be outdone, Lelaine produced Selame from the same source. The two women were crowded into Chesa’s small tent before 에그웨인 knew either existed.

The principle of the thing was wrong: *three* maids when there was not enough silver to pay the army halfway to 타르 발론, servants chosen for her without any say; and then there was the fact that she had yet another, if one who received not a copper. Everyone believed Marigan was the Amyrlin’s maidservant, anyway.

Beneath the edge of the table she felt her belt pouch, felt the bracelet inside. She should wear it more; it was a duty. Keeping her hands low, she dug the bracelet out and slipped it around her wrist, a band of silver made so the catch was invisible once closed. Made with the 하나의 힘, the bracelet snapped shut beneath the table, and she very nearly snatched it off again.

Emotion flooded into a corner of her mind, emotion and awareness, a little pocket, as if she were imagining it. Not imagination, though; all too real. Half of an *a’dam*, the bracelet created a link between her and the woman who wore the other half, a silver necklace the wearer could not remove herself. They were a circle of two without embracing *세다르*, 에그웨인 always leading by virtue of the bracelet. “Marigan” was asleep now, her feet sore from walking all day and days past, but even sleeping, fear oozed though most strongly; only hate ever came near fear in the stream that flowed through the *a’dam*. 에그웨인’s reluctance came from the constant gnawing of the other woman’s terror, from having worn the necklace end of an *a’dam* once, and from knowing the woman on the far end. She hated sharing any part of her.

Only three women in the camp knew that 모그헤디엔 was a prisoner, hidden in the midst of 에스 세다이. If it came out, 모그헤디엔 would be tried, stilled and executed in short order. If it came out, 에그웨인 might not be far behind her, and 시우안 and 리안, as well. They were the other two who knew. At best she would have the stole stripped away.

*For hiding one of the 버림받은 자들 from justice*, she thought grimly, *I’ll be lucky if they just stick me back with the 허락받은 자*. Unconsciously she thumbed the golden Great Serpent ring on the first finger of her right hand.
Then again, however just such a punishment might be, it was unlikely. She had been taught that the wisest of the sisters was chosen 아미를린 석좌, yet she had learned better. The choosing of an Amyrlin was as hotly contested as electing a mayor in the 두 강, and maybe more; no one bothered to stand against her father in Emond’s Field, but she had heard about elections in Deven Ride and Taren Ferry. 시우안 had only been raised Amyrlin because the three before her each had died after just a few years on the 아미를린 석좌. The Hall had wanted someone young. Speaking of age to a sister was at least as rude as slapping her face, yet she had begun to get some idea how long 에스 세다이 lived. Rarely was anyone chosen Sitter before she had worn the shawl seventy or eighty years at least, and Amyrlins generally longer. Often *much* longer. So when the Hall deadlocked between four sisters raised 에스 세다이 less than fifty years before, and 세인 Herimon of the White suggested a woman who had worn the shawl only *ten* years, it might have been as much exhaustion as 시우안’s qualifications in administration that brought the 의석자들 to stand for her.

And 에그웨인 al’Vere, who in many eyes should still have been a 수련생? A figurehead, easily directed, a *child* who had grown up in the same village with 랜드 al’Thor. That last definitely had its part in the decision. They would not take back the stole, but she would find the little authority she had managed to accumulate gone. Romanda, Lelaine and 셰리암 might actually come to blows over which would march her about by the scruff of her neck. “That looks much like a bracelet I saw 엘레인 wearing.” The papers on 셰리암’s lap crackled as she leaned forward for a better look. “And 니나브. They shared it, as I recall.”

에그웨인 gave a start. She had been careless. “It’s the same. A remembrance gift, when they left.” Twisting the silver circlet around her wrist, she felt a stab of guilt that was all her own. The bracelet appeared segmented, but so cunningly you could not see how exactly. She had hardly thought of 니나브 and 엘레인 since their departure for Ebou Dar. Perhaps she should call them back. Their search was not going well, it seemed, though they denied it. Still, if they could find what they were after. . . . 셰리암 was frowning, whether or not at the bracelet, 에그웨인 could not say. She could not allow 셰리암 to start thinking too much on that bracelet, though; if she ever noticed that the necklace “Marigan” wore was a match, there might be painfully awkward questions.

Rising, 에그웨인 smoothed her skirt as she moved around the table. 시우안 had acquired several pieces of information today; one could be put to good use now. She was not the only one with secrets. 셰리암 looked surprised when she stopped too close for the other woman to stand.

“Daughter, I’ve learned that a few days after 시우안 and 리안 arrived in Salidar, ten sisters left, two from each 아자 there except the Blue. Where did they go, and why?”

셰리암’s eyes narrowed a fraction, but she wore serenity as comfortably as her dress. “Mother, I can hardly recall every—”

“No dancing around, 셰리암.” 에그웨인 moved a little closer, until their knees almost touched. “No lies by omission. The truth.”

A frown creased 셰리암’s smooth forehead. “Mother, even if I knew, you cannot trouble yourself with every little—”

“The truth, 셰리암. The whole truth. Must I ask before the entire Hall why I cannot have the truth from my Keeper? I will have it, daughter, one way or another. I *will* have it.”

셰리암’s head swiveled as though she was looking for a way to escape. Her eyes fell on Chesa, hunched over her sewing, and she all but gasped with relief. “Mother, tomorrow, when we are alone, I am sure I can explain everything to your satisfaction. I must speak with a few of the sisters first.”

So they could work up what 셰리암 was to tell her tomorrow. “Chesa,” 에그웨인 said, “wait outside, please.” For all that she seemed focused on her work to the exclusion of everything else, Chesa bounded to her feet in a flash and very nearly ran from the tent. When 에스 세다이 were at odds, anyone with half a brain went elsewhere. “Now, daughter,” 에그웨인 said. “The truth. All that you know. This is as private as you will be,” she added when 셰리암 glanced at 시우안.

For a moment 셰리암 adjusted her skirts, plucking at them really, avoiding 에그웨인’s eyes, no doubt still working out evasions. But the 세 가지 맹세 trapped her. She could not speak an untrue word, and whatever she thought of 에그웨인’s true position, slipping behind her back was a long way from denying her authority to her face. Even Romanda maintained the proper courtesies, if only by a hair at times.

Drawing a deep breath, 셰리암 folded her hands in her lap and spoke to 에그웨인’s chest, matter-of-fact. “When we learned the 적색 아자 was responsible for setting 로가인 up as a false Dragon, we felt something had to be done.”

“We” certainly meant the small coterie of sisters she had gathered around her; Carlinya and 베오닌 and the rest held as much real sway as most 의석자들, if not actually in the Hall. “엘라이더 was sending out demands for every sister to return to the Tower, so we chose ten sisters to do just that, by the fastest means they could manage. They all should be there long since. Quietly making sure that every sister in the Tower understands the truth of what the Reds did with 로가인. Not—” She hesitated, then finished in a rush. “Not even the Hall knows of them.”

에그웨인 stepped away, rubbing her temples again. Quietly making sure. In the hope that 엘라이더 would be deposed. Not exactly a bad scheme, really; it might even work, eventually. It might take years, too. But then, for most sisters, the longer they could go without truly *doing* anything, the better. With enough time, they could convince the world that the 백색 탑 had never really broken. It had been broken before, even if only a handful knew it. Maybe, with enough time, they could find a way to adjust everything so it had not, really. “Why keep it from the Hall, 셰리암? Surely you don’t think any of them would betray your plan to 엘라이더.” Half the sisters eyed the other half askance for fear of 엘라이더’s sympathizers. Partly for fear of that.

“Mother, a sister who decided that what we do is a mistake would hardly let herself be chosen a Sitter. Any such would have taken herself away long since.” 셰리암 had not relaxed, but her voice took on the patient, instructing tone she seemed to think had the greatest effect on 에그웨인. Usually, though, she was more adroit at changing the subject. “Those suspicions are the worst problem we face for the time being. No one really trusts anyone. If we could only see how to—”

“The 흑색 아자,” 시우안 cut in quietly. “That’s what chills your blood like a silverpike up your skirts. Who can say for sure who is Black, and who can say what a Black sister might do?”

셰리암 darted another hard look at 시우안, but after a moment the force went out of her. Or rather, one sort of tension replaced another. She glanced at 에그웨인, then nodded, reluctantly. By the sour twist to her mouth, she would have made another evasion had it not been plain 에그웨인 would not stand for it. Most sisters in the camp believed now, but after more than three thousand years denying the 흑색 아자’s existence, it was a queasy belief. Almost no one would open her mouth on that topic, no matter what they believed.

“The question, Mother,” 시우안 went on, “is what happens when the Hall does find out.” She seemed to be thinking aloud again. “I can’t see any Sitter accepting the excuse that she couldn’t be told because she might be on 엘라이더’s side. And as for the possibility she might be 흑색 아자. . . . Yes, I think they will be quite upset.”

셰리암’s face paled slightly. It was a wonder she did not go dead white. “Upset” did not begin to cover it. Yes, 셰리암 would face *much* more than upset if this came out.

Now was the time to drive home her advantage, but another question occurred to 에그웨인. If 셰리암 and her friends had sent—what were they? Not spies. Ferrets, maybe, sent into the walls after rats—if 셰리암 had sent ferrets into the 백색 탑, could . . . ?

A sudden stab of pain through that pocket of sensations in the back of her head sent everything else flying. Had she felt it directly, it would have been numbing. As it was, her eyes bulged in shock. A man who could channel was touching the necklace around 모그헤디엔’s neck; this was one link no man could be brought into. Pain, and something unheard of from 모그헤디엔. Hope. And then it was all gone, the awareness, the emotions. The necklace was off.

“I . . . need some fresh air,” she managed. 셰리암 started to rise, and 시우안, but she waved them back down. “No, I want to be alone,” she said hastily. “시우안, find out everything 셰리암 knows about the ferrets. Light, I mean the ten sisters.” They both stared at her, but thank the Light, neither followed as she snatched the lantern from its hook and hurried out.

It would not do for the Amyrlin to be seen running, yet she came close, hoisting her divided skirts as well as she could with her free hand and very nearly trotting. A cloudless sky made the moonlight bright, dappling the tents and wagons with shadows. Most people in the camp were asleep, but low fires still burned here and there. A handful of 감시자s were about, a few servants. Too many eyes to see if she ran. The last thing she wanted was someone offering help. She realized she was panting, but from alarm, not exertion.

Thrusting her head and the lantern into “Marigan’s” tiny tent, she found it empty. The blankets that made up the pallet on the ground lay in a sprawl, tossed aside by someone in a hurry.

*And what if she had still been here?* she wondered. *With the necklace off, and maybe whoever freed her?* Shivering, she withdrew slowly. 모그헤디엔 had good reason to dislike her, very personally, and the only sister who could match one of the 버림받은 자들 alone, when she could channel at all, was in Ebou Dar. 모그헤디엔 could have killed 에그웨인 without anyone noticing; even had a sister felt her channel, there would be nothing remarkable in that. Worse, 모그헤디엔 might not have killed her. And no one would have known anything until they found the pair of them gone.

“Mother,” Chesa fussed behind her, “you should not be out in the night air. Night air is bad air. If you wanted Marigan, I could have fetched her.”

에그웨인 very nearly jumped. She had not been aware of Chesa following her. She studied the people at the nearest fires. They had gathered for companionship, not warmth in this unholy heat, and they were not close, but maybe someone had seen who went into “Marigan’s” tent. She certainly had few visitors. And no men among them. A man might well have been remarked. “I think she has run away, Chesa.”

“Why, that wicked woman!” Chesa exclaimed. “I always said she had a mean mouth and a sneaking eye. Slinking away like a thief after you took her in. She’d be starving by a road, if not for you. No gratitude at all!”

She followed all the way back to the tent where 에그웨인 slept, nattering on about wickedness in general, the thanklessness of “Marigan” in particular, and how that sort should be handled, which seemed to jump between switching them till they settled down and tossing them out before they could run away, tucked around cautions that 에그웨인 check her jewelry to be sure it was all still there.

에그웨인 barely heard. Her mind spun. It could not have been 로가인, could it? He could not have known about 모그헤디엔, much less come back to rescue her. Could he? Those men 랜드 was gathering, those Asha’man. Rumor in every village carried whispers of Asha’man and the 검은 탑. Most of the sisters tried to pretend they were unaffected by dozens of men who could channel gathering in one spot—the worst of the tales had to be inflated; rumor always exaggerated—but 에그웨인’s toes wanted to curl under with fright whenever she thought of them. An Asha’man could have. . . . But why? How would he have known, any more than 로가인?

She was trying to avoid the only reasonable conclusion. Something far worse than 로가인 come back, or even Asha’man. One of the 버림받은 자들 had freed 모그헤디엔. 라빈 was dead by 랜드’s hand, according to 니나브, and he had killed 이샤마엘 as well, or so it seemed. And 아지노르 and 발타멜. 모이라인 had killed Be’lal. That left only 아스모데안, 디만드레드 and 사마엘 among the men. 사마엘 was in 일리안. No one knew where the others were, or any of the women who survived. 모이라인 had done for 란피어 too, or they had done for each other, but all the other women were still alive, so far as anyone knew. Forget the women. It had been a man. Which? Plans had been laid long since in case one of the 버림받은 자들 struck at the camp. No one sister here could equal any of the 버림받은 자들 by herself, but linked in circles was another matter, and any 버림받은 자들 who stepped into their camp would find circles forming on every side of him. Or her. Once they realized who she was. The 버림받은 자들 showed no signs of agelessness, for some reason. Maybe it was some effect of being connected to the 어둠의 존재. They. . . .

This was dithering. She had to start thinking clearly.

“Chesa?”

“. . . . look like you need your head rubbed for the ache again is what, is what you. . . . Yes, Mother?”

“Find 시우안 and 리안. Tell them to come to me. But don’t let anyone hear you.”

Grinning, Chesa dropped a curtsy and scampered out. She could hardly avoid knowing the currents that swirled around 에그웨인, yet she found all the plotting and scheming fun. Not that she knew more than surface, and little enough of that. 에그웨인 did not doubt her loyalty, but Chesa’s opinion of what was exciting might change if she learned the depth of those swirls.

Channeling the oil lamps inside the tent alight, 에그웨인 blew out the lantern and set it carefully in a corner. Maybe she had to think clearly, but she still felt as if she was stumbling in the dark.

A Pair of Silverpike

에그웨인 was sitting in her chair—one of the few real chairs in the camp, with a little plain carving like a farmer’s best armchair, roomy and comfortable enough that she felt only a touch of guilt about taking up valuable wagon space for it—she was sitting there trying to pull her thoughts together when 시우안 swept aside the entry flaps and ducked into the tent. 시우안 was not happy.

“Why in the Light did you run off?” Her voice had not changed with her face, and she chided with the best even when she did it in respectful tones. Barely respectful. Her blue eyes remained the same, too; they could have done for a saddlemaker’s awls. “셰리암 brushed me aside like a fly.” That surprisingly delicate mouth twisted bitterly. “She was gone almost as soon as you were. Don’t you realize she handed herself to you? She certainly does. Her, and Anaiya and Morvrin and the lot of them. You can be sure they’ll spend tonight trying to bail water and patch holes. They could manage it. I don’t see how, but they might.”

Almost as the last word left her mouth, 리안 entered. A tall, willowy woman, her coppery face was as youthful as 시우안’s, and for the same reason; she also was more than old enough to be 에그웨인’s mother, in truth. 리안 took one look at 시우안 and threw up her hands as much as the roof of the tent would allow. “Mother, this is a foolish risk.” Her dark eyes went from dreamy to flashing, but her voice had a languorous quality even when she was irritated. Once, it had been brisk. “If anyone sees 시우안 and me together this way—”

“I don’t care if the whole camp learns your squabbling is a fraud,” 에그웨인 broke in sharply, weaving a small barrier against eavesdropping around the three of them. It could be worked through with time, but not without detection, so long as she held the weave instead of tying it off.

She did care, and perhaps she should not have called them both, but her first half-coherent thought had been to summon the two sisters she could count on. No one in the camp so much as suspected. Everyone knew the former Amyrlin and her former Keeper detested one another every bit as much as 시우안 detested being tutor to her successor. Should any sister uncover the truth, they might well find themselves doing penance for a long time to come, and not an easy one—에스 세다이 appreciated being made fools of even less than other people; *kings* had been made to pay for that—but in the meanwhile their supposed animosity resulted in a certain leverage with the other sisters, including 의석자들. If *they* both said the same thing, it must be so. Another incidental effect of being stilled was very useful, one no one else knew about. The 세 가지 맹세 no longer held them; they could lie like wool merchants, now.

Schemes and deceptions on every side. The camp was like some fetid swamp where strange growths sprouted unseen in mists. Maybe anywhere 에스 세다이 gathered was like that. After three thousand years of plotting, however necessary, it was hardly surprising that scheming had become second nature to most sisters and only a breath away for the rest. The truly horrible thing was that she found herself beginning to enjoy all the machinations. Not for their own sake, but as puzzles, though no twisted bits of iron could intrigue her a quarter so much. What that said about her, she did not want to know. Well, she *was* 에스 세다이, whatever anyone thought, and she had to take the bad of it with the good.

“모그헤디엔 has escaped,” she went on without pause. “A man removed the *a’dam* from her. A man who can channel. I think one of them took the necklace away; it wasn’t in her tent, that I saw. There might be some way to find it using the bracelet, but if there is, I don’t know it.”

That took the starch right out of them. 리안’s legs gave way, and she dropped like a sack onto the stool Chesa sometimes used. 시우안 sat down on the cot slowly, back very straight, hands very still on her knees. Incongruously, 에그웨인 noticed that her dress had tiny blue flowers embroidered in a wide 타이런 maze around the bottom, a band that made the divided skirts seem one when she was still. Another band curved becomingly across the bodice. Concern for her clothes, that they be pretty instead of just suitable, was certainly a small change, looking at it one way—she never took it to extremes—yet in another, it was as drastic as her face. And a puzzle. 시우안 resented the changes, and resisted them. Except for this one.

리안, on the other hand, in true 에스 세다이 fashion embraced what had changed. A young woman again—에그웨인 had overheard a Yellow exclaiming in wonder that both were prime childbearing age, by everything she could find—she might never have been Keeper, never have had any other face. The very image of practicality and efficiency became the ideal of an indolent and alluring 도마니 woman. Even her riding dress was cut in the style of her native land, and no matter that its silk, so thin it barely seemed opaque, was as impractical as the pale green color for traveling dusty roads. Told that having been stilled had broken all ties and associations, 리안 had chosen the 녹색 아자 over a return to the Blue. Changing 아자s was not done, but then, no one had been stilled and then Healed before, either. 시우안 had gone right back into the Blue, grumbling over the idiotic need to “entreat and appeal for acceptance” as the formal phrase went.

“Oh, Light!” 리안 breathed as she thumped onto the stool with considerably less than her usual grace. “We should have turned her over for trial the first day. Nothing we’ve learned from her is worth letting her loose on the world again. Nothing!” It was a measure of her shock; she did not normally go about stating the obvious. Her brain had not grown indolent, whatever her outward demeanor. 란guid and seductive 도마니 women might be on the outside, but they were still known as the sharpest traders anywhere.

“Blood and bloody—! We should have had her watched,” 시우안 growled through her teeth.

에그웨인’s eyebrows rose. 시우안 must be as shaken as 리안. “By who, 시우안? Faolain? Theodrin? They don’t even know you two are of my party.” A party? Five women. And Faolain and Theodrin were hardly eager adherents, especially Faolain. 니나브 and 엘레인 could be counted too, of course, and 비르기테 certainly, even if she was not 에스 세다이, but they were a long way off. Stealth and cunning were still her major strengths. Plus the fact that no one expected them of her. “How should I have explained to *anyone* why they were supposed to watch my serving woman? For that matter, what good would it have done? It had to be one of the 버림받은 자들. Do you really think Faolain and Theodrin together could have stopped him? I’m not sure I could have, even linked with Romanda and Lelaine.” They were the next two strongest women in the camp, as strong in the Power as 시우안 used to be.

시우안 visibly forced a scowl from her face, but even so, she snorted. She often said that if she could no longer be Amyrlin, then she would teach 에그웨인 how to be the best Amyrlin ever, yet the transition from lion on a hill to mouse underfoot was difficult. 에그웨인 allowed her no little latitude because of that.

“I want the two of you to ask about among those near the tent 모그헤디엔 was sleeping in. Someone must have seen the man. He had to come afoot. Anybody opening a gateway inside a space that little risked cutting her in two, however small he wove it.”

시우안 snorted, louder than the first time. “Why bother?” she growled. “Do you mean to go chasing after like some fool hero in a gleeman’s fool story and bring her back? Maybe tie up all the 버림받은 자들 at one go? Win the Last Battle while you’re at it? Even if we get a description head to toe, nobody knows one 버림받은 자들 from another. Nobody here, anyway. It’s the most bloody useless barrel of fish guts I ever—!”

“시우안!” 에그웨인 said sharply, sitting up straighter. Latitude was one thing, but there were limits. She did not put up with this even from Romanda.

Color bloomed slowly in 시우안’s cheeks. Struggling to master herself, she kneaded her skirts and avoided 에그웨인’s eyes. “Forgive me, Mother,” she said finally. She almost sounded as if she meant it.

“It has been a difficult day for her, Mother,” 리안 put in with an impish smile. She was very good at those, though she generally used them to set some man’s heart racing. Not promiscuously, of course; she possessed discrimination and discretion in ample supply. “But then, most are. If she could only learn not to throw things at Gareth Bryne every time she gets angry—”

“Enough!” 에그웨인 snapped. 리안 was only trying to take a little of the pressure from 시우안, but she was in no mood for it. “I want to know anything I can learn about whoever freed 모그헤디엔, even if it’s just whether he was short or tall. Any scrap that makes him less a shadow creeping in the dark. If that’s not more than I have a right to ask.” 리안 sat quite still, staring at the flowers in the carpet in front of her toes.

The redness spread to cover nearly 시우안’s whole face; with her fair skin, it made her look like a sunset. “I . . . humbly beg your pardon, Mother.” This time, she did sound penitent. Her difficulty meeting 에그웨인’s gaze was obvious. “Sometimes it’s hard to. . . . No, no excuses. I humbly beg pardon.”

에그웨인 fingered her stole, letting the moment set itself as she looked at 시우안 without blinking. That was something 시우안 herself had taught her, but after a bit she shifted uneasily on the cot. When you knew you were in the wrong, silence pricked, and the pricks drove home that you were wrong. Silence was a very useful tool in a number of situations. “Since I can’t recall what I should forgive,” she said at last, quietly, “there seems to be no need. But, 시우안. . . . Don’t let it happen again.”

“Thank you, Mother.” A hint of wry laughter curled the corners of 시우안’s mouth. “If I may say so, I seem to have taught you very well. But if I may suggest . . . ?” She waited for 에그웨인’s impatient nod. “One of us should carry your order to Faolain or Theodrin to ask the questions, very sulky at being made a messenger. They’ll occasion a deal less comment than 리안 or I. Everyone knows you are their patron.”

에그웨인 agreed immediately. She still was not thinking clearly, or she would have seen that for herself. The headachy feeling was back again. Chesa claimed it came from too little sleep, but sleeping was difficult when your head felt taut as a drumhead. It would take a larger head than hers not to feel tight, stuffed with as many worries as she had. Well, at least now she could pass on the secrets that had kept 모그헤디엔 hidden, how to weave disguises with the Power and how to mask your ability from other women who could channel. Revealing those had been too risky when they might have led to unmasking 모그헤디엔.

*A bit more acclaim*, she thought wryly. There had been great petting and exclaiming when she announced the once-lost secret of 이동, which at least had been her own, and more praise since for every one of the secrets she had wrenched out of 모그헤디엔, like pulling a back tooth each time. None of the acclaim made an ounce of difference in her position, though. You could pat a talented child on the head without forgetting she was a child.

리안 departed with a curtsy and a dry comment that she was not sorry somebody else would have less than a full night’s rest for once. 시우안 waited; no one could be allowed to see her and 리안 leaving together. For a time 에그웨인 merely studied the other woman. Neither spoke; 시우안 seemed lost in thought. Finally she gave a start and stood, straightening her dress, plainly preparing to go.

“시우안,” 에그웨인 began slowly, and found herself uncertain how to continue.

시우안 thought she understood. “You were not only right, Mother,” she said, looking 에그웨인 straight in the eye, “you were lenient. Too lenient, though I say it who shouldn’t. You are the 아미를린 석좌, and no one may be insolent or impertinent to you. If you’d given me a penance that made even Romanda feel sorry for me, it would have been no more than I deserved.”

“I will remember that next time,” 에그웨인 said, and 시우안 bowed her head as if in acceptance. Maybe it was. Unless the changes in her ran deeper than seemed possible, there almost certainly would be a next time, and more after that. “But what I want to ask about is Lord Bryne.” All expression vanished from 시우안’s face. “Are you sure you wouldn’t like me to . . . intervene?”

“Why would I want that, Mother?” 시우안’s voice was blander than cold water soup. “The only duties I have are teaching you the etiquette of your office and handing 셰리암 reports from my eyes-and-ears.” She still retained some of her former network, though it was doubtful any knew who their reports went to now. “Gareth Bryne hardly requires enough of my time to interfere with that.” She almost always referred to him that way, and even when she used his title, she put a bite into it.

“시우안, a burned barn and a few cows couldn’t cost that much.” Not compared with paying and feeding all those soldiers, certainly. But she had offered before, and the stiff reply was the same.
“I thank you, Mother, but no. I won’t have him saying I break my word, and I swore to *work* the debt off.” Abruptly, 시우안’s stiffness dissolved in laughter, rare when she spoke about Lord Bryne. Scowls were much more common. “If you need to worry about somebody, worry about him, not me. I need no help handling Gareth Bryne.”

And that was the strange part. Weak she might be in the 하나의 힘, now, but not so weak that 시우안 had to keep on as his servant, spending hours up to her elbows in hot soapy water with his shirts and smallclothes. Perhaps she did so in order to have someone at hand on whom she could loose the temper she was otherwise forced to keep in a sack. Whatever the reason, it occasioned no little talk, and confirmed her oddness in many eyes; she *was* 에스 세다이, after all, if rather far down. His methods of dealing with her temper—once she threw plates and boots, anyway—outraged her and provoked threats of dire consequences, yet though she could have wrapped him up unable to stir a finger, 시우안 never touched *세다르* around him, not to do his chores and not even when it meant being turned over his knee. That fact she had kept hidden from most so far, but some things slipped out when she was in a rage, or when 리안 was in a humor. There seemed to *be* no explanation. 시우안 was not weak-spirited or a fool, she was neither meek nor afraid, she was not. . . .

“You might as well be on your way, 시우안.” Clearly, some secrets were not going to be revealed tonight. “It’s late, and I know you want your bed.”

“Yes, Mother. And, thank you,” she added, though 에그웨인 could not have said for what.

After 시우안 left, 에그웨인 rubbed her temples once more. She wanted to pace. The tent would not do; it might be the largest in the camp occupied by just one person, but that meant less than two spans by two, and it was crowded with cot and chair and stool, washstand and stand-mirror and no fewer than three chests full of clothes. Chesa had seen to those last, and 셰리암, and Romanda and Lelaine and a dozen more 의석자들. They kept seeing to them; a few more gifts of silk shifts or stockings, one more dress grand enough to receive a king, and there would be need for a fourth chest. Maybe 셰리암 and the 의석자들 hoped all the fine dresses would blind her to anything else, but Chesa just thought the 아미를린 석좌 had to be clothed suitably for her station. Servants, it seemed, believed in following the correct rituals as much as the Hall ever did. Shortly Selame would be there; it was her turn to undress 에그웨인 for bed, another ritual. Only, between her head and her restless feet, she was not ready for bed yet.

Leaving the lamps burning, she hurried out before Selame could arrive. Walking would clear her head, and maybe tire her enough that she could sleep soundly. Putting herself to sleep would be no problem—the Wise One dreamwalkers had taught her that skill early on—yet finding any rest in it was another matter. Especially when her mind boiled with a list of worries that began with Romanda and Lelaine and 셰리암, then ran through 랜드, 엘라이더, 모그헤디엔, the weather and on out of sight.

She avoided the area near 모그헤디엔’s tent. If she asked questions herself, too much importance would be given to a servant running away. Discretion had become part of her. The game she played allowed few slips, and being careless where you knew it did not matter could lead to being careless where it did. Worse, you could discover you had been wrong about where it mattered. *The weak must be bold cautiously*. That was 시우안 again; she truly did her best to teach, and she knew this particular game very well.

There were no more people out and about in the moon-shadowed camp than had been there before, handfuls slouched wearily around low fires, exhausted by their evening’s labors after a hard day’s journey. Those who saw her rose tiredly to make their courtesies as she passed, murmuring “빛 shine on you, Mother” or something like, occasionally asking her blessing, which she gave with a simple “빛 bless you, my child.” Men and women old enough to be her grandparents sat back down beaming from that, yet she wondered what they actually believed about her, what they knew. All the 에스 세다이 presented an unbroken front to the outside world, including their own servants. But 시우안 said that if you believed a servant knew twice what he should, you only knew half the truth. Still, those bows and curtsies and murmurs followed her from one clump of people to the next, comforting her with the possibility that there were some at least who did not see her as a child the Hall brought out when they needed her.

As she passed an open area surrounded by ropes tied to posts driven into the ground, a gateway’s silver slash of light flashed vivid in the darkness as it rotated open. It was not really light, though; it cast no shadows. She paused to watch beside a corner post. No one at the nearby fires even looked up; they were used to this by now. A dozen or more sisters, twice as many servants and a number of 감시자s bustled out, returning with messages and wicker cages of pigeons from the dovecotes in Salidar, a good five hundred miles west and south as the goose flew.

They began scattering before the gateway closed, carrying their burdens to 의석자들, to their 아자s, a few back to their own tents. Most nights, 시우안 would have been with them; she seldom trusted anyone else to fetch messages destined for her even if most were in codes or ciphers. Sometimes the world seemed to hold more networks of eyes-and-ears than it did 에스 세다이, though most were severely truncated by circumstance. The majority of agents for the various 아자s seemed to be lying low until the “difficulties” in the 백색 탑 subsided, and a good many of the individual sisters’ eyes-and-ears had no idea where the woman they served was at present.

Several of the 감시자s saw 에그웨인 and made careful bows, with a respect proper to the stole; sisters might eye her askance, but the Hall had raised her Amyrlin and the Gaidin needed no more. A number of the servants offered bows or curtsies, too. Not one of the 에스 세다이 hurrying away from the gateway so much as glanced in her direction. Perhaps they did not notice her. Perhaps.

In a way, that anybody could still hear from any of their eyes-and-ears at all was one of 모그헤디엔’s “gifts.” The sisters with the strength to make gateways had all been in Salidar long enough to know it well. Those who could weave a gateway of useful size were able to Travel almost anywhere from there, and land right on the spot. Trying to Travel *to* Salidar, however, would have meant spending half of each night learning the new roped-off patch of ground, more for some, every time they made camp. What 에그웨인 had pried from 모그헤디엔 was a way to journey from a place you did not know well to one you did. Slower than 이동, 스키밍 was not one of the lost Talents—no one had ever heard of it—so even the name was credited to 에그웨인. Anyone who could Travel could Skim, so every night sisters Skimmed to Salidar, checking the dovecotes for birds that had returned to where they had been hatched, then Traveled back.

The sight should have pleased her—the rebel 에스 세다이 had gained Talents the 백색 탑 thought lost forever, as well as learned new ones, and those abilities would help cost 엘라이더 the 아미를린 석좌 before all was done—yet instead of pleasure, 에그웨인 felt sourness. Being snubbed had nothing to do with it, or not much, anyway. As she walked on, the fires grew farther between, then faded behind; all around her lay the dark shapes of wagons, most with canvas tops stretched over iron hoops, and tents glowing palely in the moonlight. Beyond, the army’s campfires climbed the surrounding hills all around, the stars brought to ground. The silence from Caemlyn tied her middle into knots, whatever anyone else thought.

The very day they left Salidar a message had arrived, though 셰리암 had not bothered to show it to her until a few days ago, and then with repeated warnings on the need to keep the contents secret. The Hall knew, but no one else must. More of the ten thousand secrets that infested the camp. 에그웨인 was sure she never would have seen it if she had not kept going on about 랜드. She could recall every carefully chosen word, written in a tiny hand on paper so thin it was a wonder the pen had not torn through.

> We are well settled at the inn of which we spoke, and we have met with the wool merchant. He is a *very* remarkable young man, everything that 니나브 told us. Still, he was courteous. I think he is somewhat afraid of us, which is to the good. It will go well.

> You may have heard rumors about men here, including a fellow from 살다에아. The rumors are all too true, I fear, but we have seen none of them and will avoid them if we can. If you pursue two hares, both will escape you.

> Verin and Alanna are here, with a number of young women from the same region as the wool merchant. I will try to send them on to you for training. Alanna has formed an attachment to the wool merchant which may prove useful, though it is troubling too. All will go well, I am sure.

> Merana

셰리암 emphasized the good news, as she saw it. Merana, an experienced negotiator, had reached Caemlyn and been well received by 랜드, the “wool merchant.” Wonderful news, to 셰리암. And Verin and Alanna would be bringing 두 강 girls to become 수련생s. 셰리암 was sure they must be coming down the same road they themselves were headed up. She seemed to think 에그웨인 would be all aglow at the expectation of seeing faces from home. Merana would handle everything. Merana knew what she was doing.

“That’s a bucket of horse sweat,” 에그웨인 muttered at the night. A gap-toothed fellow carrying a large wooden bucket gave a start and gaped at her, so amazed he forgot to bow.

랜드, *courteous*? She had seen his first meeting with Coiren Saeldain, 엘라이더’s emissary. “Overbearing” summed it up nicely. Why should he be different with Merana? And Merana thought he was afraid, thought that was good. 랜드 was seldom afraid even when he should be, and if he was now, Merana should remember that fear could make the mildest man dangerous, remember that 랜드 was dangerous just being who he was. And what was this attachment Alanna had formed? 에그웨인 did not entirely trust Alanna. The woman did extremely odd things at times, maybe impetuously and maybe with some deeper motive. 에그웨인 would not put it past her to find a way into 랜드’s bed; he would be clay in the hands of a woman like her. 엘레인 would break Alanna’s neck if that was so, but that was the least of it. Worst of all, no more of the pigeons Merana had taken with her had appeared in the Salidar dovecotes.

Merana should have had some word to send, if only that she and the rest of the embassy had gone to 케렌. Lately the 현명한 이들 did little more than acknowledge 랜드 was alive, yet it seemed he was there, sitting on his hands as far as she could make out. Which should have been a warning beacon. 셰리암 saw it differently. Who could say why any man did what he did? Probably not even the man himself, most of the time, and when it came to one who could channel. . . . Silence proved all was well; Merana surely would have reported any real difficulty. She must be on her way to 케렌, if not there already, and there was no need to report further until she could send word of success. For that matter, 랜드 in 케렌 *was* success of a sort. One of Merana’s goals, if not the most important, had been to ease him out of Caemlyn so that 엘레인 could return there safely and take the Lion Throne, and the dangers of 케렌 had dissipated. Incredible as it seemed, the 현명한 이들 said Coiren and her embassy had left the city on their way back to 타르 발론. Or maybe not so incredible. It all made a sort of sense, given 랜드, given the way 에스 세다이 did things. Even so, to 에그웨인, it all felt . . . wrong.

“I have to go to him,” she muttered. One hour, and she could straighten everything out. Underneath, he was still 랜드. “That’s all there is to it. I have to go to him.”

“That isn’t possible, and you know it.”

If 에그웨인 had not had herself on a tight rein, she would have jumped a foot. As it was, her heart pounded even after she made out 리안 by the light of the moon. “I thought you were . . .” she said before she could stop herself, and only just managed not to say 모그헤디엔’s name.

The taller woman fell in beside her, keeping a careful watch for other sisters as they walked. 리안 did not have 시우안’s excuse for spending time with her. Not that being seen together once should cause any harm, but . . .

*“Should not” isn’t always “will not,”* 에그웨인 reminded herself. Slipping the stole from her shoulders, she folded it to carry in one hand. At a glance, from a distance, 리안 might well be taken for an 허락받은 자 despite her dress; many 허락받은 자 lacked enough of the banded white dresses to wear one all the time. From a distance, 에그웨인 might be taken for one, too. Not the most pacifying thought.

“Theodrin and Faolain are asking around near Marigan’s tent, Mother. They weren’t especially pleased. I did a fine sulk over carrying messages, if I do say so. Theodrin had to stop Faolain dressing me down for it.” 리안’s laughter was quiet and breathy. Situations that grated 시우안’s teeth usually amused her. She was cosseted by most of the other sisters for how well she had adjusted.

“Good, good,” 에그웨인 said absently. “Merana misstepped somehow, 리안, or he wouldn’t be staying in 케렌, and she wouldn’t be keeping quiet.” Off in the distance, a dog bayed at the moon, then others, until they were abruptly silenced by shouts that, perhaps luckily, she could not quite understand. A number of the soldiers had dogs tagging along; there were none in the 에스 세다이 camp. Any number of cats, but no dogs.

“Merana does know what she is doing, Mother.” It sounded very like a sigh. 리안 and 시우안 both agreed with 셰리암. Everyone did, except her. “When you give someone a task, you have to trust it to them.”

에그웨인 sniffed and folded her arms. “리안, that man could strike sparks from a damp cloth, if it wore the shawl. I don’t know Merana, but I’ve never seen an 에스 세다이 who qualified as a damp cloth.”

“I’ve met one or two,” 리안 chuckled. This time her sigh was plain. “But not Merana, true. Does he really believe he has friends inside the Tower? Alviarin? That might make him difficult for Merana, I suppose, but I can hardly see Alviarin doing anything to risk her place. She was always ambitious enough for three.”

“He has a letter supposedly from her.” She could still see 랜드 gloating over receiving letters from 엘라이더 and Alviarin both, back before she herself left 케렌. “Maybe her ambitions make her think *she* can replace 엘라이더 with him on her side. That’s if she really wrote it. He thinks he’s clever, 리안—maybe he is—but he doesn’t believe he needs anyone.” 랜드 would go on thinking he could handle anything by himself right up until one of those anythings crushed him. “I know him inside and out, 리안. Being around the 현명한 이들 seems to have infected him, or maybe he infected them. Whatever the 의석자들 think, whatever any of you think, an 에스 세다이’s shawl doesn’t impress him any more than it does the 현명한 이들. Sooner or later he’ll exasperate a sister until she does something about it, or one of them will push him the wrong way, not realizing how strong he is, and what his temper is now. After that there might be no going back. I’m the only one who can deal with him safely. The only one.”

“He can hardly be as . . . irritating . . . as those 아일women,” 리안 murmured wryly. Even she found it difficult to be amused by her experiences with the 현명한 이들. “But it hardly matters. ‘The 아미를린 석좌 being valued with the 백색 탑 itself. . . .’ ”

A pair of women appeared between the tents ahead, moving slowly as they talked. Distance and shadows obscured their faces, yet it was clear they were 에스 세다이 from the way they carried themselves, an assurance that nothing hiding in any darkness could harm them. No 허락받은 자 on the brink of the shawl could manage quite that degree of confidence. A queen with an army at her back might not. Scowling with frustration, 에그웨인 nearly pulled her out again and marched on. Let it all come into the open. Only one Tower law specifically limited the power of the 아미를린 석좌. A fistful of irritating customs and a barrel full of inconvenient realities, but only one law, yet it could not have been a worse for her purposes. “The 아미를린 석좌 being valued with the 백색 탑 itself, as the very heart of the 백색 탑, she must not be endangered without dire necessity, therefore unless the 백색 탑 be at war by declaration of the 탑의 회의실, the 아미를린 석좌 shall seek the lesser consensus of the 탑의 회의실 before deliberately placing herself in the way of any danger, and she shall abide by the consensus that stands.” What rash incident by an Amyrlin had inspired that, 에그웨인 did not know, but it had been law for something over two thousand years. To most 에스 세다이, any law that old attained an aura of holiness; changing it was unthinkable.

Romanda had quoted that . . . that *bloody* law as though lecturing a half-wit. If the Daughter-Heir of 안도르 could not be allowed within a hundred miles of the 용의 환생, how much more they must preserve the 아미를린 석좌. Lelaine sounded almost regretful, most likely because she was agreeing with Romanda. That had nearly curdled both their tongues. Without them, both of them, the lesser consensus lay as far out of reach as the greater. Light, even that declaration of war only required the lesser consensus! So if she could not obtain permission. . . . 리안 cleared her throat. “You can hardly do much if you go in secret, Mother, and the Hall will find out, soon or late. I think you would find it difficult to have an hour to yourself after that. Not that they’d dare put a guard on you, precisely, but there are ways. I can quote examples from . . . certain sources.” She never mentioned the hidden records directly unless they were behind a ward.

“Am I so transparent?” 에그웨인 asked after a moment. But there were tents and furnishings and foodstuffs, and a thousand things needed to keep the sisters and those who served them. The loudest sounds here were snores, a chorus of frogs.

“No, Mother,” 리안 laughed softly. “I just thought what I would do. But it’s well known I’ve lost all my dignity and sense; the 아미를린 석좌 can hardly take me for a model. I think you must let young Master al’Thor go as he will, for a time anyway, while you pluck the goose that’s in front of you.”

“His way may lead us all to the Pit of Doom,” 에그웨인 muttered, but it was not an argument. There had to be a way to pluck that goose and still keep 랜드 from making dangerous mistakes, but she could not see it now. Not frogs; those snores sounded like a hundred saws cutting logs full of knots. “This is as bad a spot for a soothing walk as I’ve ever visited. I think I might as well go to bed.”

리안 tilted her head. “In that case, Mother, if you will forgive me, there’s a man in Lord Bryne’s camp. . . . After all, whoever heard of a Green without even one 감시자?” From the sudden quickening in her voice, you might have thought she was off to meet a lover. Considering what 에그웨인 had heard about Greens, perhaps there was not that much difference.

Back among the tents, the last of the fires had been doused with dirt; no one took risks with fire when the countryside was tinder dry. A few tendrils of smoke rose lazily in the moonlight where the job had not been well done. A man murmured drowsily in his sleep inside a tent, and here and there a cough drifted out or a rasping snore, but otherwise the camp lay silent and still. Which was why 에그웨인 was surprised when someone stepped from the shadows in front of her, especially someone wearing the simple white dress of a 수련생.

“Mother, I need to speak to you.”

“Nicola?” 에그웨인 had made a point of fixing name to face for every 수련생, no easy chore given how sisters hunted all along the army’s path for girls and young women who could learn. Active search was still not well thought of—custom was to wait for the girl to ask, best of all to wait for her to come to the Tower—but ten times as many 수련생s studied in the camp now as the 백색 탑 had held in years. Nicola was one to be remembered, though, and besides, 에그웨인 had often noticed the young woman staring at her. “Tiana won’t be pleased if she finds you up this late.” Tiana Noselle was the 수련생 감독관, known equally for a comforting shoulder when a 수련생 needed to cry and an unyielding stance when it came to rules.

The other woman shifted as if to hurry away, then straightened her back. Sweat glistened on her cheeks. The darkness was cooler than the light had been, but not what anyone would call cool, and the simple trick of ignoring heat or cold came only with the shawl. “I know I’m supposed to ask to see Tiana Sedai and then ask her to see you, Mother, but she’d never let a 수련생 approach the 아미를린 석좌.”

“About what, child?” 에그웨인 asked. The woman was older by six or seven years at least, but that was the proper address for a 수련생.

Fidgeting with her skirt, Nicola stepped closer. Large eyes met 에그웨인’s perhaps more directly than a 수련생’s should have. “Mother, I want to go as far as I can.” Her hands plucked at her dress, but her voice was cool and self-possessed, fit for an 에스 세다이. “I won’t say they are holding me back, but I am sure I can become stronger than they say. I just know I can. You were never held back, Mother. No one has ever gained so much of her strength as fast as you. All I ask is the same chance.”

Movement in the shadow behind Nicola turned into another sweaty-faced woman, this one in short coat and wide trousers, carrying a bow. Her hair hung to her waist in a braid tied with six ribbons, and she wore short boots with raised heels.

Nicola Treehill and Areina Nermasiv seemed an odd pair to be friends. Like many of the older 수련생s—women with nearly ten years on 에그웨인 were tested now, though many sisters still grumbled that they were ten years too old to accept 수련생 discipline—like many of those older women, Nicola was ferocious in her desire to learn, by all reports, and she had a potential bettered only by 니나브, 엘레인 and 에그웨인 herself among living 에스 세다이. In fact, Nicola apparently was making great strides, often great enough that her teachers had to slow her down. Some said she had begun picking up weaves as if she already knew them. Not only that, but she already demonstrated two Talents, although the ability to “see” *ta’veren* was minor, while the major Talent, Foretelling, emerged so that no one understood what she had Foretold. She herself did not remember a word she said. All in all, Nicola was already marked by the sisters as someone to watch despite her late start. The begrudging agreement to test women older than seventeen or eighteen probably could be laid at Nicola’s feet.

Areina, on the other hand, was a Hunter for the Horn who swaggered as much as a man and sat around talking of adventures, those she had had and those she would, when she was not practicing with her bow. Very likely she had picked that weapon up from 비르기테, along with her manner of dress. She certainly seemed to have no interest in anything beside the bow, except flirting occasionally, in a rather forward manner, though not lately. Perhaps long days on the road left her too tired for it, if not for archery. Why she was still traveling with them, 에그웨인 could not understand; it was hardly likely that Areina believed the 발레르의 뿔 would turn up along their march, and impossible that she even suspected it was hidden away inside the 백색 탑. *Very* few people knew that. 에그웨인 was not certain even 엘라이더 did.

Areina seemed a posturing fool, but 에그웨인 felt a certain sympathy for Nicola. She understood the woman’s discontent, understood wanting to know it all now. She had been that way, too. Maybe she still was. “Nicola,” she said gently, “we all have limits. I’ll never match 니나브 Sedai, for example, whatever I do.”

“But if I could only have the chance, Mother.” Nicola actually wrung her hands in pleading, and there was a touch of it in her voice, yet her eyes still met 에그웨인’s levelly. “The chance you had.”

“What I did—because I had no choice, because I didn’t know better—is called forcing, Nicola, and it is dangerous.” She had not heard that term until 시우안 apologized for doing it to her; that was one time 시우안 truly had seemed repentant. “You know if you try to channel more of *세다르* than you’re ready to handle, you risk burning yourself out before you ever come close to your full strength. Best you learn to be patient. The sisters won’t let you be anything else until you are ready, anyway.”

“We came to Salidar on the same riverboat as 니나브 and 엘레인,” Areina said suddenly. Her gaze was more than direct; it was challenging. “And 비르기테.” For some reason, she said the name bitterly.

Nicola made shushing motions. “There’s no need to bring that up.” Oddly, she did not sound as if she meant it.

Hoping she was keeping her face half so smooth as Nicola’s, 에그웨인 tried to quell a sudden uneasiness. “Marigan” had come to Salidar on that boat, too. An owl hooted, and she shivered. Some people thought hearing an owl in moonlight meant bad news was coming. She was not superstitious, but. . . . “No need to bring up what?”

The other two women exchanged looks, and Areina nodded.

“It was on the walk from the river to the village.” For all her supposed reluctance, Nicola peered straight into 에그웨인’s eyes. “Areina and I heard 톰 Merrilin and Juilin Sandar talking. The gleeman, and the thief-taker? Juilin said if there were 에스 세다이 in the village—we weren’t sure, yet—and they learned 니나브 and 엘레인 had been pretending to be 에스 세다이, then we were all jumping into a school of silverpike, which I take it isn’t very safe.”

“The gleeman saw us and hushed him,” Areina put in, fingering the quiver at her waist, “but we heard.” Her voice was hard as her stare.
“I know they’re both 에스 세다이 now, Mother, but wouldn’t they still be in trouble if anyone found out? The sisters, I mean? Anybody who pretends to be a sister is in trouble if they find out, even years later.” Nicola’s face did not change, but her gaze suddenly seemed to be trying to fix 에그웨인’s. She leaned a little forward, intent. “Anybody at all. Isn’t that so?”

Emboldened by 에그웨인’s silence, Areina grinned. An unpleasant grin in the night. “I hear 니나브 and 엘레인 were sent out of the Tower on some task by the 산체 woman back when she was Amyrlin. I hear you were sent off by her, too, at the same time. Got into all sorts of trouble when you came back.” Sly insinuation slithered into her voice. “Do you remember them playing at 에스 세다이?”

They stood there looking at her, Areina leaning insolently on her bow, Nicola so expectant the air should have crackled.

“시우안 산체 is 에스 세다이,” 에그웨인 said coldly, “and so are 니나브 al’Meara and 엘레인 Trakand. You will show them proper respect. To you, they are 시우안 Sedai, 니나브 Sedai and 엘레인 Sedai.” The pair blinked in surprise. Inside, her stomach quivered. With outrage. After everything she had been through tonight, she was confronted with *blackmail* from these . . . ? She could not think of a word bad enough. 엘레인 could have; 엘레인 listened to stablemen and wagon drivers and every sort, memorizing the words she should have refused to hear. Unfolding the striped stole, 에그웨인 draped it carefully across her shoulders.

“I don’t think you understand, Mother,” Nicola said hastily. Not fearfully, however; just attempting to force her point. “I merely worried that if anyone found out that you had—” 에그웨인 gave her no chance to go further.

“Oh, I understand, child.” The fool woman *was* a child, however old she was. Any number of the older 수련생s gave trouble, usually in the form of insolence toward 허락받은 자 set to teach them, but even the silliest had sense enough to avoid impertinence to the sisters. It fanned her anger to white heat, that the woman had the gall to try this on with her. They were both taller than she, if not by much, but she planted her fists on her hips and drew herself up, and they shrank away as though she loomed. “Do you have any notion how serious it is to bring charges against a sister, especially for a 수련생? Charges based on a conversation you claim to have heard between men now a thousand miles away! Tiana would skin you alive and put you to scrubbing pots the rest of your natural life.” Nicola kept trying to push a word in—apologies, they sounded like this time, and more protests that 에그웨인 did not understand, frantic attempts to change everything—but 에그웨인 ignored her and rounded on Areina. The Hunter took another step back, wetting her lips and looking remarkably uncertain. “You needn’t think you would walk away clear, either. Even a Hunter could be hauled to Tiana for a thing like this. If you’re lucky enough not to be flogged at a wagon tongue, the way they do soldiers caught stealing. Either way, you’ll be tossed out by the road with your welts for company.”

Drawing a deep breath, 에그웨인 folded her hands at her waist. Clutched together, they would not tremble. All but cowering, the pair looked suitably chastened. She hoped those downcast eyes and slumped shoulders and shifting feet were not feigned. By rights, she should send them to Tiana right now. She had no idea what the penalty might be for trying to blackmail the 아미를린 석좌, but it seemed likely that being turned out of the camp would be the least of it. In Nicola’s case, the turning out would have to wait until her teachers were satisfied she knew enough of channeling not to hurt herself or others by accident. Nicola Treehill would never be 에스 세다이, though, once that charge was laid against her; all that potential would go for nothing.

Except. . . . Any woman caught pretending to be 에스 세다이 was set down so hard she would still be whimpering years later, and an 허락받은 자 caught might very well consider the other woman fortunate, but surely 니나브 and 엘레인 were safe now they really were sisters. Herself, as well. Only, it might take no more than a whisper of this to erase any chance of making the Hall acknowledge her truly the 아미를린 석좌. As well jaunt off to 랜드, and then tell the Hall to their faces. She dared not allow these two to see her doubt, or even suspect.

“I will forget this,” she said sharply. “But if I hear so much as a whisper of it again, from anyone. . . .” She drew a ragged breath—if she heard *shouts* of it, there might be little she could do—but by the way they jumped, they read a threat that pricked deep. “Get to your beds before I change my mind.”

In an instant they became a flurry of curtsies, of “Yes, Mother” and “No, Mother” and “As you command, Mother.” They scurried away looking back over their shoulders at her, every step faster than the last, until they were running. She had to walk on sedately, but she wanted to run too.
