My eyes see as if in a fog, my hand is burned away, and the old wounds in my side rip open if I do anything more strenuous than breathe. I’m dry, like an overused well. I need to finish my work here and get to 세이올 굴.*

*Otherwise, there won’t be anything left of me for the 어둠의 존재 to kill.*

That wasn’t a thought to cause laughter; it was one to cause despair. But 랜드 did not weep, for tears could not come from steel.

For the moment, 르웨어스 테린’s cries seemed enough for both of them.

**C*HAPTER** **2**

![](images/00302.jpg)

The Nature of Pain

에그웨인 stood up straight, backside aflame with the now-familiar agony of a solid beating beneath the hands of the 수련생 감독관. She felt like a rug that had just been pounded free of its dust. Despite that, she calmly straightened her white skirts, then turned to the room’s mirror and calmly dabbed the tears from the corners of her eyes. Only one tear in each eye this time. She smiled to her reflection, and her twin selves nodded to one another in satisfaction.

A small, dark-paneled room reflected behind her on the mirror’s silvery surface. Such a stern place it was, a sturdy stool in the corner, the top darkened and smoothed from years and years of use. A blockish desk, set with the 수련생 감독관’ thick tome. The narrow table directly behind 에그웨인 had some carvings, but its leather padding was far more distinctive. Many a 수련생—and not a few 허락받은 자—had bent down across that table, bearing the punishment for disobedience. 에그웨인 could almost imagine that the table’s dark color had come from repeated tearstains. Many of her own had been shed there.

But none today. Only two tears, and neither had fallen from her cheeks. Not that she didn’t hurt; her entire body seemed to burn from the pain. Indeed, the severity of those beatings had increased the longer she continued to defy the powers in the 백색 탑. But as the beatings had grown more frequent and more painful, 에그웨인’s resolve to endure had grown as well. She hadn’t yet managed to embrace and accept the pain as the 아일 did, but she felt that she was close. The 아일 could laugh during the most cruel of tortures. Well, she could smile the moment she stood up.

Each lash she endured, each pain she suffered, was a victory. And victory was always a reason for happiness, no matter how one’s pride or one’s skin burned.

Standing beside the table behind 에그웨인, reflected in the mirror, was the 수련생 감독관 herself. Silviana looked down at the leather strap in her hands, frowning. Her ageless square face seemed just faintly confused; she regarded the strap as one might a knife that refused to cut or a lamp that refused to light.

The woman was of the 적색 아자, a fact reflected in the trim on the hem of her simple gray dress and the fringed shawl on her shoulders. She was tall and stocky and she had her black hair back in a bun. In most ways 에그웨인 considered her a superior 수련생 감독관. Even if she *had* administered a ridiculous number of punishments to 에그웨인. Perhaps because of that. Silviana did her duty. Light knew there were few enough in the Tower lately of whom that could be said!

Silviana looked up and met 에그웨인’s eyes in the mirror. She quickly put down the strap and washed all emotion from her face. 에그웨인 turned around calmly.

Uncharacteristically, Silviana sighed. “When will you give this up, child?” she asked. “You’ve proven your point quite admirably, I must say, but you must know that I will continue to punish you until you submit. Proper order must be maintained.”

에그웨인 held in her shock. The 수련생 감독관 rarely addressed 에그웨인 except to offer instruction or reprobation. Still, there had been cracks before. . . .

“Proper order, Silviana?” 에그웨인 asked. “As it has been maintained elsewhere in the Tower?”

Silviana’s lips drew back in a line. She turned and made a notation in her book. “I will see you in the morning. Off to dinner with you.”

The morning punishment would be because 에그웨인 had called the 수련생 감독관 by her name without adding the honorific “Sedai” to the end. And likely because both knew that 에그웨인 would not curtsy before she left.

“I will return in the morning,” 에그웨인 said, “but dinner must wait. I have been ordered to attend 엘라이더 this evening as she eats.” This session with Silviana had gone long—에그웨인 had brought quite a list of infractions with her—and now she wouldn’t have time to eat. Her stomach complained at the prospect.

Silviana showed just a brief moment of emotion. Was it surprise? “And you said nothing of this earlier?”

“Would it have changed anything if I had?”

Silviana did not respond to the question. “You will eat after attending the Amyrlin, then. I shall leave instructions for the Mistress of the Kitchens to hold you some food. Considering how often you are being given 치유 these days, child, you will need to take your meals. I won’t have you collapsing from lack of nourishment.”

Stern, yet fair. A pity this one had found her way to the Red. “Very well,” 에그웨인 said.

“And after eating,” Silviana said, raising a finger, “you shall return to me for showing disrespect to the 아미를린 석좌. She is never to be known as simply ‘엘라이더’ to you, child.” She turned down to her ledger, adding, “Besides, Light only knows what kind of trouble you’ll be in by this evening.”

As 에그웨인 left the small chamber behind—entering a wide, gray-stoned hallway with floor tiles of green and red—she considered that last comment. Perhaps it *hadn’t* been surprise that Silviana had shown upon hearing of 에그웨인’s visit to 엘라이더. Perhaps it had been sympathy. 엘라이더 would not react well when 에그웨인 stood up to her the way she had to all others in the Tower.

Was that why Silviana had decided to bring 에그웨인 back for a final strapping after eating? With the orders Silviana had given, 에그웨인 would be *required* to take food before returning for her punishment, even if 엘라이더 heaped the strappings upon her.

It was a small kindness, but 에그웨인 was grateful for it. Enduring the daily punishments was difficult enough without skipping meals.

As she pondered, two Red sisters—Katerine and Barasine—approached her. Katerine held a brass cup. Another dose of forkroot. 엘라이더 wanted to make certain that 에그웨인 couldn’t channel a trickle during the meal, it seemed. 에그웨인 took the cup without protesting and downed it in a single gulp, tasting the faint, yet characteristic, hint of mint. She handed the cup back to Katerine with an offhanded gesture, and the woman had no choice but to accept it. Almost as if she were a royal cupbearer.

에그웨인 didn’t head for 엘라이더’s quarters immediately. The overly long punishment’s intrusion into the dinner hour ironically left her with a few spare moments—and she didn’t want to arrive early, for that would show 엘라이더 deference. So instead she lingered outside the door of the 수련생 감독관 with Katerine and Barasine. Would a certain figure come to visit the study?

In the distance, small clusters of sisters walked the hallway’s tiles of green and red. There was a furtive cast to their eyes, like hares venturing into a clearing to nibble at leaves, yet fearing the predator who hid in the shadows. Sisters in the Tower these days always wore their shawls, and they never went about alone. Some even held the Power, as if afraid of being jumped by footpads here in the 백색 탑 itself.

“Are you pleased with this?” 에그웨인 found herself asking. She glanced at Katerine and Barasine; both were, coincidentally, also part of the group that had first captured 에그웨인.

“What was that, child?” Katerine asked coolly. “Speaking to a sister without being asked a question first? Are you so eager for more punishment?” She wore a conspicuous amount of red, her dress a bright crimson slashed with black. Her dark hair curled slightly in its cascade down her back.

에그웨인 ignored the threat. What more could they do to her? “Set aside the bickering for a moment, Katerine,” 에그웨인 said, watching a group of Yellows pass, their step quickening as they saw the two Reds. “Set aside the posturing for authority and the threats. Put these things away and *look*. Are you proud of this? The Tower spent centuries without an Amyrlin being raised from the Red. Now, when you finally have a chance, your chosen leader has done *this* to the Tower. Women who won’t meet the eyes of those they do not know familiarly, sisters who travel in clusters. The 아자s behave as if they are at war with one another!”

Katerine sniffed at the comment, though the lanky Barasine hesitated, glancing over her shoulder at the group of Yellows hurrying down the corridor, several of them firing glances back at the two Reds.

“This was not caused by the Amyrlin,” Katerine said. “It was created by your foolish rebels and their betrayal!”

*My rebels?* 에그웨인 thought with an inward smile. *So you now see them as “mine,” rather than regarding me as just a poor 허락받은 자 who was duped? That’s progress.*

“Were we the ones who pulled down a sitting Amyrlin?” 에그웨인 asked. “Were we the ones who turned 감시자 against 감시자, or the ones who failed to contain the 용의 환생? Have we chosen an Amyrlin who is so power-hungry, she’s ordered the construction of her own *palace*? A woman who has every sister wondering if she’ll be the next to be stripped of the shawl?”

Katerine didn’t respond, as though realizing that she shouldn’t be drawn into an argument with a mere 수련생. Barasine still watched the distant Yellows, her eyes wide. Worried.

“I should think,” 에그웨인 said, “that the Red should not be the ones sheltering 엘라이더, but should instead provide her fiercest critics. For 엘라이더’s legacy will be your own. Remember that.”

Katerine glanced at her, eyes flaring, and 에그웨인 suppressed a cringe. Perhaps that last had been too straightforward.

“You will report to the 수련생 감독관 tonight, *child*,” Katerine informed her. “And explain how you showed disrespect to sisters and to the Amyrlin herself.”

에그웨인 held her tongue. Why was she wasting her time trying to convince Reds?

The aged wooden door behind her snapped shut, making 에그웨인 jump and glance over her shoulder. The tapestries to either side stirred slightly, then went still. 에그웨인 hadn’t realized that she’d left the door open just a crack as she’d left. Had Silviana listened to the conversation?

There was no more time to dawdle. It appeared that Alviarin wasn’t going to come this evening. Where was she? She always arrived for punishment right around the time that 에그웨인 finished. 에그웨인 shook her head, then strode away down the hallway. The two Reds followed—they stayed with her increasingly now, following her, watching her, at all times except when 에그웨인 visited the quarters of other 아자s for training. She tried to act as if those two sisters were an honorary retinue, rather than her jailers. She also tried to ignore the pain of her backside.

All signs indicated that 에그웨인 was winning her war against 엘라이더. Earlier, at lunch, 에그웨인 had heard the 수련생s gossiping about the dramatic failure 엘라이더 had suffered in failing to keep 랜드 captured. The event was several months past, now, and was supposed to have been secret. And then there was the rumor of Asha’man bonding sisters who had been sent to destroy them. Another mission of 엘라이더’s that wasn’t supposed to be known. 에그웨인 had taken steps to keep these failures strong in the minds of the Tower’s occupants, much as she had with 엘라이더’s irregular treatment of Shemerin.

Whatever the 수련생s were gossiping about, the 에스 세다이 were hearing. Yes, 에그웨인 was winning. But she was beginning to lose the satisfaction she’d once felt at that victory. Who could take joy in seeing the 에스 세다이 unraveling like aged canvas? Who could feel glad that 타르 발론, the grandest of all great cities, was piled with refuse? As much as 에그웨인 might despise 엘라이더, she could not exult at seeing an 아미를린 석좌 lead with such incompetence.

And now, tonight, she would face 엘라이더 in person. 에그웨인 walked slowly through the hallways, pacing herself so as to not arrive early. How should she proceed at the dinner? During her nine days back in the Tower, 에그웨인 had not so much as glimpsed 엘라이더. Attending the woman would be dangerous. If she offended 엘라이더 just a hair too much, she could find herself being sent for execution. And yet, she could not simper and pander. She would *not* bow before the woman, not if it cost her life.

에그웨인 turned a corner, then pulled up short, nearly stumbling. The hallway ended abruptly in a stonework wall set with a bright tile mural. The image was that of an ancient Amyrlin, sitting on an ornate golden seat, holding forth her hand in warning to the kings and queens of the land. The plaque at the bottom declared it to be a depiction of Caraighan Maconar, ending the rebellion in Mosadorin. 에그웨인 vaguely recognized the mural; the last she’d seen it, it had been on the wall of the Tower library. But when she’d seen it there, the Amyrlin’s face hadn’t been a mask of blood. The dead bodies depicted hanging from the eaves hadn’t been there either.

Katerine stepped up beside 에그웨인, face paling. Nobody liked to speak of the unnatural way rooms and corridors changed places in the Tower. The transformations made for a solemn reminder that squabbles over authority were secondary to larger, horrible troubles in the world. This was the first time 에그웨인 had seen not only a corridor moved, but a depiction altered as well. 어둠의 존재 stirred, and the very Pattern itself was shaking.

에그웨인 turned and stalked away from the misplaced mural. She couldn’t focus on those problems right now. You scrubbed a floor clean by first picking a single spot and getting to work. She’d picked her spot. The 백색 탑 *had* to be made whole.

Unfortunately, this detour was going to take more time. 에그웨인 reluctantly hastened her pace; it wouldn’t do to be early, but she’d prefer not to be late either. Her two watchers hurried as well, skirts swishing as they backtracked through several corridors. As they did, 에그웨인 caught sight of Alviarin hurrying around a corner, head down, walking toward the study of the 수련생 감독관. So she was going to her punishment after all. What had caused her to delay?
Two more turns and one flight of cold stone steps later, 에그웨인 found herself cutting through the 적색 아자 section of the Tower, as that now provided the quickest route up to the Amyrlin’s quarters. Red tapestries hung on the walls, accented by crimson tiles on the floor. The women walking the corridors wore expressions of a near uniform austerity, their shawls draped carefully over their shoulders and arms. Here, in their own 아자’s quarters where they should be confident, they seemed insecure and suspicious, even of those servants who bustled about, bearing the Flame of 타르 발론 on their chests. 에그웨인 passed through the hallways, wishing she didn’t have to hurry so, as it made her look cowed. There was nothing to be done about it. At the center of the Tower, she climbed several flights of stairs, eventually reaching the hallway that led to the Amyrlin’s quarters.

Her busyness with 수련생 chores and lessons had left her with little time to consider her confrontation with the false Amyrlin. This was the woman who had pulled down 시우안, the woman who had beaten 랜드, and the woman who had pushed the 에스 세다이 themselves to the very brink of collapse. 엘라이더 needed to know 에그웨인’s anger, she needed to be humiliated and made ashamed! She. . . .

에그웨인 stopped in front of 엘라이더’s gilded door. *No.*

She could imagine the scene easily. 엘라이더 enraged, 에그웨인 banished to the dark cells beneath the Tower. What good would that do? She could *not* confront the woman, not yet. That would only lead to momentary satisfaction followed by a debilitating failure.

But light, she couldn’t bow to 엘라이더 either! The Amyrlin did no such thing!

Or . . . no. The Amyrlin did what was required of her. Which was more important? The 백색 탑, or 에그웨인’s pride? The only way to win this battle was to let 엘라이더 think that *she* was winning. No . . . No, the only way to win was to let 엘라이더 think there *was no battle*.

Could 에그웨인 keep a civil tongue long enough to survive this night? She wasn’t certain. However, she *needed* to leave this dinner with 엘라이더 feeling that she was in control, that 에그웨인 was properly cowed. The best way to achieve that while maintaining some measure of pride would be to say nothing at all.

Silence. That would be her weapon this evening. Steeling herself, 에그웨인 knocked.

Her first surprise came when an 에스 세다이 opened the door. Didn’t 엘라이더 have servants to perform that function? 에그웨인 didn’t recognize the sister, but the ageless face was obvious. The woman was of the Gray, as indicated by her shawl, and she was slender with a full bust. Her golden brown hair fell to the middle of her back, and she had a haunted cast to her eyes, as if she’d been under great strain recently.

엘라이더 sat inside. 에그웨인 hesitated in the doorway, looking in at her rival for the first time since departing from the 백색 탑 with 니나브 and 엘레인 to hunt the 흑색 아자, a turning point that seemed an eternity ago. Handsome and statuesque, 엘라이더 seemed to have lost a small measure of her sternness. She sat, secure and smiling faintly, as if thinking on some joke that only she understood. Her chair was almost a throne, carved, gilded and painted with red and white. There was a second place set at the table, presumably for the nameless Gray sister.

에그웨인 had never visited an Amyrlin’s own quarters before, but she could imagine what 시우안’s might have looked like. Simple, yet not stark. Just enough ornamentation to indicate that this was the room of someone important, but not enough to become a distraction. Under 시우안, everything would have served a function—perhaps several functions at once. Tables with hidden compartments. Wall hangings that doubled as maps. Crossed swords over the hearth that were oiled, should the 감시자s need them.

Or perhaps that was just fancy. Regardless, not only had 엘라이더 taken different rooms for her quarters; her decorations were notably rich. The entire suite hadn’t been decorated yet—there was talk that she was adding to her rooms day by day—but what was there was very lavish. New silk brocades, all of red, hung from the walls and ceilings. The 타이런 rug underfoot depicted birds aflight, and was so finely woven that it could almost be mistaken for a painting. Scattered through the room were pieces of furniture of a dozen different styles and makes, each one lavishly carved and inlaid with ivory. Here a series of vines, there a knobby ridged design, there crisscrossing serpents.

More infuriating than the extravagance was the stole across 엘라이더’s shoulders. It was striped with six colors. Not seven, but six! Though 에그웨인 had not chosen an 아자 herself, she would have taken the Green. But that didn’t stop her from feeling a surge of anger at seeing that shawl with blue removed. One did not simply *disband* one of the 아자s, even if one were the 아미를린 석좌!

But 에그웨인 held her tongue. This meeting was about survival. 에그웨인 could bear straps of pain for the good of the Tower. Could she bear 엘라이더’s arrogance as well?

“No curtsy?” 엘라이더 asked as 에그웨인 entered the room. “They *said* that you were stubborn. Well, then, you shall visit the 수련생 감독관 when this supper is through and inform her of the lapse. What do you say to that?”

*That you are a plague upon this structure as vile and destructive as any disease that has struck city and people in all years past. That you—*

에그웨인 broke her gaze away from 엘라이더’s. And—feeling the shame of it vibrate through her very bones—she bowed her head.

엘라이더 laughed, obviously taking the gesture the right way. “Honestly, I expected you to be more trouble. It appears that Silviana *does* know her duty. That is well; I had worried that she, like far too many in the Tower lately, had been shirking. Well, be busy with you. I won’t wait all night to dine.”

에그웨인 clenched her fists, but said nothing. The back wall was set with a long serving table bearing several silver platters, their polished domed lids dripping with condensation from the heated contents. There was also a silver soup tureen. To the side, the Gray sister hovered near the door. Light! The woman was terrified. 에그웨인 had rarely seen such an expression on a sister. What was causing it?

“Come, Meidani,” 엘라이더 said to the Gray. “Are you going to hover all night? Sit down!”

에그웨인 covered a moment of shock. Meidani? She was one of those sent by 셰리암 and the others to spy on the 백색 탑! As 에그웨인 checked the contents of each platter, she shot a glance over her shoulder. Meidani had found her way to the small, less ornate seat at 엘라이더’s side. Did the Gray always wear such finery to supper? Her neck sparkled with emeralds and her muted green dress was of the most expensive silk, accentuating a bosom that might have been average on another woman, but that seemed ample on Meidani’s slender body.

베오닌 said she’d warned the Gray sisters that 엘라이더 knew they were spies. So why hadn’t Meidani fled the Tower? What was holding her here?

Well, at least now the woman’s expression of terror made sense. “Meidani,” 엘라이더 said, sipping from a goblet of wine, “you are rather wan this day. Have you been getting enough sun?”

“I have been spending a great deal of time with historical records, 엘라이더,” Meidani said, voice uneven. “Have you forgotten?”

“Ah, that is right,” 엘라이더 said musingly. “It will be good to know how traitors have been treated in the past. Beheading seems too easy and simple a punishment to me. Those who split our Tower, those who flaunt their defection, a very *special* reward will be needed for them. Well, continue your search then.”

Meidani sat down, hands in lap. Anyone other than an 에스 세다이 would have had to mop her brow free of sweat. 에그웨인 stirred the silver tureen, hand clutching the ladle with a white-knuckled grip. 엘라이더 *knew*. She knew that Meidani was a spy, and yet she still invited the woman to dinner. To play with her.

“Hurry up, girl,” 엘라이더 snapped at 에그웨인.

에그웨인 plucked up the tureen, the handles warm beneath her fingers, and walked over to the small table. She filled the bowls with a brownish broth bobbing with Queen’s Crown mushrooms. It smelled so heavily peppered that any other flavor would be indistinguishable. So much food had gone bad that without spice, the soup would be inedible.

에그웨인 worked mechanically, like a wagon wheel rolling behind the oxen. She didn’t have to make choices; she didn’t have to respond. She just worked. She filled the soup bowls precisely, then fetched the bread basket and placed one piece—not too crusty—on each small porcelain bread saucer. She returned with a circular dab of butter for each, cut quickly but precisely from the larger brick with a couple of flicks of the knife. One did not spend long as an innkeeper’s daughter without learning to serve a proper meal.

Even as she worked, she stewed. Each step was agony, and not because of her still-burning backside. That physical pain, oddly, seemed insignificant now. It was secondary to the pain of remaining silent, the pain of not allowing herself to confront this awful woman, so regal, so arrogant.

As the two women began their soup—pointedly ignoring the weevils in their bread—에그웨인 retreated to the side of the room and stood, hands clasped before her, posture stiff. 엘라이더 glanced at her, then smiled, apparently seeing another sign of subservience. In reality, 에그웨인 didn’t trust herself to move, for she feared that any activity would end with her slapping 엘라이더 across the face. Light, but this was hard!

“What talk is there in the Tower, Meidani?” 엘라이더 asked, dipping her bread in the soup.

“I . . . don’t have much time to listen. . . .”

엘라이더 leaned forward. “Oh, surely you know something. You have ears, and even Grays must gossip. What are they saying about those rebels?”

Meidani paled further. “I . . . I . . .”

“Hmm,” 엘라이더 said. “When we were 수련생s, I don’t remember you being so slow of wit, Meidani. You haven’t impressed me these last few weeks; I begin to wonder why you were ever given the shawl. Perhaps it never belonged on your shoulders in the first place.”

Meidani’s eyes opened wide.

엘라이더 smiled at her. “Oh, I’m only teasing you, child. Back to your meal.”

She joked! Joked about how she had stolen the shawl from a woman, humiliating her to such an extent that she fled the Tower. Light! What had happened to 엘라이더? 에그웨인 had met this woman before, and 엘라이더 had struck her as stern, but not tyrannical. Power changed people. It appeared that in 엘라이더’s case, holding the 아미를린 석좌 had taken her sternness and solemnity and replaced them with a heady sense of entitlement and cruelty.

Meidani looked up. “I . . . I have heard sisters express worry about the 쇼엔찬.”

엘라이더 waved an indifferent hand, sipping her soup. “Bah. They are too distant to be of danger to us. I wonder if they’re secretly working for the 용의 환생. Either way, I suspect that the rumors about them are largely exaggerated.” 엘라이더 glanced at 에그웨인. “It’s a source of constant amusement to me that *some* will believe anything that they hear.”

에그웨인 couldn’t speak. She could barely have sputtered. How would 엘라이더 feel about these “exaggerated” rumors if the 쇼엔찬 slapped a cold *a’dam* around her idiot neck? 에그웨인 could sometimes feel that band on her own skin, itching, impossible to move. Sometimes, it still made her faintly sick to move around freely, as if she felt that she should be locked away, chained to the post on the wall by a simple loop of metal.

She *knew* what she had dreamed, and knew those dreams to be prophetic. The 쇼엔찬 would strike at the 백색 탑 itself. 엘라이더, obviously, discounted her warnings.

“No,” 엘라이더 said, waving for 에그웨인 to bring another ladle of soup. “These 쇼엔찬 are not the problem. The *real* danger is the complete lack of obedience shown by the 에스 세다이. What will I have to do to end those foolish talks at the bridges? How many sisters will have to do penance before they acknowledge my authority?” She sat, tapping her spoon against her soup cup. 에그웨인, at the serving table, picked up the tureen, retrieving the ladle from its silver holder.

“Yes,” 엘라이더 mused, “if the sisters had been *obedient*, then the Tower wouldn’t be divided. Those rebels would have obeyed rather than running off like a silly flock of startled birds. If the sisters were *obedient*, we would have the 용의 환생 in our hands, and those horrid men training in their ‘검은 탑’ would have been dealt with long ago. What do you think, Meidani?”

“I . . . obedience is certainly important, 엘라이더.”

엘라이더 shook her head as 에그웨인 ladled soup into her bowl. “Anyone would admit *that*, Meidani. I asked what should be done. Fortunately, I have an idea myself. Doesn’t it strike you as strange that the 세 가지 맹세 contain no mention of obedience to the 백색 탑? Sisters cannot lie, cannot make a weapon for men to kill other men, and cannot use the Power as a weapon against others except in defense. Those oaths have always seemed too lax to me. Why no oath to obey the Amyrlin? If that simple promise were part of all of us, how much pain and difficulty could we have avoided? Perhaps some revision is in order.”

에그웨인 stood still. Once, she herself hadn’t understood the importance of the oaths. She suspected that many a 수련생 and 허락받은 자 had questioned their usefulness. But she had learned, as every 에스 세다이 must, their importance. The 세 가지 맹세 were what *made* the 에스 세다이. They were what kept the 에스 세다이 doing what was best for the world, but more than that, they were a shelter from accusations.

Changing them . . . well, it would be an unprecedented disaster. 엘라이더 should *know* that. The false Amyrlin just turned back to her soup, smiling to herself, no doubt contemplating a fourth oath to demand obedience. Couldn’t she see how that would undermine the Tower itself? It would transform the Amyrlin from a leader to a despot!

에그웨인’s rage boiled within her, steaming like the soup in her hands. This woman, this . . . creature! *She* was the cause of the problems in the 백색 탑, *she* was the one who caused division between rebels and loyalists. *She* had taken 랜드 captive and beaten him. She was a disaster!

에그웨인 felt herself shaking. In another moment, she’d burst and let 엘라이더 hear truth. It was boiling free from her, and she could barely contain it.

*No!* she thought. *If I do that, my battle ends. I lose my war.*

So 에그웨인 did the only thing she could think of to stop herself. She dumped the soup on the floor.

Brownish liquid sprayed across the delicate rug of red, yellow and green birds aflight. 엘라이더 cursed, jumping up from her seat and backing away from the spill. None of the liquid had gotten on her dress, which was a shame. 에그웨인 calmly snatched a serving towel off of the table and began to mop up the spill.

“You clumsy idiot!” 엘라이더 snapped.

“I’m sorry,” 에그웨인 said, “I wish that hadn’t happened.” And she did. She wished none of this evening had occurred. She wished 엘라이더 weren’t in control; she wished the Tower had never been broken. She wished she hadn’t been forced to spill the soup on the floor. But she had. And so she dealt with it, kneeling and scrubbing.

엘라이더 sputtered, pointing. “That rug is worth more than your entire village, wilder! Meidani, help her!”

The Gray didn’t offer a single objection. She scurried over and grabbed a bucket of chilled water, which had been cooling some wine, and hurried back to help 에그웨인. 엘라이더 moved over to a door on the far side of the room to call for servants.

“Send for me,” 에그웨인 whispered as Meidani knelt down to help clean.

“What?”

“Send for me to give me instruction,” 에그웨인 said quietly, glancing at 엘라이더, whose back was turned. “We need to speak.”

에그웨인 had originally intended to avoid the Salidar spies, letting 베오닌 act as her messenger. But she had too many questions. Why hadn’t Meidani fled the Tower? What were the spies planning? Had any of the others been adopted by 엘라이더 and beaten down as soundly as Meidani?

Meidani glanced at 엘라이더, then back at 에그웨인. “I may not seem it sometimes, but I’m still 에스 세다이, *girl*. You cannot order me.”

“I am your Amyrlin, Meidani,” 에그웨인 said calmly, wringing a towelful of soup into a pitcher. “And you would do best to remember it. Unless you want the 세 가지 맹세 replaced with vows to serve 엘라이더 for eternity.”

Meidani glanced at her, then cringed at 엘라이더’s shrill calls for servants. The poor woman had obviously seen a hard time lately.

에그웨인 laid a hand on her shoulder. “엘라이더 *can* be unseated, Meidani. The Tower *will* be reunited. I will see it happen, but we must keep courage. Send for me.”

Meidani looked up, studying 에그웨인. “How . . . how do you do it? They say you are punished three and four times a day, that you need 치유 between so that they can beat you further. How can you take it?”

“I take it because I must,” 에그웨인 said, lowering her hand. “Just as we all do what we must. Your service here watching 엘라이더 is difficult, I can see, but know that your work is noticed and appreciated.”

에그웨인 didn’t know if Meidani really had been sent to spy on 엘라이더, but it was always better for a woman to think that her suffering was for a good purpose. It seemed to have been the right thing to say, for Meidani straightened, taking heart and nodding. “Thank you.”

엘라이더 was returning, behind her three servants.

“Send for me,” 에그웨인 ordered Meidani again, voice a whisper. “I am one of the few in this Tower who has a good excuse to move between the various 아자 quarters. I can help heal what has been broken, but I will need your help.”

Meidani hesitated, then nodded. “Very well.”

“You!” 엘라이더 snapped, stepping up to 에그웨인. “Out! I want you to tell Silviana to strap you as she’s never strapped a woman before! I want her to punish you, then Heal you on the spot, then beat you again! Go!”

에그웨인 stood, handing her towel to one of the servants. Then she walked to the exit.

“And don’t think that your clumsiness has allowed you to escape your duties,” 엘라이더 continued from behind. “You will return and serve me again on another date. And if you so much as spill another *drop*, I will have you locked away in a cell with no windows or lights for a week. Do you understand?”

에그웨인 left the room. Had this woman ever been a true 에스 세다이, in control of her emotions?

Yet 에그웨인 herself had lost control of her emotions. She should never have let herself get to a point where she’d been forced to drop the soup. She had underestimated how infuriating 엘라이더 could be, but that would not happen again. She calmed herself as she walked, breathing in and out. Rage did her no good. You didn’t get mad at the weasel who was sneaking into your yard and eating your hens. You simply laid a trap and disposed of the animal. Anger was pointless.

Hands still smelling faintly of pepper and spices, she made her way down to the lowest level of the Tower, to the 수련생s’ dining hall beside the main kitchens. 에그웨인 had worked in those kitchens herself frequently during the last nine days; every 수련생 was required to work chores. The smells of the place—charcoal and smoke, simmering soups and sharp, unscented soaps—were very familiar to her. The smells weren’t that different, actually, from the kitchen of her father’s inn back in the 두 강.

The white-walled room was empty, the tables sitting unattended, though there was a small tray on one of them, covered with a pot lid to keep it warm. Her cushion was there as well, left by the 수련생s to soften the hard bench. 에그웨인 approached, but ignored the cushion as she always did, though she was grateful for the gesture. She sat and removed the lid from the meal. Unfortunately, all she found was a bowl of the same brownish soup. There was no hint of the roast, gravy or long, thin buttered beans that had made up the rest of 엘라이더’s meal.

Still, it was food, and 에그웨인’s stomach was grateful for it. 엘라이더 hadn’t ordered that she *immediately* go for punishment, and so Silviana’s order that she eat first took precedence. Or, at least, there was enough of an argument there to protect her.

She ate quietly, alone. The soup was indeed spicy, and it tasted as much of pepper as it had smelled, but she didn’t mind. Other than that, it was actually quite good. She’d also been left a few slices of bread, though she’d gotten the ends of the loaf. All in all, not a bad meal for someone who had thought she might get nothing.

에그웨인 ate contemplatively, listening to Laras and the scullions bang pots at washing up in the other room, surprised at how calm she felt. She had changed; something was different about her. Watching 엘라이더, finally confronting the woman who had been her rival all of these months, forced her to look at what she was doing in a new light.

She had imagined herself undermining 엘라이더 and seizing control of the 백색 탑 from within. Now she realized that she didn’t need to undermine 엘라이더. The woman was fully capable of doing that herself. Why, 에그웨인 could picture the reaction of the 의석자들 and 아자 heads when 엘라이더 announced her intention to change the 세 가지 맹세!

엘라이더 would topple eventually, with or without 에그웨인’s help. 에그웨인’s duty, as Amyrlin, wasn’t to speed that fall—but to do whatever she could to hold the Tower and its occupants together. They couldn’t afford to fracture further. Her duty was to hold back the chaos and destruction that threatened them all, to reforge the Tower. As she finished off her soup, using the last piece of bread to wipe the remnants from the bowl, she realized she had to do *whatever* she could to be a strength to the sisters in the Tower. Time was growing very short. What was 랜드 doing to the world without guidance? When would the 쇼엔찬 attack to the north? They’d have to cut through 안도르 to get to 타르 발론, and what destruction would that cause? Surely she had some time to reforge the Tower before the attack came, but no moments to waste.

에그웨인 took her dish into the kitchen proper and washed it herself, earning a nod of approval from the hefty Mistress of the Kitchens. After that, 에그웨인 made her way up to Silviana’s study. She needed to get her punishment done quickly; she still intended to visit 리안 tonight, as was her custom. 에그웨인 knocked, then entered, finding Silviana at her desk, leafing through a thick tome by the light of two silver lamps. When 에그웨인 entered, Silviana marked the page with a small length of red cloth, then shut it. The worn cover read *Meditations on the Kindling Flame,* a history of the rise of various Amyrlins. Curious.

에그웨인 sat down on a stool before the desk—not flinching at the immediate sharp pain of her backside—and spoke calmly about the evening, omitting the fact that she’d dropped the bowl of soup on purpose. She did, however, say that she’d dropped it after 엘라이더 had talked of revoking and changing the 세 가지 맹세.

Silviana looked very thoughtful at that.

“Well,” the woman said, standing up and fetching her lash, “the Amyrlin has spoken.”

“Yes, I have,” 에그웨인 said, standing up and positioning herself on the table, skirts and shift up for the beating.

Silviana hesitated, and then the strapping began. Oddly, 에그웨인 felt no desire to cry out. It hurt, of course, but she just couldn’t scream. How ridiculous the punishment was!

She remembered her pain at seeing the sisters pass in the hallways, regarding one another with fear, suspicion and distrust. She remembered the agony of serving 엘라이더 while holding her tongue. And she remembered the sheer horror at the idea of everyone in the Tower being bound by oath to obey such a tyrant.

에그웨인 remembered her pity for poor Meidani. No sister should be treated in such a way. Imprisonment was one thing. But beating a woman down, toying with her, hinting at the torture to come? It was insufferable.

Each of these things was a pain inside of 에그웨인, a knife to the chest, piercing the heart. As the beating continued, she realized that nothing they could do to her body would *ever* compare to the pain of soul she felt at seeing the 백색 탑 suffer beneath 엘라이더’s hand. Compared with those internal agonies, the beating was ridiculous.

And so she began to laugh.

It wasn’t a forced laugh. It wasn’t a defiant laugh. It was the laughter of disbelief. Of incredulity. How could they think that beating her would solve anything? It was ludicrous!

The lashing stopped. 에그웨인 turned. Surely that wasn’t all of it!

Silviana was regarding her with a concerned expression. “Child?” she asked. “Are you all right?”

“I am quite well.”

“You . . . are certain? How are your thoughts?”

*She thinks I’ve broken under the strain,* 에그웨인 realized. *She beats me and I laugh from it.*

“My thoughts are well,” 에그웨인 said. “I don’t laugh because I’ve been broken, Silviana. I laugh because it is absurd to beat me.”

The woman’s expression darkened.

“Can’t you see it?” 에그웨인 asked. “Don’t you feel the pain? The agony of watching the Tower crumble around you? Could any beating compare to that?”

Silviana did not respond.

*I understand,* 에그웨인 thought. *I didn’t realize what the 아일 did. I assumed that I just had to be harder, and that was what would teach me to laugh at pain. But it’s not hardness at all. It’s not strength that makes me laugh. It’s understanding.*

To let the Tower fall, to let the 에스 세다이 fail—the pain of that would destroy her. She had to stop it, for she was the 아미를린 석좌.

“I cannot refuse to punish you,” Silviana said. “You realize that.”

“Of course,” 에그웨인 said. “But please remind me of something. What was it you said about Shemerin? Why was it 엘라이더 got away with taking the shawl from her?”

“It was because Shemerin accepted it,” Silviana replied. “She treated herself as if she really *had* lost the shawl. She didn’t fight back.”

“I will not make the same mistake, Silviana. 엘라이더 can *say* whatever she wants. But that doesn’t change who I am, or who any of us are. Even if she tries to change the 세 가지 맹세, there will be those who resist, who hold to what is correct. And so, when you beat me, you beat the 아미를린 석좌. And that should be amusing enough to make us both laugh.”

The punishment continued, and 에그웨인 embraced the pain, took it into herself, and judged it insignificant, impatient for the punishment to cease.

She had a lot of work to do.

**C*HAPTER** **3**

![](images/00296.jpg)

The Ways of Honor

아비엔다 crouched with her spear-sisters and some True Blood scouts atop the low, grassy hill, looking down at the refugees. They were a sorry lot, these 도마니 wetlanders, with dirtied faces that had not seen a sweat tent in months, their emaciated children too hungry to cry. One sad mule pulled a single cart among the hundred struggling people; what they hadn’t piled in the vehicle they carried. There wasn’t much of either. They plodded northeast along a pathway that couldn’t quite be called a road. Perhaps there was a village in that direction. Perhaps they were just fleeing the uncertainty of the coastal lands.

The hilly landscape was open save for the occasional stand of trees. The refugees hadn’t seen 아비엔다 and her companions, despite the fact that they were less than a hundred paces away. She’d never understood how wetlanders could be so blind. Didn’t they watch, noting any oddities on the horizon? Couldn’t they see that traveling so near to a hilltop practically invited scouts to spy on them? They should have secured the hill with their own scouts before coming anywhere near.
Didn’t they care? 아비엔다 shivered. How could you *not* care about eyes watching you, eyes that might belong to a man or Maiden holding a spear? Were they so eager to wake from the dream? 아비엔다 did not fear death, but there was a very big difference between embracing death and wishing for it.

*Cities,* she thought, *they’re the problem.* Cities were stinking, festering places, like sores that never healed. Some were better than others—엘레인 did an admirable job with Caemlyn—but the best of them gathered too many people and taught them to grow comfortable staying in one place. If those refugees had been accustomed to travel and had learned to use their own feet, rather than relying on horses as wetlanders so often did, then it would not be so difficult for them to leave their towns. Among the 아일, the craftsmen were trained to defend themselves, the children could live off the land for days, and even blacksmiths could travel great distances quickly. An entire sept could be on the move within an hour, carrying everything they needed on their backs.

Wetlanders were strange, doubtless. Still, she felt pity for the refugees. The emotion surprised her. While she was not heartless, her duty lay elsewhere, with 랜드 al’Thor. She had no reason to feel heartsore for a group of wetlanders she’d never met. But time spent with her first-sister, 엘레인 Trakand, had taught her that not all wetlanders were soft and weak. Just most of them. There was *ji* in caring for those who could not care for themselves.

Watching these refugees, 아비엔다 tried to see them as 엘레인 would, but she still struggled to understand 엘레인’s form of leadership. It was not the simple leadership of a group of Maidens on a raid—that was both instinctive and efficient. 엘레인 would not watch these refugees for signs of danger or hidden soldiers. 엘레인 would feel a responsibility to them, even if they were not of her own people. She would find a way to send food, perhaps use her troops to secure a safe area for them to homestead—and in doing so, acquire a piece of this country for herself.

Once, 아비엔다 would have left these thoughts to clan chiefs and roofmistresses. But she wasn’t a Maiden any longer, and she had accepted that. She now lived under a different roof. She was ashamed that she had resisted the change for so long.

But that left her with a problem. What honor was there for her now? No longer a Maiden, not quite a Wise One. Her entire identity had been wrapped up in those spears, her *self* forged into their steel as surely as the carbon that strengthened them. She had grown from childhood certain that she would be *Far Dareis Mai*. Indeed, she had joined the Maidens as soon as possible. She had been proud of her life and of her spear-sisters. She would have served her clan and sept until the day when she finally fell to the spear, bleeding her last water onto the parched earth of the Three-fold 란d.

This was not the Three-fold 란d, and she had heard some *algai’d’siswai* wonder if the 아일 would ever return there. Their lives had changed. She didn’t trust change. It couldn’t be spotted or stabbed; it was more silent than any scout, more deadly than any assassin. No, she’d never trust it, but she would accept it. She would learn 엘레인’s ways and how to think like a chief.

She *would* find honor in her new life. Somehow.

“They are no threat,” whispered Heirn, crouching with the True Bloods on the other side of the Maidens.

Rhuarc watched the refugees, alert. “The dead walk,” the Taardad clan chief said, “and men fall at random to 시야 가리는 자’s evil, their blood corrupted like the water of a bad well. Those might be poor folk fleeing the ravages of war. Or they might be something else. We keep our distance.”

아비엔다 glanced at the increasingly distant line of refugees. She did not think Rhuarc was right; these were not ghosts or monsters. There was always something . . . wrong about those. They left her with an itch, as if she were about to be attacked.

Still, Rhuarc was wise. One learned to be careful in the Three-fold 란d, where a tiny twig could kill. The group of 아일 slipped off the hilltop and down onto the brown-grassed plain beyond. Even after months spent in the wetlands, 아비엔다 found the landscape strange. Trees here were tall and long-limbed, with too many buds. When the 아일 crossed patches of yellow spring grass among the fallen winter leaves, they all seemed so full of water that she half-expected the blades and leaves to burst beneath her feet. She knew the wetlanders said that this spring was unnaturally slow starting, but already it was more fertile than her homeland.

In the Three-fold 란d, this meadow—with the hills to provide watchpoints and shelter—would have immediately been seized by a sept and used for farming. Here, it was just one of a thousand different untouched patches of land. The fault lay again in those cities. The nearest ones were too distant from this location to make it a good spot for a wetlander farmstead.

The eight 아일 quickly crossed the grasses, weaving between hillsides, moving with speed and stealth. Horses could not match a man’s feet, what with their thunderous galloping. Terrible beasts—why did the wetlanders insist on riding them? Baffling. 아비엔다 could begin to understand how a chief or queen must think, but she knew that she’d never completely understand wetlanders. They were just too strange. Even 랜드 al’Thor.

Especially 랜드 al’Thor. She smiled, thinking of his earnest eyes. She remembered the scent of him—wetlander soaps, which smelled of oil, mixed with that particular earthy musk that was all his own. She *would* marry him. She was as determined as 엘레인 in that regard; now that they were first-sisters, they could marry him together as was proper. Only, how could 아비엔다 marry anyone, now? Her honor had been in her spears, but 랜드 al’Thor now wore those at his waist, beaten and forged into a belt buckle, given to him by her own hand.

He had offered her marriage once. A man! Offering marriage! Another of those strange wetlander customs. Even disregarding the strangeness of it—disregarding the insult his proposal had shown 엘레인—아비엔다 could never have accepted 랜드 al’Thor as her husband. Couldn’t he understand that a woman must bring honor to a marriage? What could a mere apprentice offer? Would he have her come to him as an inferior? It would shame her completely to do that!

He must not have understood. She did not think him cruel, only dense. She would come to him when *she* was ready, then lay the bridal wreath at his feet. And she couldn’t do that until she knew who she was.

The ways of *ji’e’toh* were complex. 아비엔다 knew how to measure honor as a Maiden, but 현명한 이들 were different creatures entirely. She had thought she was gaining some small amount of honor in their eyes. They had allowed her, for instance, to spend a great deal of time with her first-sister in Caemlyn. But then, suddenly, Dorindha and Nadere had arrived and informed 아비엔다 that she had been ignoring her training. They had seized her like a child caught listening furtively outside the sweat tent, towing her away to join the rest of her clan as they left for 아라드 도만.

And now . . . and now the 현명한 이들 treated her with *less* respect than they had before! They offered her no teaching. Somehow, she had misstepped in their eyes. That made her stomach twist. To shame herself before the other 현명한 이들 was almost as bad as showing fear before one as brave as 엘레인!

So far, the 현명한 이들 had allowed 아비엔다 some honor by letting her serve punishments, but she didn’t know *how* she had shamed herself in the first place. Asking would—of course—only bring more shame. Until she unwove the problem, she could not meet her *toh*. Worse, there was a real danger of her making the mistake again. Until she sorted out this problem, she would remain an apprentice, and she would *never* be able to bring an honorable bridal wreath to 랜드 al’Thor.

아비엔다 gritted her teeth. Another woman might have wept, but what good would that have done? Whatever her mistake, she had brought it upon herself, and it was her duty to right it. She *would* find honor again and she *would* marry 랜드 al’Thor before he died at the Last Battle.

That meant that whatever it was she had to learn, she needed to do so quickly. Very quickly.

They met up with another group of 아일 waiting in a small clearing amid a stand of pine trees. The ground was thick with discarded brown needles, the sky broken by the towering trunks. The group was small by the standards of clans and septs, barely two hundred people. In the middle of the clearing stood four 현명한 이들, each wearing the characteristic brown woolen skirt and white blouse. 아비엔다 wore similar attire, which now felt as natural to her as the *cadin’sor* once had. The scouting party split up, men and Maidens moving to join members of their clans or societies. Rhuarc joined the 현명한 이들, and 아비엔다 followed him.

Each of the 현명한 이들—Amys, Bair, Melaine, and Nadere—gave her a glance. Bair, the only 아일 with the group who wasn’t Taardad or Goshien, had arrived only recently, perhaps to coordinate with the others. Whatever the reason, none of them seemed pleased. 아비엔다 hesitated. If she left now, would it seem as if she were trying to avoid their attention? Did she instead dare stay, and risk incurring their further displeasure?

“Well?” Amys said to Rhuarc. Though Amys had white hair, she looked quite young. In her case, this wasn’t due to working the Power—her hair had started turning silver when she’d been a child.

“It was as the scouts described, shade of my heart,” Rhuarc said. “Another pitiful band of wetlander refugees. I saw no hidden danger in them.”

The 현명한 이들 nodded, as if this was what they had expected. “That is the tenth band of refugees in less than a week,” said aged Bair, her watery blue eyes thoughtful.

Rhuarc nodded. “There are rumors of 쇼엔찬 attacks on harbors to the west. Perhaps the people move inland to avoid the raids.” He glanced at Amys. “This country boils like water spilled on a hearthstone. The clans are uncertain what 랜드 al’Thor wishes of them.”

“He was very clear,” Bair noted. “He will be pleased that you and Dobraine Taborwin secured Bandar Eban, as he asked.”

Rhuarc nodded. “But still, his intentions are not clear. He asked for us to restore order. Are we then to be like wetlander city guardsmen? That is no place for the 아일. We are not to conquer, so we do not get the fifth. And yet it feels very much like conquest, what we do. The *Car’a’carn*’s orders can be clear yet confusing at the same time. He has a gift in that area, I think.”

Bair smiled, nodding. “Perhaps he intends for us to do something with these refugees.”

“And what would we do?” Amys asked, shaking her head. “Are we Shaido, expected to make *gai’shain* from wetlanders?” Her tone left little doubt as to what she thought of both Shaido *and* the idea of making wetlanders *gai’shain.*

아비엔다 nodded in agreement. As Rhuarc said, the *Car’a’carn* had sent them to 아라드 도만 to “restore order.” But that was a wetlander concept; 아일 brought their own order with them. There was chaos to war and battle, true, but each and every 아일 understood his place, and would act within that place. The little children understood honor and *toh*, and a hold would continue to function after all of the leaders and 현명한 이들 were killed.

It was not so with wetlanders. They ran about like a basket of wild lizards suddenly dropped onto hot stones, taking no care for provisions when they fled. As soon as their leaders were occupied or distracted, banditry and chaos ruled. The strong took from the weak, and even blacksmiths were not safe.

What could 랜드 al’Thor expect the 아일 to do about it? They could not teach *ji’e’toh* to an entire nation. 랜드 al’Thor had told them to *avoid* killing 도마니 troops. But those troops—often corrupt and turned to banditry themselves—were part of the problem.

“Perhaps he will explain more when we arrive at this manor house of his,” said Melaine, shaking her head, red-gold hair catching the light. Her pregnancy was just beginning to show beneath her Wise One blouse. “And if he does not, then surely it is better for us to be here in 아라드 도만 than to spend yet more time lounging back in the land of the treekillers.”

“As you say,” Rhuarc agreed. “Let us move on, then. There is still a distance to run.” He moved off to speak with Bael. 아비엔다 took a step away, but a harsh glance from Amys made her freeze.

“아비엔다,” said the hard, white-haired woman. “How many 현명한 이들 went with Rhuarc to scout this refugee train?”

“None but me,” 아비엔다 admitted.

“Oh, and are you a Wise One now?” Bair asked.

“No,” 아비엔다 said, quickly, then shamed herself further by blushing. “I spoke poorly.”

“Then you shall be punished,” Bair said. “You are no longer a Maiden, 아비엔다. It is not your place to scout; that is a task for others.”

“Yes, Wise One,” 아비엔다 said, looking down. She had not thought that going with Rhuarc would bring her shame—she had seen other 현명한 이들 do similar tasks.

*But I am not a Wise One,* she reminded herself. *I am an apprentice only.* Bair had not said that a Wise One could not scout; only that it had not been 아비엔다’s place to go. It was about 아비엔다 herself. And about whatever it was she had done—or perhaps continued to do—to provoke the 현명한 이들.

Did they think she had grown soft by spending time with 엘레인? 아비엔다 herself worried that that was true. During her days in Caemlyn, she had begun to find herself enjoying the silks and baths. By the end, she had objected only feebly when 엘레인 had come up with an excuse to dress her in some impractical and frivolous garment with embroidery and lace. It was well that the others had come for her.

The others just stood there, looking at her expectantly, faces like red desert stones, impassive and stern. 아비엔다 gritted her teeth again. She would complete her apprenticeship and find honor. She *would*.

The call came to begin moving, and *cadin’sor*-clad men and women did so, running together in small groups. The 현명한 이들 moved as easily as the soldiers, despite their bulky skirts. Amys touched 아비엔다’s arm. “You will run with me so that we can discuss your punishment.”

아비엔다 fell into pace beside the Wise One at a brisk jog. It was a speed any 아일 could maintain almost indefinitely. Her group, from Caemlyn, had met up with Rhuarc as he was traveling from Bandar Eban to meet with 랜드 al’Thor in the western part of the country. Dobraine Taborwin, a 케렌인, was still maintaining order in the capital city, where he’d reportedly located a member of the 도마니 ruling body.

Perhaps the group of 아일 could have Traveled through a gateway the rest of the distance. But it was not far—only a few days by foot—and they had left early enough to arrive at the appointed time without using the 하나의 힘. Rhuarc wanted to scout for himself some of the landscape near the manor house 랜드 al’Thor was using as a base. Other bodies of Goshien or Taardad 아일 would join them at the base, using gateways, if needed.

“What do you think of the *Car’a’carn*’s demands of us here in 아라드 도만, 아비엔다?” Amys asked as they ran.

아비엔다 stifled a frown. What of her punishment? “It is an irregular request,” she said, “but 랜드 al’Thor has many strange ideas, even for a wetlander. This will not be the most unusual duty he has set for us.”

“And the fact that Rhuarc finds the duty discomforting?”

“I doubt that the clan chief is uncomfortable,” 아비엔다 said. “I suspect that Rhuarc speaks what he has heard others say, passing the information to the 현명한 이들. He does not wish to shame others by revealing who has spoken of their fears.”

Amys nodded. What was the purpose of the questions? Surely the woman had guessed the same thing. She would not come to 아비엔다 for counsel.

They ran in silence for a time, with no mention of punishments. Had the 현명한 이들 forgiven her unknown slight? Surely they wouldn’t dishonor her in that way. 아비엔다 had to be given time to think out what she had done, otherwise her shame would be unbearable. She might err again, this time worse.

Amys gave no clue as to her thoughts. The Wise One had been a Maiden once, like 아비엔다. She was hard, even for an 아일. “And al’Thor himself?” Amys asked. “What do you think of him?”

“I love him,” 아비엔다 said.

“I did not ask 아비엔다 the silly girl,” Amys said curtly. “I asked 아비엔다 the Wise One.”

“He is a man of many burdens,” 아비엔다 said more carefully. “I fear that he makes many of those burdens heavier than they need be. I once thought that there was only one way to be strong, but I have learned from my first-sister that I was wrong. 랜드 al’Thor . . . I do not think he has learned this yet. I worry that he mistakes hardness for strength.”

Amys nodded again, as if in approval. Were these questions a test of some sort?

“You would marry him?” Amys asked.

*I thought we weren’t talking about 아비엔다 the “silly girl,”* 아비엔다 thought, but of course didn’t say it. One did not say such things to Amys.

“I *will* marry him,” she said instead. “It is not a possibility, but a certainty.” The tone earned her a glance from Amys, but 아비엔다 held her ground. Any Wise One who misspoke deserved to be corrected.

“And the wetlander 민 Farshaw?” Amys asked. “She obviously loves him. What will you do about her?”

“She is my concern,” 아비엔다 said. “We will reach an accommodation. I have spoken with 민 Farshaw, and I believe she will be easy to work with.”

“You would become first-sisters with her as well?” Amys asked, sounding just faintly amused.

“We will reach an accommodation, Wise One.”

“And if you cannot?”

“We will,” 아비엔다 said firmly.

“And how can you be so certain?”

아비엔다 hesitated. Part of her wished to return only silence to that question, passing the leafless brush thickets and giving Amys no answer. But she was just an apprentice, and while she could not be forced to speak, she knew that Amys would keep pushing until the answer came out. 아비엔다 hoped she would not incur too much *toh* by her response.

“You know of the woman 민’s viewings?” 아비엔다 said.

Amys nodded.

“One of those viewings relates to 랜드 al’Thor and the three women he will love. Another relates to my children by the *Car’a’carn*.”

She said no more, and Amys pressed no more. It was enough. Both knew that one would sooner find a Stone Dog who would retreat than find a viewing of 민’s that went wrong.

On one hand, it was good to know that 랜드 al’Thor would be hers, although she would have to share him. She did not begrudge 엘레인, of course, but 민 . . . well, 아비엔다 did not really know her. Regardless, the viewing was a comfort. But it was also bothersome. 아비엔다 loved 랜드 al’Thor because *she* chose to, not because she was destined to. Of course, 민’s viewing didn’t guarantee that 아비엔다 would actually be able to marry 랜드, so perhaps she had misspoken to Amys. Yes, he would love three women and three women would love him, but would 아비엔다 find a way to marry him?

No, the future was not certain, and for some reason that brought her comfort. Perhaps she should have worried, but she did not. She would get her honor back, and then she would marry 랜드 al’Thor. Perhaps he would die soon after, but perhaps an ambush would come and she would fall to an arrow this day. Worrying solved nothing.

*Toh*, however, was another matter.

“I misspoke, Wise One,” 아비엔다 said. “I implied that the viewing said I would marry 랜드 al’Thor. That is not true. All three of us will love him, and while that implies marriage, I do not know for certain.”

Amys nodded. There was no *toh*; 아비엔다 had corrected herself quickly enough. That was well. She would not add more shame on top of what she had already earned.

“Very well, then,” Amys said, watching the path ahead of her. “Let us discuss today’s punishment.”

아비엔다 relaxed slightly. So she still had time to discover what she had done wrong. Wetlanders often seemed confused by 아일 ways with punishment, but wetlanders had little understanding of honor. Honor didn’t come from *being* punished, but *accepting* a punishment and bearing it restored honor. That was the soul of *toh*—the willing lowering of oneself in order to recover that which had been lost. It was strange to her that wetlanders couldn’t see this; indeed, it was strange that they didn’t follow *ji’e’toh* instinctively. What was life without honor?

Amys, rightly, wouldn’t tell 아비엔다 what she had done wrong. However, she was having no success thinking through the answer on her own, and it would cause less shame if she discovered the answer through conversation. “Yes,” 아비엔다 said carefully. “I should be punished. My time in Caemlyn threatened to make me weak.”

Amys sniffed. “You are no more weak than you were when you carried the spears, girl. A fair bit stronger, I should think. Your time with your first-sister was important for you.”

So that wasn’t it. When Dorindha and Nadere had come for her, they had said she needed to continue her training as an apprentice. Yet in the time since the 아일 had departed for 아라드 도만, 아비엔다 had been given no lessons. She had been assigned to carry water, to mend shawls, and to serve tea. She had been given all manner of punishments with little explanation of what she had done wrong. And when she did something obvious—like going scouting when she shouldn’t have—the severity of her punishment was always greater than the infraction should have merited.

It was almost as if the punishment *was* the thing the 현명한 이들 wanted her to learn, but that could not be. She was not some wetlander who needed to be taught the ways of honor. What good would constant and unexplained punishment do, other than to warn of some grave mistake she had made?

Amys reached to her side, untying something hanging at her waist. The woolen bag she held up was about the size of a fist. “We have decided,” she said, “that we have been too lax in our instruction. Time is precious and we have no room left for delicacy.”

아비엔다 covered her surprise. Their previous punishments were *delicate*?

“Therefore,” Amys said, handing over the small sack, “you will take this. Inside are seeds. Some are black, others are brown, others are white. This evening, before we sleep, you will separate the colors, then count how many there are of each one. If you are wrong, we will mix them together and you will start again.”

아비엔다 found herself gaping, and she nearly stumbled to a stop. Hauling water was necessary work. Mending clothing was necessary work. Cooking meals was important work, particularly when no *gai’shain* had been brought with the small advance group.

But this . . . this was *useless* work! It was not only unimportant, it was frivolous. It was the kind of punishment reserved for only the most stubborn, or most shameful, of people. It almost . . . almost felt as though the 현명한 이들 were calling her *da’tsang*!

“By 시야 가리는 자’s eyes,” she whispered as she forced herself to keep running. “What did I *do*?”

Amys glanced at her, and 아비엔다 looked away. Both knew that she didn’t want an answer to that question. She took the bag silently. It was the most humiliating punishment she had ever been given.

Amys moved off to run with the other 현명한 이들. 아비엔다 shook off her stupor, her determination returning. Her mistake must have been more profound than she had thought. Amys’ punishment was an indication of that, a hint.

She opened the bag and glanced inside. There were three little empty *algode* bags inside to help with the separation, and thousands of tiny seeds nearly engulfed them. This punishment was *meant* to be seen, meant to bring her shame. Whatever she’d done, it was offensive not just to the 현명한 이들, but to all around her, even if they—like 아비엔다 herself—were ignorant of it.

That only meant she had to be more determined.

**C*HAPTER** **4**

![](images/00227.jpg)

Nightfall

가윈 watched the sun burn the clouds to death in the west, the final light fading. That haze of perpetual gloom kept the sun itself shrouded. Just as it hid the stars from his sight at night. Today the clouds were unnaturally high in the air. Often, 용산’s tip would be hidden on cloudy days, but this thick, gray haze hovered high enough that most of the time, it barely brushed the mountain’s jagged, broken tip.

“Let’s engage them,” Jisao whispered from where he crouched beside 가윈 on the hilltop.

가윈 glanced away from the sunset, back toward the small village below. It should have been still, save perhaps for a goodman checking on his livestock one last time before turning in. It should have been dim, unlit save for a few tallow candles burning in windows as people finished evening meals.

But it was not dim. It was not quiet. The village was alight with angry torches carried by a dozen sturdy figures. By that torchlight and the light of the dying sun, 가윈 could make out that each was wearing a nondescript uniform of brown and black. 가윈 couldn’t see the three-starred insignia on their uniforms, but he knew it was there.

From his distant vantage, 가윈 watched a few latecomers stumble from their homes, looking frightened and worried as they gathered with the others in the crowded square. These villagers welcomed the armed force with reluctance. Women clutched children, men were careful to keep their eyes downcast. “We don’t want trouble,” the postures said. They’d undoubtedly heard from other villages that these invaders were orderly. The soldiers paid for goods they took, and no young men were pressed into service—though they weren’t turned away either. A very odd invading army indeed. However, 가윈 knew what the people would think. This army was led by 에스 세다이, and who could say what was odd or normal when 에스 세다이 were involved?

There were no sisters with this particular patrol, thank the Light. The soldiers, polite but stern, lined up the villagers and looked them over. Then a pair of soldiers entered each house and barn, inspecting it. Nothing was taken and nothing was broken. All very neat and cordial. 가윈 could almost hear the officer offering apologies to the village mayor.

“가윈?” Jisao asked. “I count barely a dozen of them. If we send Rodic’s squad to come in from the north, we’ll cut off both sides and smash them between us. It’s getting dark enough that they won’t see us coming. We could take them without so much as running up a lather.”

“And the villagers?” 가윈 asked. “There are children down there.”

“That hasn’t stopped us other times.”

“Those times were different,” 가윈 said, shaking his head. “The last three villages they’ve searched point a direct line toward Dorlan. If this group vanishes, the next one will wonder what it was they nearly uncovered. We’d draw the entire army’s eye in this direction.”

“But—”

“No,” 가윈 said softly. “We have to know when to fall back, Jisao.”

“So we came all this way for nothing.”

“We came all this way for an opportunity,” 가윈 said, backing away from the hilltop, making certain he didn’t show a profile on the horizon. “And now that I’ve inspected that opportunity, we’re not going to take it. Only a fool looses his arrow just because he’s got a bird in front of him.”

“Why wouldn’t you loose it if it’s right there in front of you?” Jisao asked as he joined 가윈.

“Because sometimes the prize isn’t worth the arrow,” 가윈 said. “Come on.”
Below, waiting in the dark with lanterns hooded, were some of the very men the soldiers in the village were searching for. Gareth Bryne must have been very displeased to learn there was a harrying force hiding somewhere nearby. He’d been diligent in trying to flush it out, but the countryside near 타르 발론 was liberally sprinkled with villages, forests and secluded valleys that could hide a small, mobile strike force. So far, 가윈 had managed to keep his Younglings out of sight while pulling off the occasional raid or ambush on Bryne’s forces. There was only so much you could do with three hundred men, however. Particularly when you faced one of the five Great Captains.

*Am I destined to end up fighting against each and every man who has been a mentor to me?* 가윈 took the reins of his horse and gave a silent order to withdraw by raising his right hand, then gestured sharply away from the village. The men moved without comment, dismounting and leading their mounts for both stealth and safety.

가윈 had thought he was over 햄mar and Coulin’s deaths; Bryne himself had taught 가윈 that the battlefield sometimes made allies into sudden foes. 가윈 had fought his former teachers, and 가윈 had won. That was the end of it.

Recently, however, his mind seemed determined to dredge up those corpses and carry them about. Why now, after so long?

He suspected his sense of guilt had to do with facing Bryne, his first and most influential instructor in the arts of war. 가윈 shook his head as he guided Challenge across the darkening landscape; he kept his men away from the road in case Bryne’s scouts had placed watchers. The fifty men around 가윈 walked as quietly as possible, the horses’ hoofbeats deadened by the springy earth.

If Bryne had been shocked to discover a harrying force striking at his outriders, then 가윈 had been equally shocked to discover those three stars on the uniforms of the men he slew. How had the 백색 탑’s enemies recruited the greatest military mind in all of 안도르? And what was the Captain-General of the Queen’s Guard doing fighting with a group of 에스 세다이 rebels in the first place? He should have been in Caemlyn protecting 엘레인.

Light send that 엘레인 *had* arrived in 안도르. She couldn’t still be with the rebels. Not with her homeland lacking a queen. Her duty to 안도르 outweighed her duty to the 백색 탑.

*And what of your duty, 가윈 Trakand?* he thought to himself.

He wasn’t certain he had duty, or honor, left to him. Perhaps his guilt about 햄mar, his nightmares of war and death at Dumai’s Wells, were due to the slow realization that he might have given his allegiance to the wrong side. His loyalty belonged to 엘레인 and 에그웨인. What, then, was he still doing fighting a battle he didn’t care about, helping a side that—by all accounts—was *opposed* to the one 엘레인 and 에그웨인 had chosen?

*They’re just 허락받은 자,* he told himself. *엘레인 and 에그웨인 didn’t choose this side—they are just doing what they’ve been ordered to do!* But the things that 에그웨인 had said to him all those months ago, back in 케렌, suggested that she had made her decision willingly.

She had chosen a side. 햄mar had chosen a side. Gareth Bryne had, apparently, chosen a side. But 가윈 continued to want to be on *both* sides. The division was ripping him apart.

An hour out of the village, 가윈 gave the order to mount and take to the road. Hopefully, Bryne’s scouts wouldn’t think to search the land outside the village. If they did, the tracks of fifty horsemen would be hard to miss. There was no avoiding that. The best thing now was to reach firm ground, where the signs of their passing would be hidden by a thousand years of footfalls and traffic. Two pairs of soldiers rode off in front and two pairs hung back to watch. The rest maintained their silence, though their horses now pounded a thunderous gallop. None asked why they were withdrawing, but 가윈 knew that they were wondering, just as Jisao had.

They were good men. Perhaps too good. As they rode, Rajar pulled his mount up beside 가윈’s. Just a few months ago, Rajar had been a youth. But now 가윈 couldn’t think of him as anything other than a soldier. A veteran. Some men gained experience through years spent living. Other men gained experience through months spent watching their friends die.

Glancing upward, 가윈 missed the stars. They hid their faces from him behind those clouds. Like 아일 behind black veils. “Where did we go wrong, Rajar?” 가윈 asked as they rode.

“Wrong, Lord 가윈?” Rajar asked. “I don’t know that we did anything wrong. We couldn’t have known which villages that patrol would choose to inspect, or that they wouldn’t turn along the old Wagonright Road, as you had hoped. Some of the men may be confused, but it was right to withdraw.”

“I wasn’t talking about the raid,” 가윈 said, shaking his head. “I’m talking about this whole bloody situation. You shouldn’t have to go on supply raids or spend your time killing scouts; you should have become a 감시자 to some freshly minted 에스 세다이 by now.” *And I should be back in Caemlyn, with 엘레인*.

“수레바퀴 weaves as the Wheel wills,” the shorter man said.

“Well, it wove us into a hole,” 가윈 muttered, glancing at the overcast sky once again. “And 엘라이더 doesn’t seem too eager to pull us out of it.”

Rajar looked at 가윈 reproachfully. “The 백색 탑’s methods are its own, Lord 가윈, and so are its motives. It isn’t for us to question. What good is a 감시자 who questions the orders of his 에스 세다이? A good way to get both of you killed, that is.”

*You’re not a 감시자, Rajar. That’s the problem!* 가윈 said nothing. None of the other Younglings seemed to be plagued with these questions. To them, the world was much simpler. One did as the 백색 탑, and the 아미를린 석좌, commanded. Never mind if those commands seemed designed to get you killed.

Three hundred youths against a force of over fifty thousand hardened soldiers, commanded by Gareth Bryne himself? Will of the Amyrlin or not, that was a deathtrap. The only reason the Younglings had survived as long as they had was because of 가윈’s familiarity with his teacher’s ways. He knew where Bryne would send patrols and outriding scouts, and knew how to evade his search patterns.

It was still a futile effort. 가윈 didn’t have nearly the troops needed for a true harrying force, particularly with Bryne entrenched in his siege. Beyond that, there was the remarkable matter of the army’s complete lack of a supply line. How were they getting food? They purchased supplies from the surrounding villages, but not nearly enough to feed themselves. How could they possibly have carried all they needed while still moving quickly enough to appear, without warning, in the middle of winter?

가윈’s attacks were next to meaningless. It was enough to make a man think that the Amyrlin just wanted him, and the other Younglings, out of the way. Before Dumai’s Wells, 가윈 had suspected that was the case. Now he was growing certain. *And yet you continue to follow her orders,* he thought to himself.

He shook his head. Bryne’s scouts were getting dangerously close to his base of operations, and 가윈 couldn’t risk killing any more of them without giving himself away. It was time to head back to Dorlan. Perhaps the 에스 세다이 there would have a suggestion on how to proceed.

He hunkered down on his horse and continued riding into the night. *Light, I wish I could see the stars,* he thought.

**C*HAPTER** **5**

![](images/00179.jpg)

A Tale of Blood

랜드 crossed the trampled manor green, banners flapping before him, tents surrounding him, horses whinnying in their pickets on the far west side. In the air hung the scents of an efficient war camp: smoke and savor from the stewpots were much stronger than the occasional whiff of horse dung or an unwashed body.

바쉐어’s men maintained a tidy camp, busying themselves with the hundreds of little tasks that allowed the army to function: sharpening swords, oiling leathers, mending saddles, fetching water from the stream. Some practiced charges to the left, on the far side of the green, in the space between tent lines and the scraggly trees growing alongside the stream. The men held gleaming lances at the level as their horses trampled the muddy ground in a long swath. The maneuvers not only kept their skills sharp, but exercised the horses as well.

As always, 랜드 was trailed by a flock of attendants. Maidens were his guards, and the 아일 watched the 살다에안 soldiers with wariness. Beside him were several 에스 세다이. They were always about him, now. 패턴 had no place for his onetime insistence that all 에스 세다이 be kept at arm’s length. It wove as it willed, and experience had shown that 랜드 needed these 에스 세다이. What he wanted no longer mattered. He understood that now.

It was little comfort that many of these 에스 세다이 in his camp had sworn allegiance to him. Everyone knew that 에스 세다이 followed their oaths in their own ways, and they would decide what their “fealty” to him would require.

Elza Penfell—who accompanied him this day—was one of those who had sworn to him. Of the 녹색 아자, she had a face that might be considered pretty, if one didn’t recognize the ageless quality that marked her as 에스 세다이. She was pleasant, for an 에스 세다이, despite the fact that she had helped kidnap 랜드 and lock him in a box for days, to be pulled out only for the occasional beating.

In the back of his mind, 르웨어스 테린 growled.

That was past. Elza had sworn. That was enough to allow 랜드 to use her. The other woman attending him today was less predictable; she was a member of Cadsuane’s retinue. Corele Hovian—a slim Yellow with blue eyes, wild dark hair, and a perpetual smile—had sworn no oaths to do as he said. Despite that, he felt a temptation to trust her, since she had once tried to save his life. It was only because of her, Samitsu and Damer Flinn that 랜드 had survived. One of two wounds in 랜드’s side that would not heal—a gift from Padan Fain’s cursed dagger—still lingered as a reminder of that day. The constant pain of that festering evil overlaid the equal pain of an older wound beneath, the one 랜드 had taken while fighting 이샤마엘 so long ago.

Soon, one of those wounds—or perhaps both—would spill 랜드’s blood onto the rocks of 세이올 굴. He wasn’t certain if they would be what killed him or not; with the number and variety of the different factors competing to take 랜드’s life, even 맷 wouldn’t have known which one was the best bet.

As soon as 랜드 thought of 맷, the colors swirled in his vision, forming into the image of a wiry, brown-eyed man wearing a wide-brimmed hat and tossing dice before a small crowd of watching soldiers. 맷 wore a grin and seemed to be showing off, which was not unusual, though there didn’t seem to be any coin changing hands for his throws.

The visions came whenever he thought of 맷 or 페린, and 랜드 had stopped dismissing them. He did not know what caused the images to appear; probably his *ta’veren* nature interacting with the other two *ta’veren* from his home village. Whatever it was, he used it. Just another tool. It appeared that 맷 was still with the Band, but was no longer camped in a forested land. It was hard to tell from the angle, but he looked to be outside a city somewhere. At least, that was a large road in the near distance. 랜드 had not seen the small, dark-skinned woman with 맷 for some time. Who was she? Where had she gone?

The vision faded. Hopefully, 맷 would return to him soon. He would need 맷 and his tactical skills at 세이올 굴.

One of 바쉐어’s quartermasters—a thick-mustached man with bowlegs and a squat body—saw 랜드 and approached with a quick step. 랜드 waved the 살다에안 back; he had no mind for supply reports at the moment. The quartermaster saluted immediately and retreated. Once, 랜드 might have been surprised at how quickly he was obeyed, but no longer.
